title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Preface: How to Use This Book
Change one number in a dataset, and how many documents are now wrong? If the number was copied by hand into a report, a slide, an email and a web page, nobody knows without searching. This book teaches a way of publishing with nothing to search for: you write once, in plain text, and a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog and a dashboard all rebuild from that one source with one command. The program that rebuilds them is Quarto.
This book is about producing publication-quality documents that are reproducible from their data and code, at a speed that coding agents have only recently made possible. Reproducible means every number, table and figure is computed by code from the data, kept beside the prose, so one command rebuilds them all and anyone can check how they were made. Publication quality means each output is fit for the reader who will use it: laid out, captioned, cited and checked. The speed comes from the agent. The cryptic commands and fragile configuration that used to stand between an analysis and its published, interactive form are no longer the bottleneck: you describe the step, the agent writes the code and runs the commands, and you check the result.
Quarto is one of three parts. With git, which records every version of the source, and a hosting service such as GitHub Pages, which puts the result on the web, it lets one person produce reproducible, publication-quality work for a wide range of settings and formats: a page read on a phone, a report printed for a meeting, slides on a projector, an e-book, an interactive dashboard. A coding agent does the typing for all three, and this book shows you how to direct it and check its work.
crumbs: Preface: How to Use This Book

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Prompt, Check, Publish
The title names the method, a loop you run at every step of both projects. You prompt a coding agent, a program that writes files and runs commands at your request, describing one small piece of work with its files and columns named. It is an agent, not a chat, because it acts: where a web chat replies with code for you to copy and run, an agent edits your files and runs the commands itself, then reports back. You check what it did: read what changed, look at the result, compare it with the data. An agent can be fluent, fast and wrong, so this step is never skipped, and it is always yours. Then Quarto publishes, rebuilding every output from the checked source the same way every time. Chapter 1 explains why the last step can be trusted, and Chapter 2 how to make the first two reliable.
Every hands-on step in Parts II and III goes once round the loop in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Prompt, Check, Publish: the loop this book teaches, with who acts at each step.

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Who this book is for
I wrote this book for researchers, software practitioners, data experts and students: anyone who works with data and code and needs to share the results. It shows how to publish everything from one plain-text source, prose and code together, with Quarto. Quarto is free and open source, and it is traditional software, not AI, so the same source always builds the same report, slide deck or web page: reproducible, interactive and of publication quality. With a coding agent, work that once took days now takes minutes. Along the way, I explain the concepts, the arguments and the decisions behind each step.
Reproducibility is why I wrote this book. Work that others can rebuild earns their trust, justifies the decisions made on it, and gives them something to build on, which is how science, technology and understanding move forward. More automation means fewer errors and a better experience, for the people who make the work and for those who read it.
Publishing is half the job; the other half is being read. Content works only if it engages the people it is for, so the book treats every output as something a particular reader will use, and checks it as that reader would. I hope it improves the interactions, and the outcomes, of everyone who works with data, software and AI applications and has to communicate them.
You may be new to Quarto, to coding agents or to both. No programming is assumed: I explain the Python the agent writes, but you do not have to write it. If the terminal is new to you, Chapter 3 teaches the little you need, one checked step at a time, and Chapter 4 has you use it by hand on a real report before you give an agent its first edit. Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits collects the keys, paths and error messages worth knowing.
You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free GitHub account, and an account with one coding agent (Before you start lists what each needs).

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
The two running examples
Every concept is tied to one of two projects, both built on real, cited data.
A London visitor guide (Part II). For the city’s tourism office, you write one guide that becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and a published website. Every visitor number in it, from the 7,116,929 visits to the Natural History Museum (South Kensington) in 2025 down, is computed from the counts published by the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions.
Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities (Part III). You group Colombia’s municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, from 2016 to 2023, compare health and education outcomes between the kinds, and publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all from one analysis script. Most of the data are Colombian open data, joined by official municipality codes; rainfall comes from the Climate Hazards Center’s CHIRPS data and altitude from NASA’s SRTM elevation data (Appendix G — Data Sources, Licences and Credits).

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Your first afternoon
Part I fits in an afternoon, and it ends with something to show for it. Chapters 1 and 2 are reading: nothing to install, nothing to type. Chapter 3 sets up your computer in six steps, each with a check; allow about an hour. Chapter 4 is the first payoff, about 45 minutes at the keyboard: you copy a small report, render it yourself, check its numbers against the data and find the one that is wrong, start a Git history, change an input and undo it, and make three common mistakes on purpose to read their errors. Everything in it is typed by hand except the last step, the agent’s first edit, which you check with Git before you keep it.

section: What a hands-on step looks like
text:
What a hands-on step looks like
Each step is a three-part box, explained in How to read the agent boxes: the exact prompt to give your agent, what it will probably run, and the few things only you can do. Prompts are examples, not transcripts: agents vary, so check the result rather than the wording. Five kinds of aside step out of the main text; here is one of each.






NoteWhy this works



A number computed from the data cannot disagree with the data. Asides like this one explain the mechanism behind a step, so that you can adapt it to your own project.








WarningCommon pitfall



A render started while a live preview is rendering the same file collides with it. Asides like this one describe failures seen in practice, and how to avoid them.








TipIn practice



Ask for one step per prompt: a small change is quick to check, and when something breaks you know which step broke it. Asides like this one hold judgement calls and habits.




Pause and think


The agent reports a render with no errors. Is the work checked?



Answer

Not yet: a clean render proves that the code ran, not that its numbers are right. Asides like this one ask a question to answer before you read on; the answer follows it.








ImportantTry it



Asides like this one are exercises. Think of one document you produce more than once, and note where each of its numbers comes from.

You’re done when you can say which of its numbers are typed by hand and which come from a file.



Steps marked optional are for readers who are ahead; nothing later depends on them.

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
Two ways through
Self-paced. Read in order. Part I can be read and done in one sitting, your first afternoon; each chapter of Parts II and III ends at a checkpoint or at the finished example, where you can stop and resume later.
The core path. Parts II and III are long because they explain, but the path through them is shorter. On a first reading, leave for later the sections marked (optional) in their headings, Part III’s further challenges and its route that builds the model rather than using it: nothing later depends on them. What remains is the core:

Part II: Markdown and the guide’s rules (5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules); computed numbers and one source in three formats (6  Documents That Compute); three audiences from one prompt (7  One Guide, Five Audiences); Git, publishing and one changed input (8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild).
Part III: the question, the data and the rules (9  The Question, the Data and the Rules); one chapter for each step of the analysis, from exploring (10  Look Before You Model) to the within-cluster check (14  Correlation Is Not Causation), copying each block’s finished script from clustering on (Use the model, or build it); then the report, the slides, the website and one changed setting (15  Publish Many).

Workshop-paced. The book grew out of a six-hour workshop and keeps its shape, while explaining what the workshop only had time to show: why each step works, where it fails, and when not to take it. Appendix I — Running This as a Workshop has the day’s agenda and the chapters each block covers (Table I.1 and Table I.2).

title: Prompt, Check, Publish
text:
When you get stuck
You will get stuck: an install fails, a prompt goes wrong, a render stops with an error you have never seen. That is expected, and the book is built for it. Every hands-on block ends at a checkpoint, a folder in the workshop’s repository (checkpoints/), the copy of the workshop’s files you download during setup (Step 5: Run the setup check). It holds the project as it should be at that point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. In a workshop the rule is simple: stuck for two minutes, catch up. Where the book reaches a checkpoint, a catch-up box gives the one line to paste into your agent (Figure 2).
Reading on your own, you have time the room does not, so spend a few minutes on a diagnosis first. Each step uses only what Chapters 3 and 4 teach:

Where are you? pwd prints the folder; the project’s commands work only inside it.
What changed? git status lists the files changed since your last commit, and git diff shows how, including changes you did not mean to make.
What does the error say? Read its first line (Reading an error) and look it up in Appendix D — Troubleshooting.
Try one fix, the one that line points to, and run the command again.

If that fix does not work, catch up. Afterwards, make one short check of your own: open the output that the checkpoint’s README names, and see that it shows what the book describes at that point.






Figure 2: Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.



The README’s last step names the workshop slide to rejoin at. In the book, that place is the catch-up box itself, so after catching up you carry on reading from the box. If you were stuck partway through a block, go straight to its box: the checkpoint already holds the steps between where you stopped and the box. Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers lists every checkpoint.

title: About the Author
text:
Ravi Kalia holds a PhD in statistical machine learning from the University of Oxford and has spent twenty years working with data, in several industries and on many continents.
This book is the written edition of Ravi’s hands-on Quarto workshop. The workshop’s slides are online, and its worked examples and catch-up checkpoints are in its GitHub repository.

title: Part I: Foundations
text:
Four chapters stand between you and the first project: one for the Publish step of the loop, one for Prompt and Check, one for the machine that runs them all, and one in which you use that machine by hand.
Chapter 1, Publishing That Rebuilds Itself. Why hand-made reports drift out of date, and how Quarto rebuilds every output from one source so that they cannot. You will follow one file through the three steps of a render, learn exactly what “reproducible” promises, and see when Quarto is the wrong tool.
Chapter 2, Working With a Coding Agent. What an agent is, what it costs, how far its reach goes, and how to ask it for work you can verify. You will learn to read the book’s hands-on boxes, and how to account for an agent’s use when the work is research.
Chapter 3, Setting Up Your Machine. Six steps, each with a check you can see, from an empty terminal to a working agent, Quarto and Python. It ends when a web page and a PDF that your own computer built both say 42.
Chapter 4, A First Report, by Hand. A one-page report with a wrong number in it, which renders without an error. You copy it, render it and find the wrong number by checking the report against its data. Then you record it with Git, change the data and undo the change, and read three errors made on purpose. Only then does the agent make its first edit, and you check its diff before you commit it.
The first two chapters are mostly reading. The last two are hands-on: do them at a desk, with a good connection, about an hour for the setup and about 45 minutes for the first report.



Where we are: Part I.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.1 Why reports drift
Most reports are built by hand. An analyst runs a script, copies a number into a Word document, pastes a chart into a slide, retypes the same number in an email, and exports a PDF for the website. Every copy is a small act of faith that the number was right and is still right. When the data change, someone has to find every copy, and nobody can say for sure where each one came from.
That faith is the problem, because the reason to publish data is that people rely on it. Work that can be reproduced earns trust: a reader, a reviewer or a manager can see where each number came from, and rebuild it. It justifies decisions, because the evidence behind a choice can be shown, checked again and defended later. And it can be built on: someone else starts from your source rather than from scratch, extends it and corrects it, which is how science, technology and understanding improve. Work that cannot be reproduced offers none of this; it asks to be taken on trust.
The alternative is one source that rebuilds every output, the Publish step of this book’s loop. The more of that work a program does, the fewer places an error can slip in, and the better the experience for everyone involved: the people who make the documents, and the people who read documents that agree with each other and with the data.
The London visitor guide that runs through Part II is a small example of a common problem. The tourism office publishes the same facts to several audiences: a web guide for visitors, a dashboard for managers, a Word brief for partners, a square social-media card and, later, a white paper. In the finished project, five pages read the same table of attraction visits, and between them they write ten files: the guide alone becomes a web page, a Word document, a PDF, a PowerPoint deck, an e-book and a slide deck that runs in the browser.
Suppose the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions (ALVA), the source of those counts, corrects one figure. In a copy-and-paste workflow, that correction has to reach ten files by hand. Three things tend to go wrong:
None of these is a failure of care. They are what happens when the output is treated as the thing you edit. The fix is structural: edit the source, and let a program rebuild the outputs (Figure 1.1).

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
Stale numbers. One copy is missed, and the partner brief disagrees with the dashboard.
Lost provenance. Six months later, nobody can say which version of the data produced the number in the white paper.
Slow change. Because every update is expensive, updates stop happening, and the documents quietly age.








Figure 1.1: One correction, two workflows. By hand, each copy waits to be retyped and some go stale; from one source, one render updates every output.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.2 What Quarto is
Quarto is an open-source publishing system, free for anyone to use: a command-line program, one you run by typing a command in a terminal (Section 3.3), that turns plain-text source files into finished documents.
The input is either a plain Markdown file (.md) or a Quarto document (.qmd). Markdown is a way of writing structured text with a few punctuation marks, such as # before a heading (Chapter 5). A .qmd file is Markdown with two additions: a block of settings at the top, written in YAML, a format for settings in which indentation is meaning (Section 6.1), and code cells, fenced blocks of code that run when the document is built. Here is a complete one, the file the test run in Chapter 3 asks your agent to write:
---
title: "Hello"
format:
  html: default
  typst: default
---

```{python}
answer = 6 * 7
```

The answer is `{python} answer`.
Between the two --- lines are the settings: a title and two formats, a web page (html) and a PDF (typst). The fenced block below them is a code cell. The sentence at the bottom contains inline code: when the document is built, Quarto runs answer and writes its value into the sentence. When this book was built, the same calculation gave 42, and that number was computed, not typed.

1.2.1 Three steps: execute, convert, typeset
To render a document is to build its outputs from its source, and quarto render does it in three steps (Figure 1.2).






Figure 1.2: What quarto render does. One source becomes Markdown with results, which Pandoc converts to each output format; for PDF, Typst typesets the result.




Execute. A computation engine runs the code cells: Jupyter for Python, knitr for R. The results (numbers, tables, figures) replace the code in an intermediate Markdown file. The cells run once for each format, so each output gets results made for it (Section 6.5). This book uses Python only.
Convert. For each format, Pandoc, a long-established document converter, reads that Markdown and writes the output: HTML, Word (docx), EPUB, PowerPoint (pptx) or a Reveal.js slide deck.
Typeset. For PDF, Pandoc writes source for Typst, a modern typesetting system that ships inside Quarto, and Typst produces the PDF. No LaTeX installation is needed. (Quarto can also make PDFs through LaTeX, format: pdf, if you install a TeX distribution.)

The split matters in practice. A failure in step 1 is a failure of your code: a missing package, a wrong column name, a cell that raises an error. A failure in step 2 or 3 is a failure of the document: a malformed table, an image too large for the page, a format-specific option that does not exist. When a render fails, the error message tells you which step stopped, and that tells you where to look.


Pause and think


A render of london.qmd stops with KeyError: 'visits_2025'. Which step failed, and where do you look first?



Answer

Step 1, execute. A code cell asked the data for a column it does not have, so compare the cell with the column names in the data file. The format settings are not the problem: Pandoc and Typst never ran.








NoteWhy this works



Pandoc converts between many formats by reading every input into one internal document model and writing every output from that model. That is why one Markdown file can become both a Word document and a slide deck: neither output is derived from the other. Both come from the same kind of structured intermediate, built from the same source, so a heading is a heading everywhere.




1.2.2 What comes out
The official list of formats is long and grouped by kind (Quarto, All Formats, checked 2026-11-12):



Table 1.1: Quarto’s output formats, as grouped in the official list.










Kind
Formats used in this book
Others

HTML, PDF (Typst), Word, EPUB
OpenDocument, PDF through LaTeX

Reveal.js, PowerPoint
Beamer

GitHub, CommonMark, Hugo and others

MediaWiki, DokuWiki and others

Jupyter, JATS, AsciiDoc and many more






Websites and blogs are project types built from the same .qmd files; a dashboard is a format of its own, whose headings lay out pages and rows (Chapter 7).

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.3 Quarto is not AI
This book pairs Quarto with a coding agent, and the pairing invites a misunderstanding: that Quarto itself is an AI tool. It is not. Quarto is conventional software. Given the same source files and the same data, it writes the same outputs every time. It does not generate text, code or figures of its own, and it sends nothing to an AI service.
The agent is a separate program. It reads and writes the files in your project folder and runs commands you approve; Quarto then turns those files into formats. The two have different failure modes, and the workflow in this book is designed around the difference:



Table 1.2: Two tools with different failure modes.











Coding agent
Quarto




Output for the same input
varies from run to run
identical


Typical mistake
plausible but wrong code or prose
a precise, reproducible error


How you check it
read its changes, run them, compare with the data
read the rendered output






Because generation and rendering are separate, every mistake the agent makes lands in a file you can read or a command you approve before anything is published: that gap is where the Check step of the loop happens. And because the render is repeatable, anyone can rebuild your outputs to confirm them, without trusting the agent at all.


Pause and think


Asked twice for the same chart, the agent writes two different code cells. If you keep one and render it twice, do you get two different charts?



Answer

No. The agent varies; Quarto does not. Once the cell is in the file, every render runs the same code on the same data, so you check the cell once and every rebuild inherits that check.








WarningCommon pitfall



Quarto runs whatever code your cells contain. If a cell calls an AI service, the document becomes as unpredictable as that service, and the cause is your code, not Quarto. Keep calls to models out of rendered documents unless the variation is the point.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.4 Reproducible: same source, same result
Reproducible is used loosely, so here is the precise sense this book means: someone else, or you in six months, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command, and can see where every number came from. Four properties make that possible:
One source. Text, code and data live in plain files in one folder. Nothing important exists only inside an application.
Numbers are computed. Every figure, table and number in a sentence comes from a code cell or inline code that reads the data. Nothing is typed in or pasted from elsewhere.
One command. quarto render rebuilds everything. There is no sequence of manual export steps to remember.
Versioned. Git, the version-control tool installed in Chapter 3, is something like Word’s Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history; a project folder with its history is a repository. Each state of the source, data and settings that you choose to record becomes a commit, with a message saying why it changed. Any earlier state can be restored, two states can be compared, and a result can be tied to the exact files that made it. The project’s Python packages are pinned too, in a lockfile (uv.lock, introduced in Section 5.10), so a colleague’s machine builds the same environment, the Python version and packages the code runs with, as yours.
The promise has conditions, and they are worth knowing from the start: the same result comes from the same inputs, the same declared environment and the same settings. Three things quietly break it. Data read live from a website can change between two renders, so a project keeps a dated copy of its data in its folder. Anything random, such as the starting points of a clustering method, gives the same answer only when its seed, the number that starts the random sequence, is fixed. And a cache, below, can serve an old result.
Together these turn the drift problem around. Correct one value in the data, render, and the table, the chart and the sentence that quote it all update together, in every format. Section 4.5 has you do exactly that, on a five-row file, in your first hands-on chapter.


Pause and think


You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?



Answer

Nothing. You fix the data file and render again. If the answer is anything else, some number in the report was typed rather than computed, and that is the bug to fix.








WarningCommon pitfall



Reproducible does not mean correct. A wrong analysis reproduces perfectly: the same wrong number appears in every format, every time. Reproducibility makes errors findable, because anyone can trace a number back to its code and data, but you still have to check results against their sources. Chapter 14 is an extended example of a result that reproduces cleanly and still must not be read the way it first appears.


There is one more subtlety, which matters once projects grow. Rendering every page from scratch can be slow, so Quarto can cache results with a setting called freeze. A cache is only as good as its rule for throwing results away, and Quarto re-executes a frozen page when that page’s source changes, not when a data file it reads changes. Chapter 15 shows how to use the cache safely. This book itself uses one, with a documented way to clear it (Appendix H).

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
section: 1.5 When Quarto is the wrong tool
text:
1.5 When Quarto is the wrong tool
Quarto earns its keep when the same content is rebuilt, either because the data change or because the content goes to several audiences. It costs you a plain-text workflow, a command line and some setup. That trade is not always worth making:

Collaborators who edit in Word. If the people who revise the document work in a word processor with tracked changes, they can comment on the Word output, but their edits have to be carried back into the source by hand. For documents whose main work is multi-author line editing, a shared word processor may simply fit better.
Designed layouts. Quarto produces structured documents: headings, paragraphs, figures, tables. Typst and CSS can take the look a long way, but a poster or a brand-heavy brochure laid out to the millimetre is easier in a design tool.
Format fidelity at the edges. Each format can only carry what it supports. Pandoc writes good Word and PowerPoint files, but a PowerPoint table cannot hold pictures, for example, so the London guide’s photo table shows each photo’s alt text in its pptx version instead. Check every format you promise to deliver.
One-off documents. A two-paragraph note with no data and no second audience gains little from a build system.







TipIn practice



A useful test: will this document be built a second time? If the data will change, if a second audience will need it in another format, or if someone will ask “where did this number come from?”, the plain-text workflow pays for itself quickly. If none of these is likely, use whatever is fastest.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
Summary


Reports drift when their outputs are edited by hand; editing one source and letting a program rebuild every output removes the copies.
quarto render executes the code cells, converts the result with Pandoc and, for PDF, typesets it with Typst; the step that stops tells you where to look.
Quarto is conventional software, not AI: the same source and data give the same outputs, so you check the agent’s work once and anyone can rebuild yours without trusting it.
Reproducible work earns trust, justifies decisions and can be built on. It means one source, computed numbers, one command and versioned files, and it makes errors findable, not absent.
A cache such as freeze re-runs a page when its source changes, not when its data do, so it needs a rule for clearing it.
Quarto pays for documents that will be built again, and is the wrong tool for co-editing in Word, designed layouts and one-off notes.


Quarto, though, renders only what it is given. In this book a coding agent writes those sources, and its output varies from run to run and can be confidently wrong. How do you ask such a program for work, and how do you check what comes back before anything is published? Chapter 2 answers.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
text:
2.1 Model plus harness
Simon Willison, a developer, has asked most major new models the same question since 2024: “Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle” (an SVG is a drawing written as text, so a model writes one as it writes code). Four Claude models, each at three effort levels (how long the model reasons before answering), answered it with 12 drawings, and every one is recognisably a pelican on a bicycle. The dearest cost 13.09 cents, about 93 times as much as the cheapest that was good enough, at 0.14 cents (Figure 2.2).
Choosing between those drawings is the first of many judgements this chapter teaches. A coding agent is a program that writes and edits files and runs commands at your request: you write the Prompt, it does the typing, and you Check whether the result is right. It can produce in a minute what would take an hour by hand, and it can produce plausible, confident, wrong work just as quickly. How do you get the first kind of work without being fooled by the second?
A coding agent is two programs working together (Figure 2.1).
The model is a large language model, such as Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT or Google’s Gemini. It runs on the vendor’s servers. It reads text and writes text, and it can reply with a structured request to use a tool: “read this file”, “run this command”.
The harness is the program on your computer that surrounds the model. Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are harnesses. The harness gives the model its tools (reading and writing files, running commands, searching), carries out the model’s tool requests, asks you before it does anything consequential, and sends the results back to the model. That loop repeats until the model replies with an answer instead of another request. That loop, run on your own files and commands, is what makes it an agent: it acts in your project folder, one tool request after another, until the step is done, where a web chat hands you text to copy.
A short way to remember the split: the model decides, the harness does, you direct and check. It has a practical consequence. Many harnesses can run several models, so the same harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently inside a different harness. When an agent disappoints you, the cause can be either half, and the fix is different: a stronger model for reasoning that falls short, better rules or permissions for a harness that does the wrong thing.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
text:
Figure 2.1: How a coding agent works. The harness on your computer passes the conversation and the results of each tool to the model, which replies with text or a request to use a tool; the harness acts in the project folder and asks you before it runs commands.










NoteWhy this works



The model cannot touch your computer. Everything it “does” is a request that the harness carries out, and the harness can show you each request before acting on it. That is the basis of every safety habit in this chapter: you approve commands you have read, and you review files after they change.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
section: 2.2 Choosing an agent and a model
text:
2.2 Choosing an agent and a model
This book covers three agents. Each comes from the same company as its default models:



Table 2.1: The agents this book covers. Antigravity replaced Gemini CLI for unpaid-tier and Google One users on 18 June 2026 (Gemini CLI installation page, checked 2026-11-12).





Agent
You type
Made by
Default models




Claude Code
claude
Anthropic
Claude


Codex
codex
OpenAI
GPT


Antigravity
agy
Google
Gemini






What “covers” means differs between them. For all three, the install command, the account it needs and how it reads project rules were checked against the vendor’s documentation (dated in Chapter 3 and Section 2.5). The first screens of Claude Code and Codex were captured for the workshop on 2026-11-07; Antigravity’s were not. Other agents exist; this book does not check them, so it does not list them. Every prompt in the book is written to work in any of the three. A vendor’s own pairing of harness and model is the easiest to set up, but it is not automatically the best fit for a task: the harness and the model are separate choices.

2.2.1 Pick a model by task, not by rank
Each vendor offers a family of models, from small and cheap to large and capable. They are not simply better and worse versions of one thing. Larger, more recent models usually follow longer instructions, plan multi-step work and recover from their own errors better. Small models are faster and cheaper, and often good enough for short, well-specified edits such as fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Joining two datasets or debugging a failed render rewards the stronger model.
The prompts in this book are short and specific, so a mid-sized model at a moderate effort setting is enough: Claude’s Sonnet on medium effort, or Haiku for small edits, or OpenAI’s Sol on low (checked 2026-11-12). For unfamiliar, hard work, the vendors’ own advice starts higher: Anthropic suggests starting with Opus 5.5 for most workloads, and OpenAI with GPT-6 Astra for complex reasoning and coding. The names change every few months, and Appendix K keeps the current ones; the advice does not. Start small, and move up only when a task keeps failing.
Models are priced by the token, a fragment of text of a few characters, with one rate for the text sent to the model (input) and another for the text it writes (output). List prices are API prices: what a program pays per token when it sends requests to the model directly, through the vendor’s programming interface (the API), rather than through a monthly subscription.






TipIn practice



Prices change monthly; the principle does not. On 2026-11-12, the list prices of the eight models in Table K.2 ran from $0.50 to $50 per million output tokens, a 100-fold spread between the smallest and the largest. That table, with its sources, is in Appendix K, the one place this book keeps facts that change; read it as a snapshot of the spread, not as numbers to plan with. Subscriptions count usage differently, and which models you can choose depends on your plan and the agent’s version.


The pelican runs below used Fable 5.2’s predecessor, Fable 5.1, listed at 10 / 50 dollars per million tokens when they were made.
The cost of a fixed level of capability has been falling fast. Measuring the cheapest model that reaches a given benchmark score, the venture firm a16z found the price falling about tenfold a year, a thousandfold over the three years from November 2021, and Epoch AI found falls of between 9 and 900 times a year depending on the benchmark (both checked 2026-11-07). Both warn that the pace may slow, and neither measures the frontier, where the price of the most capable work may fall more slowly. The practical lesson is the same either way: choose by what the task needs, not by today’s price.


2.2.2 One prompt, four models, three efforts
The pelicans this chapter opened with make the trade-off concrete. Figure 2.2 shows one run of each of four Claude models at three effort levels, with each reply’s cost at API list prices.












Model

medium effort
high effort




Haiku 5.5

Figure 2.2: One prompt, four models, three efforts: “Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle”. Images from Simon Willison’s pelican series, one run per cell; cost is each reply’s tokens at API list prices (checked 2026-11-06).



Read the grid in two directions. Down the rows, the model grows and the price per token rises, so costs climb from fractions of a cent to more than ten cents. Across the columns, effort rises: the model reasons longer and writes more, so the cost usually rises while the picture gains details rather than becoming correct. Haiku on low effort has the weakest frame; from medium effort up, the frames are sound, which is consistent with, though no proof of, the book’s advice of medium effort.
Keep the evidence in proportion. It is one run per cell of one small, self-contained task, not a benchmark: run it again and you get different birds, and Fable on medium effort even cost less than Fable on low. More effort is not always better, either: at their maximum effort, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 each spent 128,000 tokens reasoning, the models’ output limit, and returned no drawing (Simon Willison’s transcripts, checked 2026-11-12). A drawing says little about a long job that joins datasets and recovers from errors, which is where stronger models earn their price. Whether a 93-fold difference in price is worth paying depends entirely on the task.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
text:
2.3 What a conversation costs
Whether you pay by subscription or by API, use is counted in tokens. Three things raise the cost of a session:

A bigger model costs more per token.
A higher effort setting makes the model write more reasoning tokens per reply.
A longer conversation costs more with every turn, because the model keeps no memory between requests: the harness sends the whole conversation again each time. Everything sent with a request (the conversation so far, the files read, the project’s rules) is the model’s context. Prompt caching makes the repeated part cheaper, not free, and caches expire.

The habits that follow are simple: a mid-sized model at moderate effort, one task per conversation, and a fresh conversation as soon as a task is done. Three commands, typed into the agent itself rather than run in the terminal (Section 3.4.1), cover them:



Table 2.2: Three commands that control cost and context (Claude Code commands reference and Codex CLI reference, checked 2026-11-12). Type / alone to list your agent’s commands.











Command
Claude Code
Codex
Use it when




/model
switches the model; arrows adjust the effort level where the model supports it
chooses the model and reasoning effort
a prompt keeps failing (go up) or the work is routine (go down)


/clear
starts a new conversation with empty context; the old one can be resumed
clears the terminal and starts a fresh chat
a task is finished and an unrelated one starts


/exit
exits; /quit is the same
exits; /quit is the same
you are done, or need to move to another folder






/clear matters for quality as well as cost. Old instructions and files read earlier keep steering the model while they remain in the conversation; a fresh conversation drops them. Nothing on disk changes, and the project’s rules file is read again.


Pause and think


One task is finished and an unrelated one starts. Which command first, and what does it keep?



Answer

/clear. The new task needs none of the old conversation, and carrying it along costs tokens on every turn and can mislead the model. Your files stay as they are, and the project’s rules file is read again.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
section: 2.4 The root folder is the agent’s world
text:
2.4 The root folder is the agent’s world
An agent treats the folder you start it in as its root: it reads and edits files there and in the folders below, and runs commands from there. The first time you start one in a new folder, it asks whether you trust it. Claude Code’s prompt, captured on 2026-11-07, warns that “Claude Code’ll be able to read, edit, and execute files here”; Codex asks the same question in a folder that is a Git repository, and says it can read, edit and run files “subject to your permission settings”.
That question deserves a real answer. Trust only a folder you created for the work. Never start an agent in your home folder, in Documents, or anywhere that holds other people’s projects, private documents or keys (such as ~/.ssh). Project instructions in a trusted folder are read and followed too, which is another reason to trust only your own folders.
Starting in a small project folder has three practical benefits. Paths in prompts stay short (data/attractions.csv), the project’s rules file is found, and a mistake stays inside one folder that you can restore. It is not a guaranteed boundary, though: a command can still name a path outside the folder, so read each command before you approve it.






WarningCommon pitfall



Two agents writing the same files, or rendering in one folder at once, will collide; Section 7.2 shows the safe split. To work on another project, leave with /exit, change folder, and start the agent again there.
crumbs: 2  Working With a Coding Agent

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
text:
2.5 Rules that persist: AGENTS.md
Everything you tell an agent in conversation is forgotten when the conversation ends. Rules that must hold in every session go in a file: AGENTS.md, a plain Markdown file at the top of the project folder that the agent reads at the start of each session. A good one has three parts:

Scope: what the project is, and what it is not.
Rules: what must always hold (“every number comes from a cited file in data/”).
Commands: how to build and check the project.

All three agents in this book read it (checked 2026-10-30). Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work. Antigravity reads AGENTS.md or GEMINI.md in the project’s folders. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md in the working folder or above it, from version 2.1.277; a CLAUDE.md containing the line @AGENTS.md imports it, so one file can serve all three (Claude Code memory documentation, checked 2026-11-12). The repository behind this book works exactly that way: its CLAUDE.md imports its AGENTS.md.






WarningCommon pitfall



AGENTS.md is context, not enforcement. The agent reads the rules and usually follows them, but it can still slip. Write rules that are concrete enough to check (“call ALVA counts ‘ALVA member attractions’”), and check them.




Pause and think


Yesterday you told the agent, in conversation, to say “ALVA member attractions”. Today it writes “top attractions”. Why, and what is the lasting fix?



Answer

The instruction ended with yesterday’s conversation: the model keeps no memory between sessions. Put the rule in AGENTS.md, which is read at the start of every session, and still check for it, because rules are context, not enforcement.


Part II writes the London guide’s rules in Chapter 5, and Part III writes the water analysis’s in Chapter 9.
crumbs: 2  Working With a Coding Agent

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
text:
2.6 How to ask for work
A prompt is the request you type into the agent. Four habits make prompts reliable:
Be specific. Name the files, the columns, the chart type and the output. “Make a chart” invites guessing; “add a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction from data/attractions.csv” does not.
One step at a time. One task per prompt keeps each change small enough to review, and tells you which step broke when one does.
Ask it to run and check. End with a check the agent can perform: “render it and tell me which file it wrote”, “check that the PDF is one page”. An agent that verifies its own work catches many of its own mistakes.
Check what changed. You are responsible for the result. Read the changed files (most agents can show you a diff, the lines added and removed) before moving on.
The prompts in this book were designed with AI assistance and refined to reduce errors, but they are not magic, and agents vary. When a prompt mentions something you do not understand (a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a Python call), ask before you paste:



Ask your coding agent

Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.


Asking for the documentation page matters: it turns the answer into something you can check.

2.6.1 A web chat can draft your prompt
If you know what you want but not how to ask for it, a free web chat (Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini in the browser) can turn a rough idea into a prompt. Describe the goal in plain words, name your tools, and ask for a prompt of one to four lines, with one task, concrete file names and a check (Figure 2.3). The chat cannot see your files, so it guesses; the agent can see them, so it checks. Read the drafted prompt before you paste it, and fix any file name that does not match your folder.






Figure 2.3: A web chat drafts a prompt, you read it, and the coding agent runs it. An illustration drawn for the workshop, not a recording: real replies vary.









WarningCommon pitfall



Paste only what you would be happy to publish. Web chats and agents send your text to the vendor: no passwords, keys, unpublished data or personal information.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
section: 2.7 How to read the agent boxes
text:
2.7 How to read the agent boxes
Every hands-on step in this book uses the same three-part box. Here is a simpler version of the first one you will meet in Part II:



Ask your coding agent

Create london.md with a level-1 heading "Visit London" and one welcome paragraph.



Expect it to run

writes london.md · may run quarto render london.md



You do

approve its commands · open london.html in your browser


Ask your coding agent holds the exact prompt to paste into the agent (in the HTML edition, with a copy button). Expect it to run lists what the agent will probably do, so you recognise it when it asks for approval; you do not type these yourself. You do lists the few things only you can do: start the agent, sign in to accounts, approve commands, run a live preview, open results. The agent occupies the terminal tab it runs in, so commands in a You do box go in a second terminal tab opened in the same folder (Section 3.4.1).
Together the boxes are one turn of the loop in the book’s title. Ask your coding agent is the Prompt. Expect it to run and You do are where you Check, recognising each command before you approve it and opening the result yourself. The render is the Publish. Each exercise closes the loop with You’re done when: the check, stated so that you can see whether it passed.






WarningCommon pitfall



Approving a command without reading it. Most commands in this book run a tool the prompt named (quarto, uv, git, gh) on files in the project folder. Stop and ask the agent what a command does before you approve one that deletes files (rm), runs as the administrator (sudo), or touches a folder outside the project that the prompt did not name.


The prompts are examples, not transcripts. Agents vary from version to version and run to run, so the files they write will differ in detail from the ones shown. What should not vary is the result you check. Figure 2.4 shows what a session looks like.






Figure 2.4: What running the first prompt looks like: the agent writes the file, asks before running a command, renders and reports. An illustration (a scripted replay of a typical session), not a recording: your agent’s screens will look different.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
section: 2.8 Using AI in research: say it, own it
text:
2.8 Using AI in research: say it, own it
If your work is research, using an agent raises obligations beyond getting the code right. Journals and funders differ in detail, so read your venue’s own policy, but the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), whose recommendations many journals follow, states a common core (checked 2026-11-12):

An AI tool is never an author. Chatbots and other AI-assisted tools “should not be listed as authors because they cannot be responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of the work”.
You are responsible for what it produced. Humans are responsible for any submitted material that used AI-assisted technologies, and should review and edit AI output, which “can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased”. That includes references: AI-generated material is not an acceptable primary source.
Disclose the use. Authors describe their use of AI-assisted technologies at submission, in the cover letter and in the appropriate section of the work.

Two further rules follow from ordinary research ethics rather than from any one policy. Keep unpublished manuscripts, participant data and other confidential material out of public AI tools. And never let a tool generate or alter primary data or images: presenting generated data as observed is fabrication.
A useful disclosure names the tool and version, the tasks it performed and the checks you made. The statement for this book, on its copyright page, is written that way. Where it goes depends on the use: code and analysis belong in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce them, which in a Quarto project means the code itself and the project’s AGENTS.md.


Pause and think


Which needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table?



Answer

Computing a table is analysis: describe it in the Methods, in enough detail to reproduce. Venues differ on whether language editing needs a statement; ICMJE’s recommendations make no exception for it, so when in doubt, disclose.
crumbs: 2  Working With a Coding Agent

title: 2  Working With a Coding Agent
text:
Summary


The model decides, the harness does, and you direct and check; when an agent disappoints, either half can be the cause.
Choose a model by the task, not by rank: as the pelicans showed, a cheaper model at medium effort is often enough for a small, well-specified step.
Cost grows with model size, effort and conversation length, because the whole conversation is sent again each turn, so start a fresh conversation for each unrelated task.
Start an agent only in a folder you created for the work, and read each command before you approve it.
Rules that must last go in AGENTS.md, which is context, not enforcement, so write them concretely enough to check.
Good prompts are specific, ask for one step and end in a check; in research the agent is never an author, and its use is disclosed.


All of this assumes a computer on which an agent, Quarto and Python are installed and working together. Is yours? Chapter 3 gets it there in six checked steps.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
3.1 Before you start
This chapter ends with a number: 42, printed in a web page and a PDF that your own computer built. Getting it there proves that the agent, Python, Quarto and Typst work together. That is all Parts II and III need, because everything in them happens on your machine: the agent writes files in your folders, Quarto renders them there, and you open the results in your own browser and word processor. It takes six steps, and each ends with a check you can see, so you always know whether a step worked before you move on.
Do the setup somewhere calm, with a good connection, and allow about an hour. Mac and Linux readers can follow this chapter straight through. Windows readers first install Ubuntu, a version of Linux, inside Windows with WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux; Appendix A walks through that one step at a time, and from then on they follow this chapter inside Ubuntu.
A stable, fast connection. Almost every step downloads something: on Windows the Ubuntu image (several hundred megabytes), then Quarto, uv (which manages Python for each project) and Python packages, the agent itself and the example projects with their data. The agent also sends every request to its model over the internet, so a weak connection shows up as long pauses, timeouts and half-finished installs, which are easy to mistake for your own errors. Use a wired connection or strong Wi-Fi, avoid VPNs where you can, and expect company networks with a proxy to block some downloads.
Two accounts. A free GitHub account, used to publish in Parts II and III, and an account with access to one coding agent. Claude Code needs a Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise or Console account; Codex a ChatGPT sign-in or an API key (for pay-per-use billing, Section 2.2); Antigravity a Google account (checked 2026-11-18; Appendix K keeps the current list). Sign-up and email verification can take hours, so do them first.
A plan for when a step fails. Errors during setup are normal: each step depends on your system, your network and that week’s versions, so an error does not mean you have failed. It tells you what to fix:
The six steps, and how you know each one worked:

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
Look the message up in Appendix D, whose Setup table lists failures seen in practice, with tested fixes.
If it is not there, ask a web chat in your browser (Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini each have a free plan, checked 2026-11-12), not the agent: installs can fail before it is working, and sometimes the agent is what fails. Paste the command you ran and the whole error message, with a sentence saying your system (“Mac”, or “Windows with Ubuntu on WSL”) and which step you are on.
Try one suggested fix at a time, and read each suggested command before you run it. Never paste passwords, keys or private data.
If two suggestions fail, ask a person: your group’s help channel, or a colleague.
