title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
3.2 Step 1: Get the computer ready
The later steps assume two small programs: git, for version control, and curl, for downloading. Open a terminal, the window for typing commands that Step 2 explains (on a Mac: Command-Space, type Terminal, Enter; on Ubuntu: Ctrl+Alt+T), and run the line for your system.
On a Mac, install Apple’s Command Line Tools, which include git:
xcode-select --install
A dialog asks to install them: click Install and wait. Doing this deliberately now matters, because otherwise the dialog appears the first time anything uses git, which would be in the middle of Step 4 while the agent is waiting. “Already installed” is fine.
On Ubuntu or Debian (including Ubuntu on Windows):
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git
sudo runs a command as the administrator and asks for your Linux password, which stays invisible as you type. On other Linux distributions, install curl and git with your usual package manager. On Windows, follow Appendix A first: it ends with this same command, run inside Ubuntu.






ImportantTry it



Run git --version in the terminal.

You’re done when it prints a version number. On Windows, you are in Ubuntu and wsl -l -v, run in PowerShell, shows Ubuntu with VERSION 2.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
3.3 Step 2: Move around the terminal
The rest of the book happens in a terminal, a window where you type commands instead of clicking. When it is ready for a command it shows a prompt, a line ending in $ (or % on a Mac), which tells you who and where you are (not to be confused with a prompt you give an agent):
ana@laptop:~/demo$
ana is the user, laptop the computer, and ~/demo the current folder: ~ is your home folder, so this is a folder called demo inside it. Eight commands are enough to move around:



Table 3.2: Moving around the terminal.









Command
Does




pwd
prints the folder you are in (print working directory)


date
prints the date and time


ls
lists what is in this folder


mkdir name
makes a folder


cd name
goes into a folder


cd ..
goes up one folder


cd ~
goes straight home, from anywhere


rmdir name
removes an empty folder (it refuses if anything is inside)






Figure 3.1 runs them in order. Type them yourself rather than pasting: the hands remember.






Figure 3.1: Moving around the terminal: each command, and what the terminal answers. A real recording, made with a demo account whose home folder is /tmp/home/ana; yours is /home/<you> on Linux and Windows, or /Users/<you> on a Mac.



Two keys save most typing mistakes: Tab completes a file or folder name, and the up arrow brings back the previous command. Copying and pasting work differently in a terminal: select the text, then Ctrl+Shift+C copies and Ctrl+Shift+V pastes (Command-C and Command-V on a Mac), because Ctrl+C on its own stops the running program (Table B.3). Two commands start most projects in this book, one line each:
mkdir -p london-guide
cd london-guide
The first makes the folder, and -p makes mkdir quietly accept a folder that already exists, so running it twice does no harm. The second goes into it. Later chapters often join the two lines into one with &&, which means “and then, if that worked”:
mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide
If mkdir fails, cd does not run. Appendix B has more keys and habits.






ImportantTry it



From your home folder, type the commands in Table 3.2 in the order shown in Figure 3.1.

You’re done when rmdir raised no error, and the prompt shows ~.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
3.4 Step 3: Install a coding agent
Pick one agent and run its installer, the vendor’s own documented command (checked 2026-10-30). Run only the line for your agent.
Claude Code:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Codex:
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh
Antigravity:
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash
curl … | bash downloads a small install script and runs it immediately. That is normal for these tools, and it is also exactly why you should only do it with links you trust, such as each vendor’s documented command.
Then open a new terminal tab (Ctrl+Shift+T on Ubuntu, Command-T on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+D in Windows Terminal). A terminal learns where programs are when it starts, from its PATH, the list of folders it searches for programs, so it cannot find one installed a moment ago, which is the usual cause of command not found straight after an install. On a Mac, a new tab is not enough for Claude Code: its installer puts it in ~/.local/bin, a folder the PATH leaves out, and prints the fix under “Setup notes”. Paste that fix into the terminal, press Enter, then open the new tab (Claude Code, installation troubleshooting, checked 2026-11-06).
Start the agent in a fresh folder. Type the three lines one at a time: make the folder setup in your home folder (-p: no complaint if it exists), go into it, and start the agent:
mkdir -p ~/setup
cd ~/setup
claude
That last line starts Claude Code; type codex for Codex, or agy for Antigravity.
The first start walks through three screens. Claude Code’s are shown below as captured on 2026-11-07 (version 2.1.319, in an empty folder, with folder names changed); the screens change between versions, so yours may differ in wording. Before them, Claude Code asks for a text style: press Enter to keep the one selected.
Sign in. Choose the option for your account: the first for a subscription, the second for an Anthropic Console account billed by API use. The agent opens your browser; where there is none, as in WSL, it prints a link to copy into your browser, and then a code to paste back into the terminal. Codex’s first screen (version 0.167.0, captured the same day) offers “Sign in with ChatGPT”, which works the same way, and “Sign in with Device Code”, a one-time code to use when the browser sign-in fails.

 Select login method:

 ❯ 1. Claude account with subscription · Individual, Team, or Enterprise
   2. Anthropic Console account · API usage billing
   3. 3rd-party platform · Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry, Google Vertex AI

Trust the folder. The pointer starts on “No, exit”, so pressing Enter straight away quits. Press the down arrow first. Quitting by mistake is harmless: type claude again. Codex asks nothing in a plain folder like ~/setup; it asks the same question later, in a project that is a Git repository.

 Accessing workspace:

 /home/ana/setup

 Quick safety check: Is this a project you created or one you trust?
 (Like your own code, a well-known open source project, or work from
 your team). If not, take a moment to review what's in this folder first.

 Claude Code'll be able to read, edit, and execute files here.

 ❯ No, exit
   Yes, I trust this folder

 Enter to confirm · Esc to cancel

Ready. The agent shows its version, the model and plan of the account you signed in with, and the folder, then waits for a prompt on the line marked ❯. In this capture the logo beside the first lines is left out, and the model and plan are those of the account that captured it; yours shows your own.

 Claude Code v2.1.319
 Opus 5.5 with xhigh effort
 Claude Max
 ~/setup
────────────────────────────────────────────────────
❯ Try "write a test for <filepath>"
────────────────────────────────────────────────────







ImportantTry it



Install one agent, start it in ~/setup, sign in and trust the folder.

You’re done when the agent answers when you type hello. Then type /exit.




3.4.1 Two places to type
Now that an agent is installed, there are two places to type, and mixing them up costs beginners more time than anything else.
ana@laptop:~/setup$ pwd                  <- the terminal: commands
❯ Which tools are missing?                <- the agent: requests in plain language
The agent takes over the terminal tab it runs in: what you type there goes to the agent, not to the shell, the program behind the terminal that runs your commands, until you leave with /exit. Commands in this book’s You do boxes, such as quarto preview, go in the terminal; prompts in Ask your coding agent boxes go to the agent. When the agent is busy and you need the terminal, open a second tab, as after the install.
Typing in the wrong place is usually harmless: a prompt typed at $ gives command not found, and a command typed into the agent is read as a request. Look at the line you are on and try again.


Pause and think


The agent is running and the book says to type gh auth login, the GitHub sign-in of Step 5. Where do you type it?



Answer

In a second terminal tab: gh auth login is an interactive sign-in that needs you, and the agent is using the first tab. Leaving the agent with /exit also works, but ends the conversation.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
section: 3.5 Step 4: Let the agent install the tools
text:
3.5 Step 4: Let the agent install the tools
The remaining tools are Quarto itself, uv, Git and the GitHub command-line tool gh. Each has its own official install method for each system, which is exactly the kind of detail an agent handles well. Start it again in the setup folder, now as one line joined with && (with codex or agy in place of claude if that is your agent, here and in the next steps):



You do

mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup && claude



Ask your coding agent

Check which of `git`, `curl`, `uv`, `quarto` (1.10 or newer) and the GitHub CLI `gh` are missing on this computer. Install only those, using each tool's official method for my system. Never run `sudo`, or an installer that asks for a password, yourself: print each such command alone in a code block, using full paths, then wait until I say done. Then print every version.



Expect it to run

installs uv with its official installer · Quarto from its release page (or Homebrew on a Mac) · gh from GitHub’s own package source · prints versions


Before each command it wants to run, the agent stops and asks, as in Figure 2.4: read the command (the pitfall in Section 2.7 says what to look for), then approve it.
The prompt is written around one limitation: an agent cannot type your password. So it asks the agent to hand back any command that needs one, with full paths, because the second tab you paste it into starts in your home folder. Copy the command (Ctrl+Shift+C, or Command-C on a Mac), paste it in a second tab, type your password when sudo asks (it stays invisible), and then type done in the agent’s tab. On a Mac, the password is your login password.






NoteWhy this works



Quarto has no Ubuntu package in the standard repositories, and Ubuntu’s own gh package is discouraged by GitHub, so a generic apt install would get one tool wrong and the other missing. The prompt’s “each tool’s official method” sends the agent to the right source for each (Quarto’s download page and GitHub’s install instructions for Linux, checked 2026-10-30).




Pause and think


The agent has installed uv. In a terminal tab you opened before that, you type uv --version, and the terminal answers command not found. Did the install fail?



Answer

Probably not. uv’s installer puts it in ~/.local/bin, which a terminal adds to its PATH only when it starts, so a tab opened earlier cannot find it. Open a new tab and try again; only if it fails there is the install at fault.








ImportantTry it



Paste the prompt, approve the commands you have read, and run any sudo command it hands you in a second tab.

You’re done when it prints a version for all five tools. Then type /exit: uv and Quarto are only found by a terminal started after they were installed.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
3.6 Step 5: Run the setup check
Open a new tab and start the agent again, so that it sees the newly installed tools:



You do

cd ~/setup && claude



Ask your coding agent

Print the versions of `quarto` (1.10 or newer), `uv`, `gh` and this agent, and run `quarto check` (no Jupyter or LaTeX yet is fine: count it as OK). If `git config --global user.name` or `user.email` is unset, ask me for my name and my GitHub email, then set them. Clone https://github.com/project-delphi/quarto-workshop.git to `~/quarto-workshop` (if it exists, `git pull` only when its working tree is clean) and list its `checkpoints/`. Run `gh auth status`. Run every check even if one fails, then report each as OK or not.


Three parts of this check deserve a word.
quarto check reports Quarto’s own components, including Pandoc and Typst. Its Python and Jupyter lines may say they are missing, and that is fine: each project in this book gets its own Python environment from uv, so there is nothing to install for Python now. No LaTeX is needed either, because PDFs are made with the Typst engine bundled in Quarto.
A fresh Git has no identity, and git commit refuses to run without one. The prompt makes the agent ask you for your name and email, so you type your own; check that what it set is yours, not a placeholder.
To clone is to copy a repository, with its history, to your computer: here the workshop’s, into ~/quarto-workshop. It holds the finished examples, the water dataset, the starter report for Chapter 4 and the checkpoints: snapshots of each project at the end of each hands-on block, which you will use to catch up if you fall behind.



You do

if gh is not “Logged in”: in a second tab, gh auth login → GitHub.com → HTTPS → Yes → log in with a web browser; copy the one-time code to github.com/login/device; then ask the agent to check gh again








ImportantTry it



Run the setup check.

You’re done when the agent reports every check as OK, including gh “Logged in”.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
3.7 Step 6: The test run
The setup check proves the tools are installed. The test run proves they work together: the agent can write a file and run commands you approve, uv can build a project environment, Quarto can run Python through it, and Typst can write a PDF.



You do

mkdir -p ~/quarto-test && cd ~/quarto-test && claude



Ask your coding agent

Run `uv init --bare` and `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml`. Create hello.qmd (html and typst formats): a Python cell computing `6 * 7` and an inline-code sentence showing it. Render it with `uv run quarto render hello.qmd`; check hello.html and hello.pdf both say 42.



Expect it to run

uv init --bare · uv add … · writes hello.qmd · uv run quarto render hello.qmd → hello.html, hello.pdf



You do

/exit, then open the folder: open . (Mac), xdg-open . (Linux) or explorer.exe . (WSL), and open both files


The test run uses things the next chapters explain, YAML settings, a code cell and inline code, on purpose: it is a black-box check that the tools work together, not a lesson. If you are curious, hello.qmd is the file shown in Section 1.2, and Chapter 4 opens a real report of the same kind, which you read and render yourself.






WarningCommon pitfall



Every render prints a line such as [IPKernelApp] WARNING | Kernel is running over TCP without encryption. It is harmless: Quarto talks to the Python kernel, the running Python process that executes the cells, over a local connection on your own computer, and in every dry run the warning came with a successful render and changed nothing in the output.








ImportantTry it



Run the test run and open both outputs.

You’re done when hello.html and hello.pdf both say 42. The folder is disposable: delete ~/quarto-test afterwards. If a file is missing or says something else, see the Python and Jupyter table in Appendix D.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
Summary


Everything in Parts II and III happens on your own machine, so setup proves that the agent, Python, Quarto and Typst work together there.
Each step ends with a check you can see; move on only when it passes.
Commands go at the terminal’s prompt and requests to the agent; when the agent is busy, open a second tab.
A terminal finds only programs it knew of when it started, so after an install, open a new tab before suspecting the install.
The agent cannot type your password: it hands commands that need one back to you, and you read every command before you approve it.
When a step fails, look in Appendix D, then ask a web chat with the command and the whole error, one fix at a time, and never paste secrets.


The test run was a black box: a file you did not write, settings you have not met, code you have not read. Chapter 4 puts your hands on a real report before any agent does: you copy it, render it yourself, check its numbers against its data and find the wrong one, and record it with Git, so that every later change can be seen and undone. Only then does the agent make its first edit, and you check it. Part II then explains what was in the box: starting from an empty folder, you write the London guide for the tourism office one Markdown construct at a time, and by the end of Chapter 5 it is a web page with written rules for the agent.

title: 3  Setting Up Your Machine
text:
Further reading

Quarto, Get Started and download page (checked 2026-10-30).
Astral, Installing uv (checked 2026-10-30).
GitHub, GitHub CLI and installing on Linux (checked 2026-10-30).
Claude Code setup, Codex CLI and Antigravity CLI (checked 2026-10-30).
Scott Chacon and Ben Straub, Pro Git, Installing Git (checked 2026-11-06).

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
text:
4.1 Get the files
Somewhere in this chapter’s report is a wrong number. The report renders without a single error, reads perfectly well and cites its source, and one of its figures is out by 360,000 visits. Finding it takes no programming, only a habit: put each number beside the data it came from.
That habit is the Check in this book’s title, and this chapter is where you practise it with your own hands. You type every command yourself, at the terminal, on a real report: copy it, render it, check it, record it with Git, change it and undo the change, break it three ways on purpose and read the errors. Only at the end does the agent make an edit, and you check its work with the same commands you have just learned. Allow about 45 minutes; less if the terminal is already familiar.
Step 5 of Chapter 3 cloned the workshop’s files into ~/quarto-workshop. Among them is a small report, starters/first-report. Copy it out, so that the original stays as it was. Type it with Tab completion, which saves typing and catches mistakes: type cp -R ~/quarto-workshop/st and press Tab, and the terminal finishes the name, starters/. When several names fit, press Tab again to list them. When Tab does nothing at all, no name starting that way exists there, which is worth knowing before you press Enter. In the terminal, in any folder:
cp copies, and -R (recursive) copies a folder with everything inside it. It prints nothing. Many commands work this way: cp, cd and, later, git add say nothing when they succeed, and speak only when something is wrong. In the terminal, silence is success.
Now move into the copy and look around. In the terminal:
pwd prints the folder you are in, ending in first-report (/home/ana/first-report on Linux, /Users/ana/first-report on a Mac, with your own name). ls lists six names, in an order that depends on your system:
crumbs: 4  A First Report, by Hand

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
text:
cp -R ~/quarto-workshop/starters/first-report ~/first-report







WarningCommon pitfall



If cp says No such file or directory, your copy of the workshop is older than this chapter: cd ~/quarto-workshop, then git pull, then run the cp line again.



cd ~/first-report
pwd
ls




Table 4.1: What the starter holds.









Name
Holds




report.qmd
the report’s source: settings, one code cell and its sentences


data/
visits.csv, the data the report reads


AGENTS.md
the project’s rules for the agent (Section 2.5)


README.md
what the folder is, in a few lines


pyproject.toml, uv.lock
the Python packages the report needs, with exact versions












ImportantTry it



If you have not yet, copy the starter and go into it with cd ~/first-report.

You’re done when pwd prints a path ending in first-report, and ls lists report.qmd and data.




A name with a space
The terminal splits what you type at each space, so a folder name with a space in it needs care. Try it once, from your home folder. In the terminal:
cd ~
mkdir "my reports"
cd my reports
cd complains, in words that depend on your shell:

bash: cd: too many arguments            (Ubuntu)
cd: string not in pwd: my               (Mac)

cd was given two names, my and reports. Keep the name in one piece with quotes, cd "my reports", or with a backslash before the space, cd my\ reports. Tab completion types the backslash for you: type cd my and press Tab. Then tidy up and go back:
cd ~
rmdir "my reports"
cd ~/first-report
The folders in this book have no spaces in their names, and yours need not either: a hyphen, as in first-report, does the same job.
crumbs: 4  A First Report, by Hand

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
text:
4.2 Render it yourself
In the terminal, in ~/first-report:
uv run quarto render report.qmd
uv run runs a command in the project’s own Python environment (Section 1.4; Section 5.10 has more). The first time, it builds that environment from uv.lock, which takes from a few seconds to a minute, and may print some Downloading lines first. Then Quarto renders, and prints a good deal (trimmed here where marked …):

Using CPython 3.12.13
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Installed 39 packages in 301ms

Starting python3 kernel...[IPKernelApp] WARNING | …
Done

Executing 'report.quarto_ipynb'
  Cell 1/1: ''...Done

pandoc
  to: html
  output-file: report.html
  …
Output created: report.html

When a render succeeds, its last line is Output created: report.html. The lines after pandoc are its settings, and the IPKernelApp warning is harmless (Section 3.7). Your Python version, package count and timings may differ.
Open the page. In the terminal, run open report.html (Mac), xdg-open report.html (Linux), or explorer.exe . and then double-click report.html (Windows, in Ubuntu). The browser shows:

Five London Sights
Five of London’s best-known sights had 25,036,711 visits between them in 2025. The most visited was the Natural History Museum (South Kensington), with 7,116,929, and 4 of the five are free to enter.
Tate Modern, on the South Bank, had 4,154,266 visits.
Source: ALVA, “Visits made in 2025 to visitor attractions in membership with ALVA” (only ALVA member attractions are counted).

Now open the folder itself: open . (Mac), xdg-open . (Linux) or explorer.exe . (Windows, in Ubuntu), where . means “this folder”. The file browser shows the same files as ls, plus the new ones the render made: report.html and report_files/. The terminal and the file browser are two views of one folder.






ImportantTry it



Render the report and open report.html.

You’re done when the render ends with Output created: report.html, and the page shows the five sights’ total.
crumbs: 4  A First Report, by Hand

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
section: 4.3 Check every number against the data
text:
4.3 Check every number against the data
The render worked. That proves the code ran, not that the report is right. Look at the data. In the terminal, in ~/first-report:
cat data/visits.csv
cat prints a file. A CSV is a table in plain text, with commas between the columns. This one has a first line naming its seven columns, then five rows, one for each sight. Each row carries its source, url and retrieved date, so the lines are long and wrap. Ask for just the first two columns:
cut -d, -f1,2 data/visits.csv
cut keeps some columns of each line: -d, says the columns are separated by commas, and -f1,2 keeps the first and second. It splits at every comma, even one inside quotes, so it is safe here only because the first two columns hold no commas.

attraction,visits_2025
Natural History Museum (South Kensington),7116929
The British Museum,6440120
Tate Modern,4514266
National Gallery,4147544
Tower of London,2817852



Pause and think


Put the page beside this list. Which of the page’s numbers does not match a row? (The total is the sum of the five; a calculator will confirm it, but you need not.)



Answer

Tate Modern’s. The page says 4,154,266; its row says 4514266: two digits swapped. Nothing warned you, because Quarto rendered the sentence faithfully: to Quarto it is just words. To fix it, find where that number came from.


The report’s source says where each number comes from. In the terminal:
cat report.qmd

---
title: "Five London Sights"
format: html
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
import csv

with open("data/visits.csv") as f:
    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))

total = sum(int(r["visits_2025"]) for r in rows)
top = max(rows, key=lambda r: int(r["visits_2025"]))
free = [r for r in rows if r["admission"].startswith("Free")]
```

Five of London's best-known sights had `{python} f"{total:,}"` visits
between them in 2025. The most visited was the `{python} top["attraction"]`,
with `{python} f"{int(top['visits_2025']):,}"`, and `{python} len(free)` of
the five are free to enter.

Tate Modern, on the South Bank, had 4,154,266 visits.

Source: ALVA, "Visits made in 2025 to visitor attractions in membership with
ALVA" (only ALVA member attractions are counted).

You met these parts in Section 1.2: the settings between the --- lines, a code cell that reads data/visits.csv and computes total, top and free, and inline code, the `{python} …` pieces, which Quarto replaces with computed values. Chapter 6 explains every line. For now, notice what is computed and what is not. Every other number on the page is inline code that reads the data; that sentence was typed.






NoteWhy this works



A typed number is a copy, made once by a person, and nothing connects it to the data afterwards. Swapped digits are the classic copying slip, but the deeper problem is what happens next: when the data change, the copy stays as it was. That is the drift of Section 1.1, and Section 4.5 lets you watch it happen.








ImportantTry it



Check the free count too: cut -d, -f1,3 data/visits.csv shows each sight’s admission.

You’re done when you have counted 4 rows starting “Free”, as the page says, and can name the one number that is typed rather than computed.
crumbs: 4  A First Report, by Hand

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
text:
4.4 Start a history
Before you change anything, record the report as it is, so that you can always get back to it. Git, which you installed in Chapter 3, does this (Section 1.4). In the terminal, in ~/first-report:
git init -b main

Initialized empty Git repository in /home/ana/first-report/.git/

The folder is now a repository: it has a hidden .git folder where Git keeps the history. -b main names the repository’s first branch, its line of history, main, as GitHub does. (This needs Git 2.28 or newer; git --version shows yours, and the setup in Chapter 3 installs a newer one.) Ask Git what it sees:
git status

On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
    .gitignore
    AGENTS.md
    README.md
    data/
    pyproject.toml
    report.qmd
    uv.lock

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

Untracked files are ones Git can see but does not yet record. Three things in the folder are missing from the list: .venv/, report.html and report_files/. They are left out by .gitignore, a file that lists what Git should ignore; ls hides it because its name starts with a dot, and ls -a shows it. It names everything that uv and the render rebuild, so the history holds only the sources.
Record everything else as the first commit, a saved state with a message saying why:
git add .
git commit -m "Starter report, as copied"
git add . prints nothing: it chooses what goes into the next commit, and . means “this folder”, everything not ignored. git commit records it:

[main (root-commit) 15856fe] Starter report, as copied
 7 files changed, 916 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
 …

The seven characters after root-commit name the commit; yours will differ. Check again:
git status
git log --oneline

On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
15856fe (HEAD -> main) Starter report, as copied

The working tree is the files in the folder as they are now; “clean” means they are exactly as the last commit recorded them. git log --oneline lists the commits, newest first, and (HEAD -> main) marks the commit your files are at now.






WarningCommon pitfall



If git commit says “Author identity unknown”, Git does not know your name yet (Step 5 of Chapter 3 sets it). Run the two git config --global lines it prints, with your own name and email, then commit again. If you leave out -m "…", Git opens an editor for the message: leave it without saving (in nano, Ctrl+X; in Vim, Esc, then :q! and Enter) and run the command again with -m.








ImportantTry it



Start the history and make the first commit.

You’re done when git log --oneline shows one commit, and git status says working tree clean.
crumbs: 4  A First Report, by Hand

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
text:
4.5 Predict, change, rebuild
Suppose ALVA corrects Tate Modern’s figure upwards by 1,000,000. Make that change to the data yourself, with nano, the terminal’s own small text editor. In the terminal, in ~/first-report:
nano data/visits.csv
Press the down arrow three times to reach the Tate Modern row; its long line runs off the right edge of the window, which is fine. Press the right arrow until the cursor is just after the first digit of 4514266, press Backspace to delete the 4, and type 5, so that the number reads 5514266. Save with Ctrl+O, then Enter; leave with Ctrl+X.






WarningCommon pitfall



In nano, Ctrl+O (“write Out”) asks for the file name: press Enter to keep it. Ctrl+X leaves; if you have not saved, nano asks first: Y then Enter saves, N throws the changes away. The keys are listed along the bottom of the screen, where ^ means Ctrl. On a Mac, nano opens Pico, which uses the same keys (checked on macOS 26, 2026-11-12).


Before you render, ask Git what you changed:
git status
git diff
If the diff is longer than the window, Git shows it a screen at a time, with : or (END) on the last line: press Space for more and q to get your prompt back. Removed lines are red and added lines green.

On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
    modified:   data/visits.csv

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

A diff is the lines a change removed and added. The real lines are long, so here each is cut short where you see …:

diff --git a/data/visits.csv b/data/visits.csv
index eb394b9..8c1eea7 100644
--- a/data/visits.csv
+++ b/data/visits.csv
@@ -1,6 +1,6 @@
 attraction,visits_2025,admission,note,s…
 Natural History Museum (South Kensingto…
 The British Museum,6440120,Free (paid e…
-Tate Modern,4514266,Free (paid exhibiti…
+Tate Modern,5514266,Free (paid exhibiti…
 National Gallery,4147544,Free (paid exh…
 Tower of London,2817852,Paid,,"ALVA, Vi…

Read it from the top. --- is the file before, +++ after, and @@ … @@ says which lines follow. A line starting - was removed, a line starting + was added, and a line starting with a space is unchanged context. One line changed, in one file: exactly the edit you meant.


Pause and think


Before you render: of the report’s four numbers (the total, the most visited sight’s count, the free count and Tate Modern’s), which will change?



Answer

Only the total, which rises by 1,000,000 to 26,036,711. The Natural History Museum (South Kensington) is still the most visited, the free count is still 4, and the Tate Modern sentence still says 4,154,266. It was typed, so it cannot follow the data, not even when the data change in the very row it describes.


Now rebuild and look. In the terminal:
uv run quarto render report.qmd
Reload report.html in the browser (it does not reload itself). The total now reads 26,036,711, and the Tate Modern sentence has not moved. That is Section 1.1 on your own screen: one input changed, the computed numbers followed it, and the typed one was left behind.
The trial value is not real, so undo it:
git restore data/visits.csv
git status

On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean

git restore puts a file back as it was at the last commit. It is the undo for any file Git tracks, and it is final: the change it discards was never recorded, so it is gone. Render once more, and the page is back to 25,036,711.






ImportantTry it



Change the data, predict, render, compare, then restore and render again.

You’re done when your prediction matched the page, and git status says working tree clean.
crumbs: 4  A First Report, by Hand

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
text:
4.6 Three mistakes on purpose
Errors are messages, not verdicts, and they are easiest to learn from when you caused them on purpose. For each mistake below, make it, read the message, and check one piece of evidence before you fix anything. Three rules for reading an error:

Find the first line that says ERROR or error, often in red: it says what went wrong. When a long stack trace follows, scroll up to it.
Look where the caret ^ points, when there is one: that is where the program noticed.
Skip the stack trace. Many Quarto errors end with Stack trace: and a list of lines starting at …, eight for a wrong folder and more than twenty for broken settings. A stack trace lists what was running inside Quarto when it stopped: it is for Quarto’s developers, not for you.


The wrong folder
In the terminal:
cd ~
uv run quarto render report.qmd

ERROR: No valid input files passed to render

Stack trace:
    at _Command.actionHandler (file:///…/quarto.js:142967:11)
    …



Pause and think


Quarto found no file to render. Before you change anything, what do you check?



Answer

Where you are, and what is there: pwd prints your home folder, and ls shows no report.qmd. The command was right and the folder was wrong. A misspelt name, such as reprot.qmd, gives the same message, and ls shows that too. Fix it with cd ~/first-report, then render again: the last line is Output created: report.html.




A typo in the command
In the terminal, in ~/first-report:
uv run quatro render report.qmd

error: Failed to spawn: `quatro`
  Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)



Pause and think


What does the first line tell you, and what is the fix?



Answer

uv could not start a program called quatro, because there is none. The error quotes the name back: compare it, letter by letter, with what you meant. Press the up arrow to bring the command back, correct it, and press Enter. Without uv run, the shell says the same thing in its own words: zsh: command not found: quatro on a Mac, quatro: command not found on Ubuntu.




Broken settings
Open report.qmd with nano report.qmd, delete the space after the colon in format: html so that it reads format:html, save and leave. Then, in the terminal:
uv run quarto render report.qmd

ERROR: YAMLException: can not read a block mapping
entry; a multiline key may not be an implicit key (4:1)

 1 |
 2 | title: "Five London Sights"
 3 | format:html
 4 |
-----^

Stack trace:
    at …

(The first line is one line on your screen, split here to fit; the stack trace runs to more than twenty lines.)


Pause and think


The caret points at line 4, which is empty. Where is the mistake, and how do you check?



Answer

On line 3, the line above. (4:1) means line 4, column 1, counted inside the settings block, where line 1 is the opening --- and shows as empty. Without the space, format:html is not a setting, so YAML, the format of those settings, reads on and gives up at line 4. Look at the caret’s line and the line above it. git diff shows the one line you changed.


Fix it by putting the space back, or with the general undo, git restore report.qmd. Then render again to confirm: the last line is Output created: report.html.






ImportantTry it



Make all three mistakes, read each message, check the evidence, then fix it.

You’re done when the render ends with Output created: report.html, and git status says working tree clean.
crumbs: 4  A First Report, by Hand

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
section: 4.7 Hand the fix to the agent
text:
4.7 Hand the fix to the agent
You know where the bug is, you can see any change with git diff, and you can undo one with git restore. That is the moment to delegate: not before you can check the work, but as soon as you can. Start your agent in the report’s folder. In the terminal:



You do

cd ~/first-report
claude


Type codex or agy in place of claude if that is your agent. Trust the folder when it asks, because you made it (in Claude Code, press the down arrow first: the choice starts on No). (Codex asks here, and not in ~/setup, because this folder is now a Git repository.) Then, at the agent’s prompt:



Ask your coding agent

In report.qmd, the sentence about "Tate Modern" types its visit count by hand. Replace the typed number with inline code that reads Tate Modern's `visits_2025` from data/visits.csv. Do not change data/visits.csv. Render with `uv run quarto render report.qmd` and tell me the number the sentence now shows.



Expect it to run

reads AGENTS.md, report.qmd and data/visits.csv · edits report.qmd · uv run quarto render report.qmd



You do

approve its commands · /exit · then, in the terminal, git status and git diff


The starter’s AGENTS.md already says that data/visits.csv must never be edited and that every number comes from the data through inline code, so the agent is likely to get this right. Likely is not checked.


Pause and think


The agent reports: “Done. The sentence now shows the figure from the data.” Why run git diff anyway?



Answer

The agent’s message is a claim about the files; the diff shows the files themselves, every file and line that changed, including any the agent did not mention, such as an edit to the data.



4.7.1 Three checks for every change
Every change in this book, yours or the agent’s, passes the same three checks: two before you commit it, and one after. Here they are, applied to this one:



Table 4.2: The three checks, applied to the agent’s first edit.










Check
Asks
Here




Scope
Did only the files I meant change?
git status lists report.qmd alone; git diff shows the lines


Correctness
Does one number match its source row?
the page’s Tate Modern figure against its row in cut -d, -f1,2 data/visits.csv


Rebuild
Does what you committed build on its own?
render a fresh clone of the repository (below)






Scope. git status should list one modified file, report.qmd. If data/visits.csv is listed too, the agent broke the project’s rule: git restore data/visits.csv undoes that part. The diff will look something like this one, from a version written by hand to test the step (trimmed at the …); an agent’s will differ in detail:

diff --git a/report.qmd b/report.qmd
index 4147a02..39b9454 100644
--- a/report.qmd
+++ b/report.qmd
@@ -13,6 +13,8 @@ with open("data/visits.csv…
 total = sum(int(r["visits_2025"]) for r in …
 top = max(rows, key=lambda r: int(r["visits…
 free = [r for r in rows if r["admission"].s…
+tate = next(int(r["visits_2025"]) for r in rows
+            if r["attraction"] == "Tate Modern")
 ```
 
 Five of London's best-known sights had `{py…
@@ -20,7 +22,7 @@ between them in 2025. The …
 with `{python} f"{int(top['visits_2025']):,…
 the five are free to enter.
 
-Tate Modern, on the South Bank, had 4,154,266 visits.
+Tate Modern, on the South Bank, had `{python} f"{tate:,}"` visits.
 
 Source: ALVA, "Visits made in 2025 to visit…
 ALVA" (only ALVA member attractions are cou…

The typed number has gone, and in its place is inline code that looks Tate Modern up in the data.
Correctness. Reload report.html: the sentence should now say 4,514,266, which is 4514266 in the Tate Modern row of the cut output in Section 4.3.
If either check fails, git restore report.qmd puts the file back as it was before the agent touched it, and you can ask again. Undo works on the agent’s changes exactly as on yours.
When both pass, commit, in the terminal:
git commit -am "Compute Tate Modern's visits from the data"
git log --oneline
-a adds every tracked file that changed, so you need no git add; -m gives the message. Your hash, and perhaps the count of lines, will differ:

[main d7e7f02] Compute Tate Modern's visits from the data
 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
d7e7f02 (HEAD -> main) Compute Tate Modern's visits from the data
15856fe Starter report, as copied

Rebuild. The last check asks whether everything the report needs is in the history, and not only in your folder. Clone the repository into /tmp, a folder for temporary files, which the computer empties from time to time, and render the clone. In the terminal:
git clone ~/first-report /tmp/first-report-check
cd /tmp/first-report-check
uv run quarto render report.qmd

Cloning into '/tmp/first-report-check'...
done.

The clone has no .venv/ and no report.html, because .gitignore kept them out of the history, so the render prints Creating virtual environment again and then builds the page. (If Git says the destination already exists, you have run this before: pick another name, such as /tmp/first-report-check2.) Open the clone’s page as you opened yours: open report.html (Mac), xdg-open report.html (Linux), or explorer.exe . and then double-click report.html (Windows, in Ubuntu). It should match yours, 4,514,266 and all. If the clone does not render, something the report needs was never committed: add it and commit again. Then cd ~/first-report to go back; the clone is disposable.






ImportantTry it



Run the prompt, check its diff, commit, and rebuild from a fresh clone.

You’re done when git log --oneline shows two commits, and the clone’s page says Tate Modern had 4,514,266 visits.

title: 4  A First Report, by Hand
text:
Summary


A report that renders without an error can still be wrong: put each number beside its row in the data, and trace a wrong one to where it was typed.
Typed numbers drift and computed ones follow the data. Change one input, predict, rebuild and explain.
git status says what changed, git diff shows how, git restore undoes it and git commit records a state you can return to.
Read an error from its first line and the caret, skip the stack trace, and check one piece of evidence (pwd, ls, git diff) before you fix anything.
Delegate a change once you can check it: scope, correctness and rebuild (Table 4.2), then commit.


You have now made, by hand, every check the rest of the book asks you to make of an agent’s work, on a project small enough to see whole. Part II scales it up. Each project starts as this one did, with git init, so every agent edit in it can be seen with git diff and undone with git restore. Chapter 5 starts the London guide from an empty folder and explains, one construct at a time, the Markdown you have just been reading.

title: Part II: One Guide, Many Audiences
text:
London’s tourism office has one set of facts and many readers. Visitors want a web page they can open on a phone. Managers want the numbers at a glance, partners a brief they can forward, and people who walk in off the street something to take away. The office needs every one of those versions to say the same thing, and to go on saying it when the visitor counts are revised.
In this part you play the office’s role. You write the guide once, from cited data, and let Quarto make every version from that one source:

5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules turns an empty folder into a web page that changes as you watch, with written rules that hold the agent to cited facts.
6  Documents That Compute makes the guide compute: the numbers in its sentences and its chart come from the data, in three formats at once.
7  One Guide, Five Audiences serves managers, partners and walk-ins in one step, with your agent directing three sub-agents side by side.
8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild puts the guide on the web, then changes one number and asks you to explain everything that changed with it.

The exercises at the end of the part test whether you can do it without the prompts.



Where we are: Part II.
crumbs: Part II: One Guide, Many Audiences

title: 5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
5.1 Markdown at a glance
The tourism office wants a visitor guide it can stand behind: a page anyone can open on a phone, every fact traced to a source, rebuilt rather than retyped when the facts change. Figure 5.1 is where Part II ends: the guide on its own website, with links to the same content in Word, PDF, PowerPoint, e-book and slide formats.
It starts as an empty folder and one plain-text file in Markdown, a way of writing structured text with a few punctuation marks. The agent writes most of it, but Markdown is what you check: the layer you review, compare between versions and fix by hand when a sentence is wrong.
More is new here than in any other chapter: a project the agent builds step by step, its rules, the preview and the environment. Work through it in order: read a section, paste its prompt and look at the result before moving on; each Try it box says what you should see by then. Every step ends the same way, as the first report’s did (Section 4.7): you read the change with git diff and commit it. When a step goes wrong, nothing is lost: one line pasted into the agent restores the chapter’s finished state (Section 5.11).
Markdown is plain text in which a few symbols mean formatting. A # at the start of a line makes a heading; two stars on each side of a word make it bold. You type the symbols; when Quarto renders the file, turning it into a page, they become the formatting they stand for. A Markdown file is an ordinary text file whose name ends in .md: any plain-text editor opens it, and it reads well even before it is rendered.
This section shows the marks one at a time, before the first prompt; the sections after it use each of them in the guide. Each animation pairs what you type, on the left, with what you get, on the right. The right-hand side is not drawn: each step on the left was saved in a file and rendered by Quarto 1.10.20, and the right shows that page, enlarged. Each animation opens on its finished pair, which is all that a reader without animations shows, then types the source from the beginning.
Two things make Markdown safe to learn by trying:
crumbs: Part II: One Guide, Many Audiences
5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules

title: 5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
Nothing breaks. A mark that is mistyped, or opened and never closed, usually shows on the page as an ordinary character, and at worst formats the wrong words. Either way the page still renders, the slip is easy to spot, and you fix it by editing the text.
Trying costs nothing. Type a few lines into a new file named try.md, then run quarto preview try.md in the terminal, in that file’s folder (Section 5.1.6). It opens the page in your browser, or prints an address to open, and updates the page every time you save the file; Ctrl+C in the terminal stops it.


5.1.1 Headings, paragraphs and emphasis
A line that starts with # and a space is a heading, the title of a part of the page. One # gives the largest heading, for the page’s title. Each extra # makes a heading one level smaller (Figure 5.2), down to six.






Figure 5.2: Headings: one # for the largest, then ## and ### for each level down. The page is shown at a laptop’s width, where the three sizes differ most.



Ordinary text needs no mark. Lines that follow one another join into one paragraph, wherever you break them, and a blank line, a line with nothing on it, starts a new paragraph (Figure 5.3). So you can break a long sentence over several lines of the file without changing the page.






Figure 5.3: Paragraphs: lines next to each other join into one paragraph, and a blank line starts the next.



Stars round words emphasise them: two on each side for bold, one on each side for italic. Two tildes (~) on each side strike text through, for something no longer true. These marks come in pairs. Until the closing pair is typed, the opening one shows as typed, as at the start of Figure 5.4.






Figure 5.4: Emphasis: **bold**, *italic* and ~~struck through~~. Until its closing ** is typed, the opening pair shows as two stars.





5.1.2 Lists, quotations and lines
A line that starts with - and a space is an item in a bulleted list. A number and a full stop, such as 1., then a space, start an item in a numbered list (Figure 5.5). Leave a blank line above a list: without one, its items run on as part of the paragraph before it.






Figure 5.5: Lists: - and a space for a bulleted item, 1. and a space for a numbered one, with a blank line between the two lists.



A > at the start of a line makes a block quote: a quotation, set off from the text beside a bar (Figure 5.6). Start each of its lines with >.






Figure 5.6: A block quote: > at the start of each line sets the lines off as a quotation.



Three dashes on a line of their own, with a blank line above and below, draw a horizontal rule: a line across the page that separates two parts of it (Figure 5.7).






Figure 5.7: A horizontal rule: --- on a line of its own, between blank lines.





5.1.3 Links and pictures
A link has two parts: the words to click, in square brackets, then the address they open, in round brackets, with no space between the two (Figure 5.8). Square brackets on their own show as typed. An address is often too long for one row of the screen, so the editor wraps it, showing the rest on the next row, as on the left of Figure 5.8. It is still one line, typed without pressing Enter.






Figure 5.8: A link: the words in square brackets, then the address in round brackets. With the square brackets alone, the words show as typed.



A picture is written like a link with a ! in front: its caption in square brackets, then its file in round brackets (Figure 5.9). Here the file, hall.jpg, is in the same folder as the Markdown file. Section 5.7 adds what a published picture also needs: a size, and alt text, a description for readers who cannot see it.






Figure 5.9: A picture: !, the caption in square brackets, the file in round brackets. Photo of the Natural History Museum’s Central Hall: Julian Herzog, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.



A picture can be a link too. Put the whole picture where a link’s words go, inside its square brackets: [![caption](file)](address) (Figure 5.10). The page looks the same, but a click on the photo opens the address, here the museum’s own page for visitors.






Figure 5.10: A picture that is a link: the picture takes the place of a link’s words. The page looks the same, and a click on the photo opens the museum’s page. Photo: Julian Herzog, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.





5.1.4 All the marks together
Table 5.1 and Table 5.2 gather the marks this book uses, those above and a few more, each with the section where the guide first needs it. Come back to them as you write.



Table 5.1: Markdown for text and lists.









You type
You get




# Visit London
a heading; ## is the next level down (Section 5.3)


a blank line between lines
a new paragraph (Section 5.3)


\ at the end of a line
a line break inside the paragraph


*italic*, **bold**
italic, bold (Section 5.3)


~~Car~~
Car


- Tube
a bulleted item (Section 5.6)


1. British Museum
a numbered item (Section 5.6)


- [ ] Umbrella
an item with an empty box; [x] ticks it






To break a line without starting a new paragraph, end it with \. Two spaces at the end work too, but “the backslash is easier to see, and editors that strip trailing whitespace on save won’t remove it” (Quarto, Markdown Basics).



Table 5.2: Markdown for links, pictures and blocks.





You type
You get




[TfL](https://tfl.gov.uk/)
a link, TfL (Section 5.7)


![Big Ben](big-ben.jpg)
the picture, captioned “Big Ben” (Section 5.7)


> Book ahead.
a quotation (Section 5.7)


`quarto render`
quarto render, in code type


lines between ```text and ```
a code block, shown exactly as typed (Section 5.9)


| Sight | Price | over |---|---|
a table with a header row (Section 5.8)


--- between blank lines
a horizontal rule


\*free\*
*free*, stars and all: \ before a mark keeps it as typed






Here is every one of those marks in one file, toy.md, a short London note with no settings and no code:

# A day in London

Start at the **British Museum**,
where entry is *free*.\
Get there by:

- Tube
- Bus
- ~~Car~~

> Tip: book a free timed ticket.

## Two sights

1. British Museum
2. Tower of London

| Sight           | Price |
|-----------------|-------|
| British Museum  | Free  |
| Tower of London | Paid  |

---

![Big Ben](big-ben.jpg){width=15%
fig-alt="Big Ben's clock tower."}

Photo: John Dillenbeck, CC0.
Plan a route with
[TfL](https://tfl.gov.uk/).
Built with `quarto render`.
Stars kept, not italic: \*free\*

- [x] Contactless card
- [ ] Umbrella

```text
In a fence, **marks** stay put.
```

quarto render toy.md turns it into toy.html, Figure 5.11. Compare the two line by line: the lines of each paragraph have joined, except where a \ broke one; “Car” is struck through; the escaped stars round “free” and the stars inside the fence have stayed stars.






Figure 5.11: What quarto render toy.md makes of the file, at a phone’s width: a screenshot of toy.html as Quarto 1.10.20 renders it. Photo of Big Ben: John Dillenbeck, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.





Pause and think


A line of text, and straight under it, with no blank line between, a line of three dashes. Does the page show a horizontal rule?



Answer

No: the line of text becomes a level-2 heading. A line underlined with dashes is another way of writing one, in GitHub’s Markdown and Quarto’s alike, which is why the rule in Table 5.2 needs a blank line above it.




5.1.5 GitHub’s Markdown and Quarto’s
Markdown comes in dialects. GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM) is the one GitHub uses for what people write there, such as README files and issues. It is “a strict superset of CommonMark”, a precise specification of Markdown, with five extensions: tables, task lists, strikethrough, automatic links and a ban on some raw HTML (GFM specification, version 0.29-gfm, checked 2026-11-12).
Quarto “is based on Pandoc and uses its variation of markdown as its underlying document syntax” (Quarto, Markdown Basics, checked 2026-11-12). Pandoc’s Markdown reads the same core marks as GFM, takes its task lists from it, and adds more: attributes in braces, footnotes, definition lists, citations and mathematics among them (Pandoc User’s Guide, checked 2026-11-12). Three differences catch people who learnt Markdown on GitHub:

A list needs a blank line above it; without one, it runs on as part of the paragraph.
Strikethrough needs two tildes, ~~Car~~, because a single pair, ~2~, makes a subscript.
An image’s text in square brackets is its caption in Quarto, where GitHub uses it as alt text; Quarto’s alt text goes in fig-alt (Section 5.7).



5.1.6 Two commands: render and preview
Quarto turns a file into a page with either of two commands, typed in the terminal in the file’s folder (quarto render --help and quarto preview --help, Quarto 1.10.20, checked 2026-11-12):

quarto render toy.md

writes the output once, here toy.html, and stops. --to docx picks another format. Use it to make a finished file, the one you send or publish.

quarto preview toy.md

renders the file, serves the page on a local address and renders it again each time the file is saved; Ctrl+C stops it. Use it while you write, in a terminal tab of its own.


A plain .md file needs no settings to render, as toy.md shows. Section 5.4 runs both commands on the guide.

5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules

title: 5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
5.2 A folder for the guide
The guide gets its own folder in your home folder, beside the quarto-workshop repository (a project folder with its Git history) that you cloned during setup (Section 3.6), so that its checkpoints are always at ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/. By the end of the chapter your home folder, ~, looks like this:
~
├── quarto-workshop/
└── london-guide/
    ├── .git/
    ├── .gitignore
    ├── AGENTS.md
    ├── london.md
    ├── london.html
    ├── data/
    ├── images/
    ├── pyproject.toml
    ├── uv.lock
    └── .venv/

.git/ and .gitignore: the guide’s history, which you start by hand, and the list of files it leaves out.
AGENTS.md: the rules the agent reads first.
london.md: the guide’s source, the file you check; london.html is rendered from it.
data/ and images/: cited facts and credited photos, copied in and never edited.
pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .venv/: the packages, their exact versions and the installed environment.

Make the folder and start its history by hand, as you did for the first report (Section 4.4), then open a list of what Git should leave out:



You do

cd ~
mkdir -p london-guide
cd london-guide
git init -b main
nano .gitignore


In nano, type these lines, one pattern per line, then Ctrl+O, Enter and Ctrl+X to save and leave:
.venv/
.quarto/
*.quarto_ipynb
*_files/
london*.html
*.docx
*.pdf
*.pptx
*.epub
The first four are the environment and Quarto’s working files. The rest are what the guide’s renders will write: web pages, Word files, PDFs, slides and e-books (a * stands for any characters). Each is rebuilt from the source at the next render, so a commit that held them would only hold copies that go stale. Web pages are listed by name, london*.html, not *.html, because one optional page later on, visits-3d.html (Section 7.5), is a source the agent writes, not a rendered file. Make the first commit:



You do

git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Leave the environment and rendered files out of Git"


git status now says nothing to commit, working tree clean, and it will not list london.html or .venv/ when they appear, because .gitignore names them. Keep this terminal tab for Git, and start the agent in a new tab, in the same folder (type codex or agy instead of claude if you use one of those):



You do

cd ~/london-guide
claude


Claude Code first asks whether you trust the new folder (Section 3.4): you made it for this work, so say yes. Codex asks the same question here, because the folder is now a Git repository. Later prompts copy files from ../quarto-workshop/, which is outside the project folder, so the agent asks your permission the first time it reads there. Approve it, or start Claude Code with claude --add-dir ../quarto-workshop to allow it up front (Codex has the same option, --add-dir).

5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules

title: 5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
section: 5.3 A first page: a title and a welcome
text:
5.3 A first page: a title and a welcome



Ask your coding agent

Create london.md with a level-1 heading "Visit London" and a welcome paragraph with one bold and one italic phrase.


The agent writes:
# Visit London

Welcome to **London**: free museums, royal history and *riverside walks*.
# starts a heading, and the number of # signs sets its level: ## is the next level down. Double asterisks mark bold text and single asterisks italic. A blank line separates paragraphs. That is already a complete document.
Before anything else, see what the agent changed. In your Git tab:



You do

git status



On branch main
Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        london.md

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)

One new file and nothing else: the agent wrote only what it was asked to. git diff would show nothing yet, because it compares the files Git already tracks with their last commit, and a new file has no last commit: its whole text is the change. So read the file itself (cat london.md prints it), then commit it with a message that says why:



You do

git add london.md
git commit -m "Start the guide with a title and a welcome"
crumbs: Part II: One Guide, Many Audiences
5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules

title: 5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
section: 5.4 Watch it become a web page
text:
5.4 Watch it become a web page



Ask your coding agent

Render london.md with quarto render and tell me which file it wrote.



Expect it to run

quarto render london.md → london.html



You do

in a third terminal tab:
cd ~/london-guide
quarto preview london.md
open the address it prints · Ctrl+C stops it


The render writes london.html once. The preview (Section 5.1) renders it again every time london.md is saved, including when the agent saves it, so the page in your browser follows each change (Figure 5.12). It prints a line such as Browse at http://localhost:4200/ (the number varies) and usually opens that page in your browser; if it does not, open the address yourself.






Figure 5.12: A live preview: each time london.md is saved (left), quarto preview renders it again and the page reloads (right). A real recording of quarto preview with the edits this chapter makes.



Keep the preview running from now on. It is the fastest way to check what each prompt did. git status in your Git tab lists nothing new after a render: london.html is a rendered file, and .gitignore leaves it out.






WarningCommon pitfall



A preview and a render of the same file at the same moment collide: both write temporary files with the same names, and one fails with an error such as readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'. While a preview is running, let it do the rendering. Before the agent renders several formats at once (Section 6.5), stop the preview with Ctrl+C, and restart it afterwards.








ImportantTry it



Paste the two prompts above, commit the first page, then start the preview in a third tab.

You’re done when london.html opens in your browser and updates whenever london.md changes.

title: 5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
5.5 Rules for the guide
Section 2.5 introduced AGENTS.md, the file of rules an agent reads at the start of every session. The guide needs one now, before any data or photos arrive, because every later prompt relies on it:



Ask your coding agent

Create AGENTS.md for this project. Scope: a London visitor guide for the tourism office, written once and reused for every audience. Rules: every number comes from a cited file in data/, photos are openly licensed, credited and show no people, never invent facts, keep data/ and images/ unchanged, and call ALVA counts "ALVA member attractions". Show me the file.



Expect it to run

writes AGENTS.md: a scope and a list of rules



You do

approve · read it: does it say what you meant?


Each rule is there for a reason the project will meet. Every number comes from a cited file: the guide quotes visitor counts, and an agent asked for a number it does not have may produce a plausible one; a rule that every figure is computed from a file with a source removes that temptation, and gives you something to check. Openly licensed photos with no people: a published guide needs images it may reuse, and pictures of identifiable people raise consent questions it does not need. Keep data/ and images/ unchanged: the inputs are evidence, and edits belong in the analysis, not in the evidence. “ALVA member attractions”: the counts come from the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions, which lists only its members, so “London’s most visited attractions” would overclaim.
The finished project’s version reads, in part:
## Rules

- Every number comes from a cited file in `data/`: each row carries `source`, `url` and
  `retrieved`. Never estimate or invent a figure or a fact.
- ALVA counts only its member sites: write "ALVA member attractions".
- Photos are openly licensed, credited from `images/ATTRIBUTION.md`, and show no people.
- Keep `data/` and `images/` unchanged.
Read what the agent wrote and edit it yourself if the wording is off. It is your project’s contract with the agent, and the rules work best when they are concrete enough to check. Any plain-text editor will do, or the terminal’s own: in your Git tab, nano AGENTS.md opens the file; Ctrl+O and Enter save it, and Ctrl+X leaves (Appendix B). Then commit it, as you did the first page: git add AGENTS.md, then git commit -m "Write the project's rules".

text:
5.6 Five sights and how to get around



Ask your coding agent

In london.md, add a "Five sights to start with" numbered list (British Museum, Natural History Museum, Tate Modern, National Gallery, Tower of London) and a "Getting around" bullet list: 🚇 Tube, 🚌 Bus, 🚲 Santander Cycles.


## Five sights to start with

1. British Museum
2. Natural History Museum
3. Tate Modern
4. National Gallery
5. Tower of London

## Getting around

- 🚇 Tube
- 🚌 Bus
- 🚲 Santander Cycles
1. starts a numbered list and - a bulleted one; leave a blank line before a list. The five sights are the five attractions whose visits the guide charts later, from ALVA’s data. The list is a starting point, not a ranking. Among London’s ten most visited ALVA member attractions in 2025, the five, in the order listed, stand second, first, third, fourth and eighth; three attractions not on the list drew more visits than the Tower.

5.6.1 Read the diff, then commit
This is the agent’s first change to a file Git already tracks, so git diff, in your Git tab, has something to show:

diff --git a/london.md b/london.md
index df822e3..797957c 100644
--- a/london.md
+++ b/london.md
@@ -1,3 +1,17 @@
 # Visit London

 Welcome to **London**: free museums, royal history and *riverside walks*.
+
+## Five sights to start with
+
+1. British Museum
+2. Natural History Museum
+3. Tate Modern
+4. National Gallery
+5. Tower of London
+
+## Getting around
+
+- 🚇 Tube
+- 🚌 Bus
+- 🚲 Santander Cycles

Lines that start with + were added and lines that start with - removed; the others are unchanged lines shown for context. @@ -1,3 +1,17 @@ says that the three lines starting at line 1 are now seventeen. Yours will differ wherever the agent’s wording does. Check two things: every added line is one you asked for, and no other file is listed. Then commit:



You do

git commit -am "Add five sights and ways to get around"


-a takes in every tracked file that changed, and -m gives the message, as for the first report.






TipIn practice



Make it a habit: after each prompt, once the preview shows what you asked for, run git status and git diff and commit with a message that says why. git commit -am covers changed files; a new file, or a new folder such as data/, needs git add . first, which adds everything new or changed that .gitignore does not leave out. Small commits, one checked step each, let you undo one step without losing the others. Once the habit is yours you can ask the agent to commit (“commit with a message that says why”), and read its diff before you approve.

text:
5.7 Planning a visit: a link, a photo and a tip



Ask your coding agent

Copy ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/images here. In london.md, add "Plan your visit": a TfL Journey Planner link, images/big-ben.jpg at 30% width with alt text and a credit caption from images/ATTRIBUTION.md, and a "Tip from a local" blockquote.


Plan your route with the [TfL Journey Planner](https://tfl.gov.uk/plan-a-journey/).

![Big Ben in the sun. Photo: John Dillenbeck, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons](images/big-ben.jpg){width=30% fig-alt="Big Ben's clock tower and the Palace of Westminster against a blue sky with white clouds."}

> **Tip from a local:** many big museums are free. Book a free timed ticket to skip the queue.
[text](address) is a link and ![caption](file) an image; the text in square brackets becomes the image’s caption. The {…} after the image is a Quarto and Pandoc extension: width sizes it and fig-alt holds its alt text, the description that screen readers announce and that appears if the image cannot load. > starts a quotation. Figure 5.13 is that photo.






Figure 5.13: Big Ben in the sun. Photo: John Dillenbeck, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.









NoteWhy this works



Alt text is not decoration. Without it, an image in a web page or e-book is announced as “image”, or not at all, to a reader who cannot see it, and a caption alone often says who took a photo rather than what it shows. Writing it is also a small test of whether a picture says anything: if the alt text is hard to write, the image may not be needed.


The photo was chosen by the rules: it is in the public domain (CC0), its licence and the absence of people were checked on its Wikimedia Commons page (2026-10-30), and the credit comes from images/ATTRIBUTION.md, which records each photo’s author, licence and source.

text:
5.8 Sights at a glance, from cited data
The guide’s sights table needs facts: each sight’s price band, its nearest Underground station and its official page. They come from a file the agent copies, not from its memory:



Ask your coding agent

Copy ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/data here. In london.md, add a "Sights at a glance" table from data/sights.csv: a photo from images/ (height=60, no unit; alt text), Sight, Price band, Nearest tube and a "Read more" link to its `official_page`. Credit the photos (images/ATTRIBUTION.md) and the sources.


data/sights.csv is a CSV file (comma-separated values): a table in plain text, one line per row, with commas between the columns. It holds one row per sight and fact, and every row names its own source and the date it was retrieved: fifteen facts from nine distinct pages. Table 5.3 shows three of them.



Table 5.3: Three rows of data/sights.csv. Each fact also carries its source (a description) and url.

The table in london.md is plain Markdown:
| Photo | Sight | Price band | Nearest tube | More |
|---|-----|---|-----|----|
| ![The British Museum's glass roof](images/british-museum.jpg){height=60} | British Museum | Free | Tottenham Court Road | [Read more](https://www.britishmuseum.org/visit) |
Vertical bars separate columns, and the row of dashes under the header marks it as a header; the relative number of dashes sets the relative column widths. A link or an image works inside a cell.
The guide has no code yet, so the agent reads the file and types its values into the table: a cited copy of the facts, not a link to them. The next chapter makes numbers compute, and Section 8.5 shows what a copy costs.


Pause and think


The agent has filled in the sights table. How do you check that a price band came from the file and not from the agent’s memory?



Answer

Find that sight’s price_band row in data/sights.csv: its value, source and retrieval date are there. For a whole table, ask the agent to name the row behind each cell, then check a few of them yourself.








WarningCommon pitfall



Two traps in this one table. First, the PDF format made later (with Typst) rejects image sizes in CSS pixels, so {height=60px} fails with “cannot parse length”; a number without a unit, {height=60}, works everywhere, which is why the prompt says “no unit”. Second, a PowerPoint table cannot hold pictures, so the pptx version of the guide shows each photo’s alt text in its cell instead.


Some official sites, including the British Museum’s and Historic Royal Palaces’, answer automated requests with 403 Forbidden, so an agent that checks its links may report those two as broken. Open them in a browser before you believe it.
Commit this step with git add . first, so that data/ is committed with the table: from then on, Git shows you any change to the evidence.

section: 5.9 A checklist that keeps its shape
text:
5.9 A checklist that keeps its shape



Ask your coding agent

In london.md, add a "Before you go" section: a three-item checklist inside a plain text code block.


## Before you go

```text
[ ] Contactless card or Oyster card
[ ] Free museum tickets booked
[ ] Comfortable shoes and an umbrella
```
Three backticks open and close a code fence, and the word after the opening backticks names the language: text, python, bash. Text inside a fence is shown exactly as typed, which is why the brackets and line breaks survive. In the next chapter, writing {python} after the backticks instead of python turns a fence that is displayed into one that runs.

5.9.1 Spot the change you did not ask for
Suppose that after the checklist prompt, git status lists two changed files, not one:

On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   data/sights.csv
        modified:   london.md

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")



Pause and think


The prompt asked for a checklist in london.md, and nothing else. What do you do about data/sights.csv?



Answer

Look before you undo. git diff data/sights.csv shows what changed; here, shortened with “…”, one value in one row:
-British Museum,nearest_tube,Tottenham Court Road,"British Museum, Visit: …
+British Museum,nearest_tube,Holborn,"British Museum, Visit: …
The agent replaced the station the museum’s own page names with one from its memory, against the rule that keeps data/ unchanged. git restore data/sights.csv puts back that one file as it was at the last commit and leaves the checklist in london.md alone, so git status then lists only london.md. Commit that, and tell the agent what it did and which rule it broke. The scene is an illustration, not a recorded session; it is exactly the kind of change a summary such as “Added the checklist” would not mention, which is why you read git status and not only the agent’s report.








ImportantTry it



Add the lists, the link, image and quote, the table and the code fence with the four prompts above, watching each change arrive in the preview, then reading its diff and committing it.

You’re done when london.html shows both lists, the photo with its credit, the five-row table and the checklist, and git log --oneline lists one commit for each step.

section: 5.10 An environment for the code to come
text:
5.10 An environment for the code to come
A Python environment is a folder holding one version of Python and the packages a project uses, kept apart from every other project’s. Packages are the add-on libraries that Python code imports, such as pandas for tables or matplotlib for charts. The next chapter runs Python, and code never runs in a vacuum: what it does depends on the Python version and on the exact version of each package.
Getting all of that to agree used to be a lesson of its own: install conda or a system Python, sometimes a compiler, fix the PATH (the list of folders where the terminal looks for programs), register a Jupyter kernel, then debug it on every laptop. uv now does it in one step, for one project at a time. It fetches the Python version a project needs, and its lockfile, uv.lock, records the exact version of every package: it “captures the packages that would be installed across all possible Python markers such as operating system, architecture, and Python version” (uv documentation, checked 2026-10-31), so one file reproduces the same environment on every Mac, Windows and Linux machine. Other languages pair a project file with a lockfile in the same way: R’s renv.lock, JavaScript’s package-lock.json, Rust’s Cargo.lock.






NoteWhy this works



Why does the lockfile need to know the computer? Many scientific packages contain compiled C, C++ or Fortran, built separately for each operating system and processor (Intel and AMD x86_64, or Apple and other ARM arm64). Each package file’s platform tag, such as macosx_11_0_arm64, names the system it fits (Python Packaging Authority, checked 2026-10-31), so the lockfile lists the right file for every system.





Ask your coding agent

Give this folder its own Python environment with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas matplotlib plotly`. From now on run `quarto` and `python` through `uv run`, and add that rule to AGENTS.md. Show me the Python line of `uv run quarto check jupyter`.



Expect it to run

writes pyproject.toml (the packages), uv.lock (their exact versions) and .venv/ (the installed environment) · adds a rule to AGENTS.md








Figure 5.14: Giving the guide its own environment: uv init --bare, uv add with the guide’s packages, and Quarto finding the project’s own Python. A real recording with a demo account; the 40-second first render of the engine check is cut.



The four packages ipykernel, nbclient, nbformat and pyyaml are what Quarto needs to run Python cells; pandas, matplotlib and plotly are what the guide’s code will use. The larger jupyter package, with its notebook applications, is not needed.1
1 Measured in a dry run on 2026-10-30, on one fast connection, a cold install of Part III’s larger package set took 8 seconds with uv and 31 seconds with pip plus jupyter. That compares the old route with the new one, not the two installers like for like, since the pip run also installed jupyter.





NoteWhy this works



Why uv run in front of every command? Quarto refuses to run Python next to a .venv folder that is not activated (“There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv”). uv run activates the project’s environment for that one command, and first brings .venv up to date with uv.lock. So a copied project, or a checkpoint, rebuilds its own environment on its first uv run, and the rule in AGENTS.md keeps the agent using it after a restart.




Pause and think


Which file tells you the exact version of pandas the guide uses: pyproject.toml or uv.lock?



Answer

uv.lock. pyproject.toml lists the packages the project asked for, each with only a lowest acceptable version (pandas>=…); uv.lock records the one version installed, for every system. That is the file that makes a colleague’s uv run build the same environment as yours.


Commit this step too. git status lists the new pyproject.toml and uv.lock and the changed AGENTS.md, but not .venv/: .gitignore leaves it out, because uv run rebuilds it from uv.lock. So git add . and git commit -m "Give the guide its own Python environment" record everything a colleague needs to build the same environment, and nothing they do not.






ImportantTry it



Run the environment prompt, read its diff and commit it. Keep the preview running: london.md needs no Python yet.

You’re done when uv run quarto check jupyter reports the Python in this folder’s .venv, and git status says nothing to commit, working tree clean.


Stuck for two minutes? Paste this into your agent. It backs up your work and brings the project to this point; then carry on from here.
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/01-london-markdown/README.md
