text:
5.11 If you fall behind
The preface set the rule, and drew its steps in Figure 2: stuck for two minutes, catch up. The line at the end of the last Try it is this chapter’s only catch-up, because its checkpoint holds the end of the whole chapter, whichever step you were stuck on. Pasted into the agent, it:



Expect it to run

backs up london-guide/ to ../london-guide-backup-01-<time> · copies the checkpoint in · renders london.md · checks london.html


Then carry on with the next chapter (Chapter 6). The README was written for the workshop, so the agent may also point you to one of its slides; in this book, the next step is always the one after the catch-up box. The README lists the same steps, which you can also run by hand (Figure 5.15). Nothing is lost: each backup is a new folder named with the date and time, so earlier backups are kept.






Figure 5.15: Catching up by hand, as the checkpoint’s README lists it: a time-stamped backup of the folder (all but .venv/), the checkpoint copied in, and a render that rebuilds the environment from uv.lock first. A real recording with a demo account.









NoteWhy this works



The backup leaves out .venv/ because it can hold hundreds of megabytes and is rebuilt from uv.lock on the next uv run. Copying it would be slow and pointless.


Your history is kept too. A checkpoint has no .git/ folder, so catching up leaves your commits as they were, and the checkpoint’s files arrive as changes. For a reader who had committed every step before the environment (Section 5.10), git status then shows:

On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   AGENTS.md
        modified:   london.md

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
        README.md
        pyproject.toml
        uv.lock

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")

Review them as you would an agent’s change: git diff shows how london.md and AGENTS.md changed (the checkpoint’s rules add the uv run commands), and nothing in data/ or images/ is listed, because the checkpoint’s copies are the same as yours. README.md holds the checkpoint’s catch-up steps; Section 8.4 replaces it with the guide’s own. Then git add . and git commit -m "Catch up to checkpoint 01". Your own .gitignore stays, because the checkpoint has none.

title: 5  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
Summary


Markdown is plain text in which a few marks mean formatting; a mistyped mark breaks nothing and shows on the page, where you can see it and fix it.
Markdown is the layer you read and check; Quarto reads Pandoc’s, which accepts GitHub’s marks and adds more.
Plain Markdown renders with no settings; while a preview runs, let it render.
AGENTS.md holds rules concrete enough to check, written before the data arrive: facts come from cited files, never from the agent’s memory.
After each step, git status and git diff show what the agent changed; commit what you checked, and git restore undoes one file you did not want changed.
uv pins the project’s packages in uv.lock, and uv run uses them.


The guide still has no visitor numbers, because so far a number could only be typed, and a typed number goes stale the day its source is revised. The next chapter makes the guide compute them.

title: 6  Documents That Compute
text:
6.1 The anatomy of a .qmd file
In 2024, by ALVA’s count, the most visited of the guide’s five sights was the British Museum, with 6,479,952 visits; in 2025, the Natural History Museum, with 7,116,929. A guide that said, in typed words, that the British Museum is the most visited of the five went on saying it after ALVA published its 2025 table, in every copy, until someone noticed.
This chapter makes the guide compute instead. Code reads the data at every render, so a new table corrects every sentence, the chart drawn from it and the Word and PDF versions at once, without a single number copied by hand. That is the workflow’s central promise, and the rest of the book builds on it.
A Markdown file can only say what you typed into it. A Quarto document, a .qmd file, can also compute what it says, so before the guide becomes one, here are the parts of one. Section 1.2 showed hello.qmd, the test run’s file, which multiplies two numbers. toy.qmd has the same parts, and reads the guide’s own data file, so its numbers are real:
---
title: "Top of the list"
format: html
---

Visits in 2025 to ALVA member
attractions, from a cited file.

```python
# A fence: shown, never run.
1 / 0
```

```{python}
#| label: top-attraction
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
att = pd.read_csv(
    "data/attractions.csv")
top = att.loc[
    att["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"
```

Most visited: the
`{python} top["attraction"]`,
with `{python} visits` visits.
From the top:
The braces are the whole difference, as Table 6.1 sets out.
quarto render toy.qmd makes Figure 6.1. The title comes from the front matter. The fence is there, 1 / 0 and all. The cell is not, because echo: false hid it, but its work is: the sentence names the Natural History Museum (South Kensington), with 7,116,929 visits, read from the file at the moment the page was rendered.

title: 6  Documents That Compute
text:
Front matter. The block between the two --- lines at the very top holds the document’s settings, written in YAML, a format for settings in which indentation is meaning: a nested setting is indented by two spaces, and a wrong indent changes what it belongs to. title gives the page its title and format chooses the output.
Markdown. Everything outside the fences is the Markdown of Section 5.1.
A fence that is only shown. ```python names a language, so the code is coloured as Python, but Quarto never runs it. If it did, 1 / 0 would stop the render.
A code cell. ```{python}, with the language in braces, is a fence whose code runs when the document renders. Its first lines, starting #|, are cell options: label names the cell, and echo: false hides its code from the page.
Inline code. `{python} visits` runs visits and writes its value into the sentence, so the number in the sentence is computed, not typed.





Table 6.1: Four kinds of code in a .qmd file.









You write
Quarto




```python fence
shows the code; never runs it


```{python} cell
runs it; shows the output, and the code unless echo: false


`{python} visits`
runs visits; writes its value into the sentence


```{=typst} raw block
passes it to Typst untouched; other formats leave it out (Section 7.4)













Figure 6.1: What quarto render toy.qmd makes of the file, at a phone’s width: a screenshot of toy.html as Quarto 1.10.20 renders it.





Pause and think


You put braces round the fence’s language, so that it reads ```{python}, and render toy.qmd again. What happens?



Answer

The render stops. The fence is now a cell, so Quarto runs 1 / 0, Python raises a ZeroDivisionError, and no toy.html is written. The failure is in the first step, execute (Figure 1.2): your code, not the document.

6.2 Settings at the top: the title block



Ask your coding agent

Rename london.md to london.qmd. Replace the "# Visit London" heading with YAML front matter: title "Visit London", author "London Tourism Office", date today, format html. Do not render; my preview rebuilds it.



Expect it to run

renames to london.qmd · edits the top of the file



You do

in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, then uv run quarto preview london.qmd


The .qmd extension tells Quarto to look for front matter and code cells (Section 6.1). The guide’s front matter is four settings:
---
1title: "Visit London"
author: "London Tourism Office"
2date: today
3format: html
---

1

2

3

format chooses the output; later in this chapter it becomes a list.


The page in the preview now opens with the title, the author and today’s date.






WarningCommon pitfall



Delete london.md once london.qmd exists. Both would write london.html, and the one rendered last wins, so the page you see may not come from the file you edited. Restart the preview on the new file, too: the old one is still watching london.md.


Commit the step as before (Section 5.6). git status shows london.md deleted and london.qmd new; git add . records both, and git status then reports them as one change, renamed: london.md -> london.qmd, because the two files are mostly the same text. The history of the guide’s first lines carries on under the new name.

title: 6  Documents That Compute
text:
6.3 Numbers the guide computes



Ask your coding agent

In london.qmd, add a Python cell that reads data/attractions.csv and finds the most visited attraction and total visits_2025, plus a sentence showing both with inline code. The preview re-renders it: check london.html.


The agent writes a code cell (Section 6.1) and a sentence that uses its results:
```{python}
import pandas as pd
attractions = pd.read_csv("data/attractions.csv")
top = attractions.loc[attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax()]
top_name = top["attraction"]
top_visits = f"{top['visits_2025']:,}"
total_visits = f"{attractions['visits_2025'].sum():,}"
```

Most visited in 2025: the `{python} top_name`, with `{python} top_visits` visits.
London's ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew `{python} total_visits` visits.
You do not need to write Python to check it, but you should be able to read it. The cell does four things:

import pandas as pd loads pandas, the package for tables, under the short name pd.
pd.read_csv(...) reads the CSV file into a table, attractions, one row per attraction.
attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax() finds the row with the most visits in 2025, and .loc[…] takes that row, so top["attraction"] is its name.
.sum() adds up the column, and f"{…:,}" writes a number as text with a comma between the thousands, ready for a sentence.

When the document renders, the cell runs and its variables are kept, so each piece of inline code, `{python} name`, is replaced by the value of name. Rendered in this book from the same data file, the sentence reads:

Most visited in 2025: the Natural History Museum (South Kensington), with 7,116,929 visits. London’s ten most visited ALVA member attractions drew 39,692,434 visits.

Quarto 1.4 introduced this inline syntax, one for every engine, Python included; R users already wrote inline code with knitr’s `r x`, a syntax Quarto still supports (Quarto 1.4 release notes, checked 2026-11-12).


Pause and think


If attractions.csv changes, which values in those two sentences update?



Answer

The three that are computed: the top attraction’s name, its visits and the total. They update at the next render, not when the file is saved. The word “ten” is typed, so it never updates: it is right only while the file holds ten rows, and len(attractions) would compute it. Anything typed by hand behaves the same way.


The figures come from ALVA’s table of visits made in 2025 to its member attractions, retrieved on 2026-10-30. Only ALVA’s members are counted, which is why the sentence says “ALVA member attractions”: the project’s rules made the agent write it that way.

title: 6  Documents That Compute
section: 6.4 A chart with a caption and alt text
text:
6.4 A chart with a caption and alt text



Ask your coding agent

Add a matplotlib cell: a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction. Hide its code, label it fig-top10, add a caption and alt text. The preview re-renders it: check london.html.


A cell’s options go in its first lines, as comments that start with #|, like the label and echo of toy.qmd (Section 6.1):
1#| label: fig-top10
2#| echo: false
3#| fig-cap: "Visits in 2025 (ALVA)."
4#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of visits by attraction."
top10 = attractions.sort_values("visits_2025")
top10.plot.barh(
    x="attraction", y="visits_2025",
    legend=False)

1

A label starting fig- numbers the figure and lets the text refer to it as @fig-top10, which renders as “Figure 1” with a link.

2

echo: false hides the code; readers of a visitor guide want the chart, not the Python.

3

The caption, shown under the figure.

4

The alt text, read aloud by screen readers.


Figure 6.2 is that chart, drawn by this book from the same file. Notice that its caption and alt text describe different things: the caption says what the chart is, the alt text says what it shows.








Figure 6.2: Visits in 2025 to London’s ten most visited ALVA member attractions.





Matplotlib draws a static image, so the same figure travels to every format: web page, Word, PDF, slides. Interactive charts, such as Plotly’s, are JavaScript that runs in a browser, so they belong in web pages and dashboards (Chapter 7) and not in a PDF.






ImportantTry it



Run the three prompts above, watching the preview after each.

You’re done when london.html shows the title block, the sentence with computed numbers, and a numbered chart with a caption and no code.

title: 6  Documents That Compute
text:
6.5 One source, three formats



You do

first: Ctrl+C in the preview tab, so that two renders do not collide · restart it afterwards



Ask your coding agent

In london.qmd, add docx and typst (label "PDF") formats with download links on the HTML page. Render all three; check each has the computed sentence and chart.



Expect it to run

uv run quarto render london.qmd → london.html · london.docx · london.pdf


The front matter’s format becomes a list:
format:
  html:
1    format-links:
      - docx
2      - {format: typst, text: PDF}
  docx: default
3  typst: default

1

format-links adds a download link to the web page for each other format listed.

2

An entry can be a format name, or an object with the format and the link’s text.

3

typst makes the PDF with the Typst engine inside Quarto; no LaTeX is involved.


One quarto render now writes three files. Each format runs the code cells again, so the inline numbers and the figure appear in every file without anything being copied. To render only one format, add --to docx (or --to typst). Each format is one more pass through the steps of Figure 1.2. When you restart the preview, the web page has a list of Other Formats in its margin, with a link to each file; open the Word file and the PDF from there.


Pause and think


Suppose ALVA revises one row of data/attractions.csv: the Tower of London’s visits_2025 rises by 100,000. At the next render, what changes in london.html, london.docx and london.pdf? Predict before you read on, as you did with the first report (Section 4.5).



Answer

The same things change in all three, because each format runs the cells again. The total becomes 39,792,434. The Tower’s bar grows, and in a chart sorted by visits, as Figure 6.2 is, it moves up past Somerset House, which has 2,895,010. The first half of the sentence does not change: 2,917,852 is still fewer than the Natural History Museum (South Kensington)’s 7,116,929, so idxmax() finds the same row. The typed word “ten” does not change either. To check a prediction like this one, make the change yourself with nano, render, look, then put the real count back with git restore data/attractions.csv. Section 8.5 asks the same question of the whole published project.








NoteWhy this works



Why render the code once per format? Because a format can change what code produces: a figure may be drawn at a different size or resolution, and some outputs, such as interactive charts, only make sense in HTML. Re-running is the price of each format getting output made for it. For a slow analysis, the cure is to compute once in a script and have every format read the results, which is exactly how Part III is built (Section 9.6).




Pause and think


The bar chart has to appear in the Word file and the PDF as well as the web page. Why does its prompt ask for matplotlib, when the next chapter’s dashboard uses Plotly?



Answer

Matplotlib draws a static image, which every format can hold. Plotly’s charts are JavaScript that runs in a browser, so they suit the web page and the dashboard but not Word or a PDF.

1  revealjs: {output-file: london-slides.html}

In PowerPoint and Reveal.js, each ## heading becomes a slide. The EPUB is an e-book: open it in an e-book reader such as Calibre (free, for Windows, macOS and Linux) or Books on a Mac. title: 6  Documents That Compute
section: 6.7 What a render does, and why two renders collide
text:
6.7 What a render does, and why two renders collide
Figure 1.2 in Section 1.2 showed the three steps of a render. With code in the document, the first step is worth looking at more closely, because it explains the commonest failure of this chapter.
To run the cells, Quarto writes the document out as a temporary Jupyter notebook, named after the file (london.quarto_ipynb), starts a Python kernel (a running Python process) from the project’s environment, sends it each cell in order, and collects the results. Two consequences follow. The cells share one Python session, top to bottom, so a later cell can use a variable from an earlier one, and the order of cells matters. And two renders of the same file at the same moment write the same temporary files, which is why a render started while a preview is re-rendering fails with readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'.
Every render runs every cell again. That is Quarto’s default (freeze: false), and this book’s projects keep it deliberately, so outputs always match the data. It also means a slow cell slows every render; Chapter 15 returns to the trade-off and to freeze: auto, which caches results and needs a rule for when to throw them away.
Each render also prints the harmless IPKernelApp warning described in Section 3.7.


Pause and think


A later cell uses attractions, which an earlier cell creates. You move the later cell above the earlier one. What happens at the next render?



Answer

It fails with a NameError: the cells run top to bottom in one Python session, so attractions does not exist yet when the moved cell runs.








ImportantTry it



If you have not yet, run the formats prompts (Section 6.5, and optionally Section 6.6) with the preview stopped, then restart it.

You’re done when london.docx and london.pdf show the computed sentence and the chart, as do any optional formats you made.


Stuck for two minutes? Paste this into your agent. It backs up your work and brings the project to this point; then carry on from here.
Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/02-london-qmd/README.md

title: 6  Documents That Compute
text:
Summary


A .qmd file is YAML front matter, Markdown and code cells; only a fence whose language is in braces runs.
Cells run at render time, top to bottom, in one Python session.
Inline code puts results in sentences, so they follow the data; typed words do not.
The caption says what a figure is, the alt text what it shows.
Each format re-runs the code, and two renders of one file at once collide.


Every one of those formats is still the visitor’s guide, though. The tourism office has other readers (managers, partners and people who walk in off the street), and the next chapter writes a document for each of them at once.

title: 7  One Guide, Five Audiences
text:
7.1 Content once, format per audience
Correct one fact, then count the documents that repeat it. Written by hand, a dashboard, a partner brief and a printed flyer each hold their own copy of the same facts, and every copy has to be found and fixed. The one that is missed is the one that disagrees in public.
This chapter writes all three in one step: a dashboard for managers, a Word brief and its covering email for partners, and a flyer for walk-ins. The dashboard and the brief read the same data file, so a corrected count reaches both; the flyer copies its facts from data/sights.csv, a choice Section 8.5 returns to. None of the three needs another to exist, which makes them the first job in this book worth splitting across several agents at once, and the first chance to ask when that is worth what it costs.
Correct is not enough. A document does its job only when its reader engages with it, and each reader meets it differently: a manager scans a dashboard in seconds, a partner forwards a brief, a passer-by gives a flyer a glance. So each format here is chosen for how its reader will use it, and the test for every output is the same: would that reader read it, and act on it?
Each audience gets the format that suits it, and each format is a setting. This chapter makes the first three outputs in Table 7.1 and the optional advert; Chapter 8 makes the website.
A dashboard is a page of charts and key numbers arranged in a grid. In a .qmd file with format: dashboard, a level-1 heading starts a page, a level-2 heading starts a row, and each cell’s output becomes a card in that row (Quarto dashboards documentation, checked 2026-10-31). The guide’s dashboard has two pages; its outline, without the code, is:
# Attractions and # Churches start the two pages, and {height=25%} gives the first row a quarter of the page’s height. That row holds the value boxes, each showing one key number with a label and an icon; the next row holds the charts, one card per cell. A value box is written as a div: a block of Markdown between two lines of three colons, whose class in braces, .valuebox, tells Quarto what to make of it. Quarto’s other special blocks, such as callouts, use the same syntax.
It also needs a second data file. data/visits.csv holds the yearly visits to the five sights from 2015 to 2025, from ALVA’s annual tables. Two notes travel with it, from the data’s README. The years 2020 and 2021 are pandemic years, not comparable with the others. And from 2024 the Natural History Museum’s count includes its reopened gardens, so for that museum 2024 and 2025 are not like-for-like with earlier years. data/churches.csv lists the ten cathedrals and churches on Visit London’s own list, an editorial choice with no visitor numbers.
A Word brief turns Markdown headings into Word’s heading styles, so the partner’s copy has a navigable outline and working links. Its covering email is not rendered at all: it is a plain Markdown file whose message sits in a text block, to be copied into an email client, with the brief attached. The email deliberately quotes no visitor numbers. The numbers stay in the brief, where they are computed and cited, as the project’s rules require.
A flyer is a one-page Typst PDF on A5 paper. papersize accepts any of Typst’s paper names (a5, a4, us-letter and so on), and margin sets the margins (Quarto’s Typst documentation, checked 2026-10-30).

title: 7  One Guide, Five Audiences
text:
7.2 Sub-agents: one lead, many hands
The three outputs are independent: none needs another to exist. That makes them a candidate for sub-agents, separate agent sessions that your agent starts for one task each (Figure 7.3). Each sub-agent has its own context, does its task and reports back; your agent, the lead, waits for all of them and then checks the results.






Figure 7.3: One lead, three sub-agents. Each writes only its own files and renders nothing; the lead renders the files one at a time.



The gain is time: three independent tasks take about as long as the slowest of them. The cost is tokens, because each sub-agent does its own reading, reasoning and tool calls. The three agents differ in how they offer it (all checked 2026-10-31). Claude Code starts sub-agents in parallel when a prompt asks for them. Codex enables sub-agents by default and starts them when asked, and its documentation warns both that parallel edits “can create conflicts” and that sub-agent runs use more tokens. Antigravity’s command-line agent can delegate to parallel sub-agents, but its documentation does not say a prompt can require it, so it may do the tasks itself.
Two rules make parallel work safe, and the prompt below states both. Each sub-agent writes only its own files and renders nothing, so no two of them touch the same file. The lead renders the files one at a time, because two Quarto renders, or two environment updates by uv run, in the same folder can collide. Sub-agents read AGENTS.md too, so the project’s rules still apply to their work.






TipIn practice



Use sub-agents when tasks are independent, substantial and write different files. Do not use them for tasks where one needs another’s result, for several edits to the same file, or for small tasks where the overhead of starting and briefing a sub-agent outweighs the work. A prompt that might run without sub-agents should say what to do then: the prompt below ends its first sentence with “none? do the items in turn”.




Pause and think


The office also wants the guide in French and Spanish, each a new file made from london.qmd. Is that a job for sub-agents?



Answer

Yes: the two translations are independent, substantial and write different files (say london-fr.qmd and london-es.qmd), and the lead renders them one at a time. If both first needed a shared list of place names, write that list first, then split the work.

title: 7  One Guide, Five Audiences
text:
7.3 One prompt, three audiences



Ask your coding agent

Run three sub-agents in parallel, one per item (none? do the items in turn). Each reads london.qmd, data/ and images/, hides code, follows AGENTS.md and only writes its own files: no rendering.
1. london-dashboard.qmd (format: dashboard): Attractions page (value boxes: top attraction, total `visits_2025`, number free; Plotly bars by attraction; a Plotly line of visits by `year` from data/visits.csv; end each chart cell with `fig`, assigning `fig = fig.update_layout(…)`); Churches page (data/churches.csv, names linked to `visit_london`).
2. london-email.qmd: docx partner brief (2025 numbers as inline code, five sights with official links, getting around, sources); london-email-message.md: its covering email in a text block, no numbers.
3. london-flyer.qmd: one A5 Typst page (papersize: a5): Big Ben photo, five sights with price band and nearest tube, local tip.
Then render the three .qmd files yourself, one at a time, and check each.



Expect it to run

starts three sub-agents · waits · renders the three .qmd files one at a time



You do

approve its commands · open the four outputs


The lead’s renders are uv run quarto render london-dashboard.qmd, then london-email.qmd, then london-flyer.qmd, and it reports each sub-agent’s progress as it goes. The prompt is long because it is three specifications in one, each as concrete as a single prompt would be. The lead checks each file it renders; the office’s checks are yours. Open each output as its reader would: can a manager find the top attraction without reading a sentence, can a partner forward the brief and its email as they are, and does the flyer fit on one A5 page?
Then check the two rules yourself before you commit. git status should list the four new files the prompt named, london-dashboard.qmd, london-email.qmd, london-email-message.md and london-flyer.qmd, and nothing else: no change to london.qmd, data/ or images/, and none of the rendered files, which .gitignore leaves out. A sub-agent that strayed outside its own files shows up here, whatever the lead’s report says. Then git add . and commit with a message that says why.


Pause and think


A partner asks for this year’s total visits in the covering email itself. Where should the number go, and why?



Answer

In the brief, as inline code, with the email pointing to it. The email is a plain Markdown file that is never rendered, so a number typed there is a copy that will not follow the data.








WarningCommon pitfall



“End each chart cell with fig” is there because of a failure seen in practice: a Plotly chart appears twice in a dashboard card when the cell both calls fig.show() and returns the figure. Assign the figure, end the cell with its name, and nothing else. If a chart’s legend looks clipped, ask for a horizontal legend with a fixed entrywidth; if the flyer spills onto a second page, ask for a smaller photo.








ImportantTry it



Paste the prompt and approve the renders.

You’re done when you can open a two-page dashboard, a Word brief and its email, and a one-page flyer.


Stuck for two minutes? Paste this into your agent. It backs up your work and brings the project to this point; then carry on from here.

title: 7  One Guide, Five Audiences
text:
7.4 A square advert (optional)



Ask your coding agent

Create london-social.qmd: one 12 cm square Typst page (raw Typst page size) for social media: "Visit London", the Big Ben photo, the top attraction and its `visits_2025`. Hide code, follow AGENTS.md, render it, and check that the PDF is one square page.


Typst has no square paper name, so the page size is set in a raw Typst block, which Quarto passes to Typst untouched. The finished advert’s photo runs to the edges, so its page has no margin:
```{=typst}
#set page(width: 12cm, height: 12cm, margin: 0cm,
          numbering: none, fill: rgb("#0b2545"))
#set text(fill: white)
```






Figure 7.4: The finished square advert, styled as a social-media ad: a full-bleed photo under an inset border, a gradient that keeps the text legible and a gold call to action. Rendered from examples/london/london-social.qmd.



Everything on the page is placed by raw Typst: the photo fills the square (fit: "cover"), a rectangle with a navy gradient darkens its lower half, and place() positions the border, the text and the badge. The facts are still computed. A Python cell reads attractions.csv and prints them as Typst variables (#let top-name = "Natural History Museum"), which the layout uses, so a corrected count reaches the advert at the next render like every other output.
The finished advert has no title and no level-1 heading: either would land on a page of the default size before the square one. This was tested with Quarto 1.10.20 and its bundled Typst on 2026-11-12. A raw block is a useful escape hatch, and a costly one: it ties the source to one format, so use it only for what the format’s settings cannot express.
If the advert will not come out as one square page, skip it: nothing later depends on it. The finished version is ../quarto-workshop/examples/london/london-social.qmd, which you can copy into your folder and render.

text:
7.5 The sights in three dimensions (optional)
The guide’s data can also be drawn as a map: the five sights as columns as tall as their 2025 visits, Visit London’s ten churches as short markers, and the London boroughs around the Thames (Figure 7.5). Nothing in the project changes: the scene is drawn from the same files. The tallest column is the Natural History Museum, at 7.1 million visits; the only paid sight is the Tower of London.



■ free sight■ paid sight■ church · no count, marker only■ the ThamesNatural History MuseumBritish MuseumTate ModernNational GalleryTower of LondonSt Paul's CathedralSouthwark CathedralWestminster CathedralWestminster AbbeyAll Saints Margaret StreetSt Dunstan in the EastSt Martin-in-the-Fields ChurchSt Pancras Old ChurchSt Clement Danes ChurchTemple ChurchThis 3-D view needs WebGL. 2025 visits: Natural History Museum 7,116,929; British Museum 6,440,120; Tate Modern 4,514,266; National Gallery 4,147,544; Tower of London 2,817,852.
MapTilt: height is visitsUp close: the five sights




Figure 7.5: The five sights and Visit London’s churches on the London boroughs. Drag to turn, scroll to zoom, and use the buttons to tilt the map and to fly to the sights. Visits: ALVA; places: Wikidata; boroughs: ONS, Open Government Licence v3.0, contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right 2024.



Every point, height and border is computed from the project’s files: coordinates from data/places.csv (from Wikidata, CC0), visits from data/visits.csv, price bands from data/sights.csv, and borough boundaries from the Office for National Statistics, clipped at the high-water mark so the tidal Thames appears as the gap between the boroughs on its two banks. A script written for the workshop’s slides, using the three.js library, only draws them. The borough tones tell neighbours apart and encode no data.

7.5.1 Asking for three.js
You do not need to know three.js to ask for it. Name the library, the data and what you want to do with the result, and check the numbers:



Ask your coding agent

Create visits-3d.html with `three.js` from a CDN: a labelled 3-D bar per `attraction` in data/visits.csv, as tall as its `visits` in the latest `year`, that I can drag to turn. Put the numbers in the page so it opens by double-click, then check them against the CSV.








Figure 7.6: A 3-D bar chart of 2025 visits to five ALVA member attractions, drawn by three.js from this prompt. A dry run by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) on 2026-11-06, following the prompt in a scratch folder; your page will look different.



three.js is a free JavaScript library (MIT License) that draws 3-D scenes with WebGL, the browser’s built-in 3-D graphics, so the reader installs nothing. Two details of the prompt matter. It asks for the numbers to be written into the page, because a page opened by double-click cannot read local files. And the page loads three.js from a content delivery network (CDN), so it needs the internet to work; a published page keeps that dependency, which is why this book, like the workshop’s slides, ships its own copy of the library.






WarningCommon pitfall



A 3-D chart has to earn its third dimension. Perspective makes bars harder to compare than a plain bar chart: the near bar looks taller than an equal bar behind it. Figure 6.2 is the better chart for comparing visits. Use 3-D when the third dimension means something, as height does on a map, or for delight, and say which.

Summary


Each audience’s format is a setting: a dashboard, a Word brief, an A5 flyer.
Outputs whose code reads the data follow it; the flyer’s copied facts do not.
Sub-agents suit independent, substantial tasks that write different files.
Each sub-agent writes only its own files; the lead renders one at a time.
Open each output as its reader would: the lead’s checks do not replace yours.


The office now has a version of the guide for every reader but one, and all of them sit on your computer. Visitors need a website: the next chapter publishes one, then changes one number to test whether every reader really does get the same fact.

title: 8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
8.1 Git: every change, safely
The guide is finished, and nobody but you can see it: every output sits in a folder on your computer. This chapter puts it on the web, where anyone can open it on a phone, with GitHub to keep a copy of the history you have been committing and GitHub Pages to serve the result. Then it asks the question the whole workflow is built to answer: if one input changes, which outputs change with it, and how do you know? That question comes with no prompt. It tests whether you can predict what a rebuild will do, and then check.
Section 1.4 likened Git to Word’s Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history, and since the first report (Section 4.4) you have kept one yourself: git status and git diff before each commit, a message that says why, and git restore for a change you did not want. That is what Git does inside one folder, and it already keeps every earlier version of the guide, each with a note saying why it changed. Publishing needs what Git does beyond the folder: a copy of the history that others can reach, and a way for someone else to read a change and approve it before it counts.
The vocabulary for that is short (Figure 8.1; Pro Git and GitHub’s documentation, checked 2026-10-31). Your folder is already a repository, a project folder with its history, and each of your commits is a snapshot of every tracked file with its message. The new words are about sharing them.
To push is to copy commits to the shared repository on GitHub, the website that keeps a copy of a repository online. A branch is a movable label on a line of commits, so work can go on there while the main line, main (the name git init -b main gave it), keeps working. A pull request proposes merging a branch and shows its difference, or diff, line by line, as git diff does in your terminal, but on a page that others can read; a review comments on it, approves it or asks for changes; merging adds its commits to main.
Working alone, as in this book, you commit straight to main and push; in a team, every change goes round the loop. Either way the check is the one you already make: read the diff before a change counts. From here the agent can run the Git commands too. Ask it to “commit with a message that says why”, and read its diff before you approve: a diff is the clearest check you have of what the agent actually did.

Pause and think


The agent reports “Committed the dashboard changes” and asks to push. What do you check before you approve?

title: 8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
8.2 Where a site lives
A rendered Quarto website is static: a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and documents, with no program running on a server. Any web server can serve it, so publishing means copying that folder to a host. GitHub Pages is the host this book uses, because the repository is already on GitHub and quarto publish gh-pages is built in (Figure 8.2).






Figure 8.2: Publishing to GitHub Pages. The source goes to the main branch with Git; quarto publish gh-pages renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, which GitHub serves.



There are two ways to get a site onto a host. Either you render on your own computer and upload the result, as quarto publish does for GitHub Pages and Netlify, or the host builds the site from your repository on every push. The second works only if the build installs Quarto, Python and every package the project needs, or if the rendered output is committed. The London repository leaves its rendered _site/ folder out, so a host that builds would produce nothing until the build is set up.


Pause and think


You connect london-guide to a host that builds from Git, and it publishes an empty site. Why?



Answer

The repository holds no rendered site, because .gitignore leaves _site/ out, and the host’s build has no Quarto, Python or packages unless you install them in it. Either render on your computer and upload the result, or set up the build.


Six hosts with free plans for static sites show the two routes (Table 8.1, Table 8.2). Their free plans change, so Table K.3 in Appendix K lists each one’s current limits, with the date they were checked: read them before choosing.



Table 8.1: Hosts you render for and upload to.





Host
Upload with




GitHub Pages
quarto publish gh-pages, this book’s route


Netlify
quarto publish netlify


Cloudflare
wrangler deploy









Table 8.2: Hosts that build the site from your repository.





Host
How it builds




Vercel
from the repository, on every push


GitLab Pages
publishes a public folder from a CI job


Render
rebuilds on every push






Two details matter for this project. Quarto’s Netlify build plugin runs no Python, so render on your computer and upload. GitLab builds in a CI job, a build it runs on each push: set output-dir: public and install Quarto and Python in the job. Quarto Pub, Quarto’s own free host, is being replaced by Posit Connect Cloud.

title: 8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
8.3 One folder, one website



Ask your coding agent

Make this folder a Quarto website: _quarto.yml (render only the .qmd files; navbar: Guide, Dashboard, a Downloads menu for the docx, pdf, pptx, epub and london-slides.html files that exist) and index.qmd, and add /_site/ to .gitignore. Render and check the links.



Expect it to run

writes 2 files · adds a line to .gitignore · uv run quarto render → _site/



You do

then, in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, and uv run quarto preview


A _quarto.yml file at the top of the folder turns it into a project. quarto render with no file name then builds every listed page into _site/, with shared navigation, and quarto preview with no file name previews the whole site. The dashboard becomes one page of it:
project:
  type: website
1  render:
    - index.qmd
    - london.qmd
    - london-dashboard.qmd
website:
  title: "Visit London"
  navbar:
    left:
      - {text: Guide, href: london.qmd}
      - {text: Dashboard, href: london-dashboard.qmd}
2      - {text: Downloads, menu: [...]}

1

An explicit render list keeps the README, the data notes and the photo credits from becoming pages of the site.

2

The menu links the files the other formats wrote: the Word guide, the PDF, the flyer, and whichever optional files you made.


.gitignore gains one line, for the rendered site, _site/, which is rebuilt from the source and published separately (Section 8.4). The rest of the list has been there since you started the folder (Section 5.2): the environment .venv/ (rebuilt from uv.lock), Quarto’s working files and the outputs rendered beside the sources. index.qmd becomes the site’s home page, index.html, the page a visitor sees at the site’s address.






ImportantTry it



Make the folder a website and restart the preview.

You’re done when the site opens with Guide, Dashboard and Downloads in its navigation bar, and each Downloads link opens its file.

title: 8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
8.4 Publish
Before you paste the next prompt, replace <your-github-username> with your GitHub username (the agent can look it up with gh api user if you ask it to).



Ask your coding agent

If this folder is not yet a Git repository, run `git init -b main`; check that .gitignore covers _site/, .quarto/, .venv/, *_files/, *.quarto_ipynb, london*.html, *.docx, *.pdf, *.pptx and *.epub. Replace README.md in this folder with a short one linking to https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/ and listing the files in the site's Downloads menu. Commit it with any work not yet committed (nothing that .gitignore leaves out), then create a public GitHub repository named `london-guide` with gh and push `main` to it. Set the repository's website to the same URL with `gh repo edit --homepage`. Show me the README and the website URL you set.



Expect it to run

git status · git commit · gh repo create london-guide … · gh repo edit --homepage …



You do

approve gh · in the preview tab: Ctrl+C, then uv run quarto publish gh-pages and Enter · open the address on your phone


The agent creates the repository on GitHub from your folder with gh repo create london-guide --public --source=. --push, which also pushes the commits, using the sign-in from the setup check. Every commit you have made since you started the folder goes with them, so the repository on GitHub opens with the guide’s whole history, one checked step at a time. Its README is the first thing visitors to the repository see, and its link takes them on to the live site.
The first publish is yours, typed in the terminal. Stop the preview first: the publish renders the whole site, and two renders in one folder collide. It asks one question, “Publish site … (Y/n)”, which Enter answers yes; then it renders the site, creates the gh-pages branch, pushes the rendered site and opens it. Quarto’s GitHub Pages guide says to run quarto publish gh-pages locally, once, before setting up a GitHub Action to publish (checked 2026-11-12). Make that first run interactive, too: in a dry run with Quarto 1.6.40, --no-prompt stopped the first publish with “the remote origin does not have a branch named gh-pages”. That was observed with 1.6.40 and not re-tested with 1.10.20. Once the branch exists, the agent can update the site with uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt.
In that dry run, the first publish of each site took one and a half to two minutes, and GitHub Pages then built it in 20 to 35 seconds, so a 404 page in the first minute usually means the site is still being deployed.






WarningCommon pitfall



A push that fails with HTTP 400 (“RPC failed”, “the remote end hung up unexpectedly”) was seen with larger sites, such as dashboards with embedded maps. Raise Git’s buffer for this repository with git config http.postBuffer 524288000, and push again.








TipIn practice



Publishing from your own computer is simple and keeps the build where your environment is. The alternative, a GitHub Action that renders on every push (Quarto’s quarto-dev/quarto-actions), needs Python and the project’s packages installed in the job, or freeze set so that committed results are reused, and Quarto’s guide still asks for one local quarto publish gh-pages first.








ImportantTry it



Publish the guide.

You’re done when https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/london-dashboard.html opens on your phone.


Stuck for two minutes? Paste this into your agent. It backs up your work and brings the project to this point; then carry on from here.

section: 8.5 Change one input, explain the rebuild
text:
8.5 Change one input, explain the rebuild
Chapter 1 began with a correction (Section 1.1): ALVA revises one figure, and in a copy-and-paste workflow someone has to carry it by hand into every file that quotes it. Here is that scenario for real, in a project where no visitor count was ever copied. You made the same move on a smaller scale with the first report (Section 4.5) and predicted one for the guide’s first three formats (Section 6.5); now it covers every page. No prompt is supplied: write your own, or do it by hand. Make the edit to the data yourself, for example with nano data/attractions.csv (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X): the project’s rules keep the agent out of data/, which is the point of them.






ImportantTry it




Predict. Set the Tower of London’s visits_2025 in data/attractions.csv to 8000000. Which outputs will change? Write it down before you read on.
Rebuild: stop the preview, then run uv run quarto render.
Explain which outputs changed, which did not, and why.
Undo with git restore data/attractions.csv, then rebuild.


You’re done when you can name the outputs that changed, the ones that did not, and the line of code that links each changed output to the input.



The value is fictitious: chosen to change the top attraction, so that the effect is visible, and reversible, because the real file has been committed since you copied it in (Section 5.8). git restore puts a file back as it was at the last commit, and the second rebuild leaves no trial number in your files.

Check your prediction
To check, you need to know which page reads which input. Table 8.3 is computed from the finished project’s sources, optional pages included: a page counts as reading a file only if its code loads it.



Table 8.3: Which page of the finished London project (each a .qmd file) reads which file in data/, and the formats it writes. Computed from the sources: a mark means the page’s code loads the file.





Page
Writes
attrac­tions
visits
churches
sights




london
html, docx, pdf, pptx, epub, slides
●





london-dashboard
html
●

london-social
pdf

pdf

In all, five pages load attractions.csv, and between them they write ten files, so the change reaches all of them at the next render.
What it does there depends on each page’s code. Of those pages, three (the guide, the dashboard and the partner brief) find the top attraction with attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax() and the total with .sum(), so in each of them the Tower of London becomes the most visited attraction and the total rises. The square advert uses only the first call, so it names the Tower too.
The white paper names no top attraction: its sums by admission change, but its table keeps ALVA’s rank_uk column from the file, which would still rank the Tower ninth in the UK beside the most visits of the ten. A copied column goes stale too. Still, that answers the question Chapter 1 began with: the correction reaches ten files with one command, and nobody has to go looking for them.
Copies deserve a second look. The flyer loads no data at all, and the sights tables in the guide and the partner brief are typed, although the guide’s credits name sights.csv: all three copy their facts (price bands, nearest stations) from the cited file into the Markdown. That was a reasonable choice, because those facts rarely change, but it means a correction to sights.csv updates none of them. A cited copy is still a copy.






NoteWhy this works



Why does every page recompute, even ones whose sources did not change? Because the project keeps Quarto’s default, freeze: false: every render re-runs every page’s code, which keeps this exercise’s answer simple. With caching turned on, a page whose own source did not change would keep its old numbers, and the answer would depend on the cache; Chapter 15 returns to that trade-off.


Two more things do not change: the live site, until you publish again (uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt), and any output you did not rebuild. Model answers, with the follow-up questions worth asking, are in Appendix E.

title: 8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
8.6 A white paper (optional)
The same data can also become an academic paper: an abstract, numbered sections, computed results and a reference list, set in the typeface LaTeX documents use, without installing LaTeX.



Ask your coding agent

Create london-whitepaper.qmd, an A4 Typst white paper in "New Computer Modern": an abstract (no inline code), numbered Introduction, Methods, Results and Conclusions, then References via `#set bibliography(title: [References])` (references.bib from `url`). Analyse data/visits.csv vs 2019 and data/attractions.csv by `admission`. Add it to `render` and the "Downloads" menu; render; check citations. Figures must be vector: set `fig-format: svg` and check that the files in `figure-typst/` end in .svg.


bibliography: references.bib
format:
  typst:
1    mainfont: "New Computer Modern"
2    section-numbering: "1.1"
3    bibliographystyle: ieee
4    fig-format: svg

1

Typst 0.15, bundled with Quarto 1.10.20, includes New Computer Modern, the OpenType version of LaTeX’s Computer Modern, so the paper looks like a LaTeX article without a TeX installation.

2

Numbers the headings: 1, 1.1, 2.

3

Typst’s numbered reference style; [@key] in the text cites an entry in references.bib.

4

Vector figures stay sharp at any zoom; the prompt’s check makes sure they really are vectors.








Figure 8.3: The first page of the finished London white paper: title, abstract, and numbered sections with citations. Rendered from examples/london/london-whitepaper.qmd.









WarningCommon pitfall



Three traps, all met while building the example. The paper’s settings need Quarto 1.10 or newer: Quarto 1.6.40’s Typst rejects them with “unexpected argument: spacing”. An inline expression in a YAML abstract runs before the setup cell and fails, so the finished example writes its abstract in the body, in a raw Typst block. And Typst prints its own heading above the reference list, “Bibliography” by default, which the prompt changes with #set bibliography(title: [References]) so the paper needs no References heading of its own.


A genuine LaTeX PDF is also available, as format: pdf, but it needs a TeX distribution, for example quarto install tinytex. For most reports Typst is faster and simpler.

8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild

title: 8  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
Summary


Pushing copies your commits to GitHub; a pull request shows a diff for someone else to review before it counts.
A built site is static files: upload them, or let a host build them.
A _quarto.yml with a render list makes a folder a website.
The first quarto publish gh-pages is yours; later updates can be the agent’s.
A changed input reaches every page whose code loads it; copies and the live site do not.


That completes one guide for many audiences. In Part III the hard part is the analysis itself: grouping Colombia’s municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context. That one analysis is then published as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all reading the results of one script, and its rebuild test changes a setting of the analysis instead of a number in a table.

Exercise II.1: London in Markdown

title: Exercises for Part II
text:
Write your own prompts
These build on Part II and have no checkpoints. For each, write the prompt yourself, as concrete as the book’s (the files, the columns, the output) and ending with a check you can verify without trusting the agent’s report. If you skipped them, the optional pieces come first: the square advert (A square advert (optional)), the white paper (A white paper (optional)) and the three.js page (The sights in three dimensions (optional)).

A handout of free attractions. The office wants a one-page A5 handout of the attractions in data/attractions.csv that are free to enter, each with its 2025 visits. Decide which admission values count as free and say so in the prompt. You are done when the handout lists as many attractions as the dashboard’s “Top 10 with free entry” value box counts, and no number on it was typed.
Then and now. Add a section to london.qmd comparing each of the five sights’ 2025 visits with 2019’s, from data/visits.csv. Your prompt should say why 2019 is the year to compare with, and ask for the one sight whose counts are not like-for-like to be flagged. You are done when every percentage comes from a cell and the flagged sight is the one data/README.md names.
Turn a copy into a computation. The flyer and the sights tables in the guide and the partner brief all copy their facts from data/sights.csv (Table 8.3). Make the flyer’s table read the file instead. Your check: change one station name in sights.csv yourself, rebuild, and see it on the flyer. Restore the file afterwards.
A map in two dimensions. The 3-D map’s data are in data/places.csv and the borough boundaries in data/london-boroughs.geojson. Add a third dashboard page that draws the sights and churches on a 2-D Plotly map from those files, with each point’s source in its hover text. Decide how you will check that every point is where it should be.
Update the live site. Change the guide’s welcome sentence, then write one prompt that commits with a message that says why and publishes the update with uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt. You are done when the new sentence is on your phone.

title: Exercises for Part II
text:
Review questions

The project’s rules say “ALVA member attractions”, never “London’s most visited attractions”. What would be wrong with the second phrase?
After a prompt to add a “Getting around” list, git status lists london.md and AGENTS.md as modified, and git diff AGENTS.md shows the rule “Keep data/ and images/ unchanged” removed. What do you do, and why does this matter more than a wrong word in the guide?
A colleague copies your london-guide/ folder without .venv/. What gives them the same packages as you, and what do they type first?
While quarto preview runs on london.qmd, the agent runs quarto render london.qmd and it fails with readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'. What happened, and what are two ways to avoid it?
In the guide’s sentence about visits, which parts update when attractions.csv changes, and when? Does any part not update?
The guide’s bar chart has a caption and alt text. What should each say, and why are they not the same?
You need two changes to london-dashboard.qmd: a new value box and a fix to the line chart’s legend. Should you give them to two sub-agents working in parallel?
Why is the flyer’s page size set with papersize: a5, but the square advert’s in a raw Typst block?
Netlify can build your site from the repository, or you can render it yourself and upload it. Which does the London project need, and why?
After the rebuild in Exercise II.5, the dashboard on your computer shows the Tower of London as the most visited attraction, but the flyer has not changed and the dashboard on your phone still shows the old numbers. Explain both.

title: Exercises for Part II
text:
Answers

ALVA counts only its member sites, so its table is not a list of every London attraction. “London’s most visited attractions” would claim more than the data show (Rules for the guide).
Undo that file alone with git restore AGENTS.md, check that the diff of london.md holds only the list, and commit that. A wrong word spoils one page and shows in the preview; a removed rule shows nowhere on the page, yet changes every later session, because the agent reads AGENTS.md at the start of each one, and the guard on the evidence would be gone without anyone deciding it (A checklist that keeps its shape).
uv.lock, which records the exact version of every package for every system. Their first uv run command, such as uv run quarto render london.md, builds .venv/ from it (An environment for the code to come).
A render writes a temporary notebook named after the file, and the preview was rendering the same file at the same moment, so the two collided. Let the preview do the rendering while it runs, or stop it with Ctrl+C first and restart it afterwards (What a render does, and why two renders collide).
The inline code (the top attraction, its visits and the total) updates at the next render, not when the file is saved. The word “ten” is typed, so it never updates (Numbers the guide computes).
The caption says what the chart is: the measure, the year and whose attractions. The alt text says what it shows, such as which bar is longest and which shortest, for a reader who cannot see it (A chart with a caption and alt text).
No. Both edit the same file, and both are small. Sub-agents suit independent, substantial tasks that write different files; make these two edits in turn (Sub-agents: one lead, many hands).
Typst has a paper name for A5 but none for a 12 cm square, so the advert’s size needs a raw block, which Quarto passes to Typst untouched. A raw block ties the source to one format, so use it only for what the format’s settings cannot express (A square advert (optional)).
Render it yourself and upload it: the pages run Python, and Quarto’s Netlify build plugin runs none. A host that builds would also find no rendered site in the repository, because .gitignore leaves _site/ out (Where a site lives).
The flyer loads no data at all: its facts were copied into its Markdown, so a change to attractions.csv cannot reach it. The live site shows what was last published, and changes only when you publish again (Change one input, explain the rebuild).

The second transfer task compares with 2019 because it is the last year before the pandemic years 2020 and 2021, which data/README.md says are not comparable with the others. The sight to flag is the Natural History Museum: from 2024 its count includes its reopened gardens.

title: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications
text:
Where Colombia’s tap water is tested, the countryside’s is far riskier than the towns’. In 2023, of the rural zones (a municipality’s countryside, outside its head town) with a utility-supplied water-risk score, 28% fell in the high-risk or unfit bands, against 6% of urban ones. And much rural water has no score at all: that year, 6.8 million of the 12.6 million people in rural zones lived where the open data hold none.
This part asks which kinds of municipal zone exist, judged by water safety, services and context, and how infant mortality, exam scores and school dropout differ between those kinds. Each row of its data is a zone-year: one municipality’s urban zone (the head town) or rural zone in one year. The analysis groups those rows, so a municipality’s two zones can be different kinds. You are the analyst. Your readers are officials, who need a report, and a municipal council, which needs slides, and both deserve an answer that says plainly what the data cannot show:

9  The Question, the Data and the Rules pins down what is asked, what the data mean and what the agent may not do.
10  Look Before You Model finds where the data are empty or misleading, and meets Tunja, the municipality this part follows.
11  From Table to Features turns the table into features a clustering can use, and counts the cost.
12  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means lets an algorithm group the zone-years, and decides how many groups there are.
13  Interpreting Clusters names the kinds and compares their outcomes.
14  Correlation Is Not Causation asks whether worse water goes with more infant deaths, and why that is not a cause.
15  Publish Many turns one set of results into a report, slides, a blog post and a website.

The exercises at the end of the part test whether you can do it without the prompts.



Where we are: Part III.

title: 9  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
9.1 The question and its readers
In 2023, Colombia’s national report on drinking water scored the water of its urban areas at 5.7, in the low-risk band, and the water of its rural areas at 36.5, in the high-risk band (Table 9.1). DANE’s projections put 12.6 million people, 24% of the population, in rural zones in 2023. People drink and cook with this water, so where the risk sits, and what goes with it, is worth knowing.
The question for this part is therefore: which kinds of municipal zone exist in Colombia, judged by water safety, services and context, and how do health and education outcomes differ between them? Part II’s numbers were simple counts; these are not. Every step has a way to go wrong that a clean render will not reveal: a variable that means something narrower than its name, a gap that is not random, a comparison that looks causal and is not.
The question splits in two, and the order matters:
“Kinds” will be clusters: groups of zone-years, each one municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year (Section 9.4), that are similar to each other on the chosen variables, found by an algorithm called k-means (Chapter 12). Because the unit is a zone in a year, a municipality’s two zones can belong to different kinds, and a zone can move between kinds over the years.
The answer has two readers. Officials will read it as a report, in Word or as a PDF, and a municipal council will see it as a short deck of slides (Chapter 15). Both will look for where to act, and both will be tempted to read a difference between kinds as an effect of the water. So the limits are stated now, each with its reason. The water score covers only systems run by a utility (Section 9.2). Many rural zones have no score at all, so the results describe sampled systems (Section 10.2). And the comparisons describe; they cannot establish that water causes any outcome (Chapter 14).

text:
9.2 Scoring water risk: the IRCA
Colombia scores the safety of drinking water with the IRCA, the Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano (water-quality risk index for human consumption), defined in Resolución 2115 of 2007. It runs from 0, every test passed, to 100, every test failed, and article 15 sorts the scale into five bands (Table 9.1).



Table 9.1: The IRCA risk bands (Resolución 2115 de 2007, art. 15) and where the 2023 national figures fall (MinSalud, MinVivienda, INS and Superservicios, INCA 2023, Bogotá, January 2025, Tabla 4; both checked 2026-10-30).





IRCA
Band
National figures for 2023 that fall in it




0–5
no risk (sin riesgo)



5.1–14
low (bajo)
urban areas 5.7; utility-supplied 7.4


14.1–35
medium (medio)
the whole country 16.4


35.1–80
high (alto)
rural areas 36.5; self-supplied 43.7


80.1–100
unfit (inviable sanitariamente)







The national average sits in the medium band and hides the urban–rural gap, which is why this part’s data keep each municipality’s two zones apart.






NoteWhy this works



Surveillance samples of tap water are tested against health limits. Each tested characteristic carries a risk score: Escherichia coli 25, total coliforms 15, turbidity 15, free residual chlorine 15, apparent colour 6 and pH 1.5, among others. A sample’s IRCA is the score of the characteristics that fail their limit, as a percentage of the score of all those tested, and a month’s IRCA is the mean over its samples (articles 13 and 14). That is why 0 means every test passed and 100 means every test failed.








WarningCommon pitfall



The IRCA in this part’s data is not the national figure. The open table it comes from (INS, datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3) holds the utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA: samples from systems run by a water utility. A check on 2026-10-30, recorded in the data’s README (caveat 1), found that its 2023 department totals match INCA’s utility column in 30 of 30 departments and the overall figure in only 5. Self-supplied systems, which have no utility, score far worse (43.7 against 7.4 in 2023), so the data understate the risk wherever people rely on self-supply, and say nothing where no utility exists. Label the variable “utility-supplied IRCA” everywhere it appears.

title: 9  The Question, the Data and the Rules
section: 9.3 Saber 11, and what an average covers
text:
9.3 Saber 11, and what an average covers
One of the outcomes the analysis compares (Section 9.5) is an education measure, Saber 11, the national exam taken by students finishing upper secondary school, set by ICFES. It has five tests: critical reading, mathematics, social studies and citizenship, natural sciences, and English. The global score is five times the weighted mean of the five test scores (each 0 to 100; English counts once, the others three times), from 0 to 500, and its mean was fixed at 250 in the first sitting in 2014, so that years can be compared (ICFES, Guía de orientación Saber 11.° 2017-1, pp. 101 and 104, checked 2026-10-30).
Both measures are averages, and an average describes only what it averaged over. IRCA is an average over the water samples taken, so a system that is never sampled has no IRCA at all. The Saber 11 mean in the data is an average over the students who sat the exam at schools in that municipality and zone, so it says nothing about students who had left school. Keep both facts in mind in every comparison that follows.

title: 9  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
9.4 Where the data come from
Most of the data are Colombian open data from five public bodies; rainfall and altitude come from two scientific datasets. All are joined on one code: joining two tables matches their rows by a column they share, here the code that DANE’s list of municipalities, DIVIPOLA (División Político-Administrativa), gives each municipality. It has five digits, two for the department and three for the municipality, so 05001 is Medellín, in Antioquia (05). The sources are:

INS (Instituto Nacional de Salud): the IRCA surveillance results.
DANE (the national statistics office): the list of municipalities and their codes, population projections and municipal boundaries.
ICFES and MEN (the Ministry of Education): Saber 11 results and school dropout rates.
DNP (the National Planning Department), through its TerriData portal: water and sewer coverage, multidimensional poverty, municipal performance, transfers for water and infant mortality.
CHIRPS (the Climate Hazards Center’s rainfall data) and NASA SRTM (elevation data): rainfall, and a derived altitude for each head town.

They arrive as three files, in examples/water/data/ in the workshop repository: water_municipal.csv (the analysis table), municipios.geojson (municipal boundaries for maps) and README.md, which documents every column, source, licence and caveat (Appendix G lists them all).
One row is one municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year, a zone-year: this is the analysis’s unit. The urban zone is the head town (cabecera municipal); the rural zone is the smaller settlements and the dispersed countryside. The table covers every one of DANE’s 1,122 DIVIPOLA entries, both zones and every year from 2010 to 2023: 31,416 rows and 29 columns. Of those entries, 1,103 are municipalities; the rest are the island of San Andrés and areas that are not municipalities, whose rows are mostly empty. Because every municipality has all its rows, a gap is an empty cell, never a missing row.


Pause and think


A municipality’s rural zone has no IRCA in one year. Was its water safe that year?



Answer

The data cannot say. IRCA averages the samples taken from utility-run systems, so an empty cell means no utility-supplied score was published: the zone may not have been sampled, or its water may be self-supplied, which nationally scores far worse (Table 9.1). An empty IRCA is unknown, never safe and never zero.








TipIn practice



Read data/README.md before you analyse anything, and ask the agent to read it first too. Its caveats are the analysis’s traps, written down: the IRCA source above; department capitals that have no urban and rural split for coverage; a fiscal index whose method changes in 2020; infant mortality whose method changes in 2017; Saber 11 only in some years; pesos that are not adjusted for inflation. Each one turns up in the chapters that follow.

title: 9  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
9.5 Features and outcomes
The most important design decision in Part III is which variables define the kinds and which only describe them.
The features, which the clustering sees, are nine variables about water, people and place, and government. The outcomes, which the analysis only compares, are infant mortality, the Saber 11 score and school dropout (Table 9.2, Table 9.3). Three features need a word. The multidimensional poverty index (IPM, Índice de Pobreza Multidimensional) is the share of a zone’s people who are poor in several respects at once, from the 2018 census. MDM (Medición de Desempeño Municipal) is DNP’s score of a municipality’s management and results. And SGP (Sistema General de Participaciones) is the system of national transfers to municipalities: the feature is its allocation for drinking water and basic sanitation, per person.
Both tables give each variable’s level and years, computed from the municipalities’ rows. A zone variable differs between a municipality’s urban and rural rows; a municipal one is the same on both; “one value” is repeated every year. Meanings, units and sources come from data/README.md (TerriData is DNP’s data portal).

The last column matters in every chapter that follows. A zone variable is measured separately for a municipality’s urban and rural zones; a municipal one is a single value for the whole municipality, repeated on both of its rows. Five of the nine features are municipal, so a municipality’s two rows in a year differ only in the other four. And a municipal outcome, such as infant mortality, must be counted once per municipality, not once per row.
Never cluster on an outcome. If infant mortality helped define the kinds, the kinds would differ in infant mortality by construction, and the comparison in the second question would be circular: it would find exactly what was put in. Keeping outcomes out of the clustering is what lets the comparison say anything at all.


Pause and think


A colleague wants infant mortality added to the features, “since it is what we care about”. What would the comparison of outcomes between the kinds then show?



Answer

That the kinds differ in infant mortality, which would be true by construction: the algorithm would have grouped zones partly by that very number. The comparison would find what was put in. Infant mortality stays an outcome, compared only after the kinds are found.








NoteWhy this works



The same care is why the fiscal index idf is not a feature, although it describes municipal government: its method changes in 2020 (idf to 2020, idf_new from 2020, on different scales), so it cannot form one series across the years the analysis uses. A variable that changes meaning partway through would create kinds that are artefacts of the change.

title: 9  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
9.6 Compute once, publish many
Part II computed in each page. Part III computes once (Figure 9.1). One importable script, scripts/analysis.py, does all of the computation and writes its results to outputs/; every page only reads those results and draws them. A design choice, such as how many rows to drop for missing values, is made in one place, and every output follows at the next render.






Figure 9.1: Compute once, publish many. One script turns the data into results once; every publication reads the results, and none recomputes them.



The split solves two problems from Part II. A slow computation no longer slows every page and every format, because it runs once. And no page can disagree with another, because there is only one result to disagree with. Results are saved as Parquet, which keeps column types (a code such as 05001 stays text instead of becoming the number 5001), and as CSV where people will open them.
This book follows the same rule: every number in Part III is computed when the book is built, by importing the finished project’s analysis.py and running it in memory.

section: 9.7 Setting up the project: data, rules and environment
text:
9.7 Setting up the project: data, rules and environment
The project lives beside the London one, so that the workshop repository’s checkpoints are always at ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/:
~
├── quarto-workshop/
├── london-guide/
└── water-quality/
In your home folder (~), quarto-workshop/ is the clone from Chapter 3, london-guide/ is Part II’s project and water-quality/ is this part’s.
Quit the London guide’s agent first (/exit), so that the new one starts in the new folder and takes it as its world (Section 2.4). Then make the folder, start its history as you did for the guide (Section 5.2), start the agent in it, and copy the data:



You do

cd ~
mkdir -p water-quality
cd water-quality
git init -b main
claude



Ask your coding agent

Copy ../quarto-workshop/examples/water/data into this folder as data/, then list the files in data/ with their sizes.



Expect it to run

copies the folder · lists README.md, municipios.geojson and water_municipal.csv with their sizes


The data sit outside the new folder, in ../quarto-workshop/, so the agent asks before it reads there: approve it, as for the London guide (Section 5.2).
Then write the rules. If you have never clustered anything, the worry is fair: the agent can write an analysis that runs, renders and is wrong. You do not guard against that by writing the code yourself. You guard against it by checking, and a check needs something to check against.



Ask your coding agent

Read data/README.md, then create AGENTS.md for this project. Scope: describe Colombian municipal water safety and infant mortality from data/ only. Rules: keep data/ unchanged, label IRCA as utility-supplied (prestadores), never cluster on outcomes, and say comparisons are descriptive, not causal. Show me the file.



Expect it to run

reads data/README.md · writes AGENTS.md: scope, rules, the data’s caveats



You do

approve · check that AGENTS.md holds all four rules


The four rules are this chapter in miniature: the inputs are evidence and stay unchanged; the IRCA is labelled for what it is; outcomes describe the clusters but never define them; and comparisons between clusters do not establish causal effects of water safety. Asking the agent to read the README first lets it add the data’s caveats to the rules itself.



Ask your coding agent

Give this project its own Python environment with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas numpy matplotlib plotly scikit-learn pyarrow itables tabulate`. Run `quarto` and `python` through `uv run`, and add that rule to AGENTS.md. Create a .gitignore for .venv/, .quarto/, _site/, outputs/ and *_files/. Show me the Python line of `uv run quarto check jupyter`.



Expect it to run

uv init --bare · uv add … · writes pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .venv/ · adds the uv run rule to AGENTS.md · writes .gitignore · uv run quarto check jupyter


You should see a Python whose path runs through this folder’s .venv, as for the London guide (Section 5.10). The recipe is the London guide’s, with the analysis’s packages added: scikit-learn for k-means, pyarrow for Parquet, itables for the dashboard’s searchable table and tabulate for tables written as Markdown. Packages shared with Part II come from uv’s cache.






ImportantTry it



Copy the data, write the rules and create the environment.

You’re done when AGENTS.md states the analysis’s scope and its rules, uv run quarto check jupyter shows this project’s .venv Python, and the first commit holds them. Open a new terminal tab and run cd ~/water-quality first (a tab left in ~/london-guide would commit there); then git status should list .gitignore, AGENTS.md, data/, pyproject.toml and uv.lock, and not .venv/; then git add . and git commit -m "Data, rules and environment" record them, and git status says the working tree is clean.

There is no catch-up here. If you get stuck, the one at the end of Chapter 10 restores this chapter’s work and the next chapter’s together.

title: 9  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
Summary


First find kinds of municipal zone from water, services and context; then compare outcomes between them.
The data’s IRCA is utility-supplied, so it understates risk wherever people rely on self-supply.
One row is a zone-year and every row exists, so an empty cell means unmeasured, never safe.
Zone variables differ between a municipality’s two rows; municipal ones are counted once.
Features define the kinds and outcomes only describe them: clustering on an outcome is circular.
One script computes every result once, and AGENTS.md holds the limits for the agent.


What the rules cannot say is what the table holds: where it is empty, and where a series moves for reasons unrelated to water. That is the next chapter’s question.
