title: 10  Look Before You Model
text:
10.1 What exploring is for
Before any model, look at the data. Exploring tells you what a model will and will not be able to see: which columns are sparse, which zones are never measured, and whether a series changes level for reasons that have nothing to do with the thing it measures. None of that shows up as an error. A clustering algorithm will happily group rows that have been made comparable only by filling their gaps, and a chart of a series whose method changed will draw a trend that is not there.
The water data hold two such surprises that a chart can show, and several more that show only up close, in one place. For those, this chapter meets Tunja, the municipality the rest of the part follows.
Four questions are worth answering before modelling any table, and this chapter asks each of them of the water data:
The answers decide what the analysis can claim. If one group is mostly missing, conclusions about it rest on the minority that was measured, and that minority may not be typical.
crumbs: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications

title: 10  Look Before You Model
text:
How big is it? Rows and columns, and what one row is.
What is missing, and where? Missingness by column and by group (here, by zone).
How are the key values distributed? For IRCA, the count of rows in each risk band.
How do they move over time? For IRCA, its median (the middle value, with half the rows below it) by year and zone.
crumbs: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications

title: 10  Look Before You Model
text:
10.2 Rural: less data, more risk








Figure 10.1: All rows, 2010–2023, San Andrés and the non-municipalised areas included, by zone: no IRCA reported (hatched) and the Resolución 2115 risk band of the rest. Utility-supplied IRCA, INS open data (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3).





Side by side, Figure 10.1 shows all 31,416 rows. 53% of rural rows have no IRCA at all, against 14% of urban rows, because many rural systems are never sampled, or are not run by a utility and so fall outside the utility-supplied table. Among the rural rows that do have a value, 51% fall in the high or unfit bands, against 12% of urban rows. Those shares pool all fourteen years. In 2023 alone they were 28% and 6%, the figures that open Part III, after the falls in rural IRCA that Figure 10.2 shows below.
The two facts compound, in the worst direction: the zones whose scores are worse are also the ones least often scored. The gaps are not random. They depend on zone, which the data record, and perhaps on the risk itself, which they do not: statisticians call the second kind missing not at random, and no fill can repair it. Any analysis that drops the rows without IRCA, as Part III’s must, describes sampled rural systems only, and should say so.


Pause and think


Suppose every missing rural IRCA were filled with the median of the scored rural rows. Would rural water then look safer or riskier than it really is?



Answer

Probably safer, though nobody can check. Many unscored systems are ones no utility runs, and self-supplied systems score far worse nationally (Table 9.1), so the fill would turn “unknown, and likely worse” into “typical”. That is why the analysis drops these rows instead (Section 11.1).










Figure 10.2: Median utility-supplied IRCA by year and zone, 2010–2023, over the rows that report one.





The fourth question matters, as Figure 10.2 shows. The rural median drops sharply in 2016 and again in 2020. That could be an improvement in rural water, or a change in which systems were sampled; the data’s README warns that the 2020 drop may reflect sampling, and the open data cannot tell the two apart. An analysis that compares years should not read the drop as progress without evidence from outside the table.
The rural median also ends far below the national rural figure in Table 9.1: 13.4 in 2023, in the low band, against INCA’s 36.5. Two things explain the gap. The table holds only utility-run systems (Section 9.2), and a median of zones is the middle zone, which the worst zones do not pull up, and which is not weighted by how many people drink the water.

title: 10  Look Before You Model
text:
10.3 One municipality to follow: Tunja
Aggregates hide the details that make a variable trustworthy or not, so from here on this part follows one municipality through every step. Tunja, the capital of Boyacá department, is a good case for three reasons in its rows. As a department capital, it carries the coverage caveat that every capital does. Unlike most municipalities, it has an IRCA for both zones in every year: only 117 of the 1,103 municipalities have one for their rural zone in all fourteen years, so the analysis will never lose Tunja for want of a score. And its two zones differ: its rural water scored in the high-risk band every year from 2010 to 2014, while its urban water never scored above 11.9.
Tunja has 28 rows, two zones over fourteen years. Zone variables, such as IRCA, differ between its two rows in a year; municipal ones, such as rainfall and infant mortality, repeat on both (Table 9.2), so the explorer and every summary count them once. Looking at the rows one variable at a time shows several of the README’s caveats in a single place (Figure 10.3).

Pause and think


Tunja’s infant mortality drops in 2017. Is that progress?



Answer

Not on this evidence. The series changes method that year, from what look like modelled estimates to observed rates (the data’s README, caveat 8), so the drop may be the change itself, and the table cannot tell. A series like this is compared only within one method.


Five things are worth finding (Table 10.1). Because Tunja is a department capital, its coverage has no urban and rural split, so the explorer uses the municipality’s total. That total is reported as exactly 0 in 2021, which beside its neighbouring years probably means “not reported” rather than “no service”; such points are drawn hollow. The fiscal index idf ends in 2020 and idf_new starts there, on a different scale, so the two must never be joined into one line.

title: 10  Look Before You Model
text:
10.4 The first page: explore.qmd



Ask your coding agent

title: 10  Look Before You Model
text:
Summary


Before modelling, ask a table’s size, what is missing and where, how key values are distributed and how they move over time.
Rural rows are mostly without IRCA and, where scored, riskier, so results describe sampled systems only.
The gaps may depend on the risk itself, so filling them would invent water quality nobody measured.
A jump in a series can be a change of method or sampling, which the table cannot tell from a real change.
Keep the zones apart, count municipal variables once, and read codes as text.


Seeing the gaps is not the same as deciding what to do about them: the next chapter decides which rows and numbers the clustering will see, and counts what each decision costs.

title: 11  From Table to Features
text:
11.1 Four steps from table to features
A clustering algorithm does not read a table the way a person does. It sees numbers, measures distances between rows, and groups rows that are close. Everything about the result depends on which rows it sees, which numbers, on what scale, and what it is given where a number is missing. Preparation is the name for those decisions, and they shape the clusters as much as the algorithm does. Four of them stand between the water table and the clustering, and each has a price, counted in rows and in guesses.
1. Select. Keep the years 2016 to 2023, because the municipal performance index (MDM), one of the features, starts in 2016. Keep municipalities only: San Andrés has none of DNP’s values and the non-municipalised areas are nearly empty. Keep only rows with an IRCA value, since water safety is the point of the analysis. IRCA is the one feature never filled: its gaps may depend on the risk itself (Section 10.2), so a filled score would be a guess at exactly what the analysis is about.
2. Transform. Transfers for water per person (SGP) are heavily skewed: most are moderate and a few are very large. So the analysis uses their logarithm, which measures ratios rather than differences: every doubling of a transfer adds the same amount, and the few very large transfers no longer sit far from all the rest. Department capitals have no urban and rural split for coverage, so their urban rows use the municipality’s total coverage instead, and a flag column records that they did. The total suits the urban row because most of a capital’s people live in its head town (88% in the median capital in 2023). It would not suit the rural row: in other municipalities the total exceeds the rural figure in 86% of rural zone-years, so the capitals’ rural rows are filled in the next step instead.
3. Impute, with flags. To impute is to fill a missing value with an estimate. Drop rows missing more than two of the nine features. Fill the remaining gaps with the median of the same year and zone, and add a flag column, such as water_coverage_imputed, that marks every filled value. The median, because a few extreme values cannot pull it; the same year and zone, because rural and urban zones differ (Section 10.2) and years shift.
4. Standardise within each year. Replace each feature by its z-score within its year:
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}_{\text{year}}}{s_{\text{year}}}\]
where \(x\) is a row’s value of the feature, and \(\bar{x}_{\text{year}}\) and \(s_{\text{year}}\) are the feature’s mean and standard deviation over that year’s kept rows. The standard deviation is, roughly, the typical distance of a value from the mean, in the feature’s own unit. A z-score of +1 means one standard deviation above that year’s average; a z-score has no unit.
crumbs: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications

title: 11  From Table to Features
text:
NoteWhy this works



Why within each year rather than over all years? Two reasons. SGP is in nominal pesos, not adjusted for inflation, so its values drift upwards over time for reasons unrelated to any municipality. And other features shift as a whole from year to year, as rural IRCA does in Figure 10.2. Standardising within each year removes both shifts. A zone is compared only with that year’s other zones, so a nationwide shift, real or an artefact of sampling, does not move it between clusters, and one clustering over all years gives labels that mean the same relative position in every year. The price is that a real improvement shared by every zone is invisible to the clusters too.








WarningCommon pitfall



Every fill is a guess, and an unflagged guess becomes indistinguishable from data. The flags make the guesses countable and checkable later: a cluster made mostly of imputed values would be a cluster of medians, not of places. The data’s README says it of the capitals’ coverage (“Do not do it silently”), and the project’s AGENTS.md, written from that README, carries its caveats to the agent: nothing is filled silently.

The kept rows cover 1,090 municipalities. 653 rows have at least one imputed value, and 214 urban rows of department capitals took the municipal total for coverage.
Almost all the loss is the first drop: rows without an IRCA value, most of them rural zones that are never sampled or have no utility (Section 10.2). So the rural cluster that appears in the next chapter describes sampled rural systems only. The imputed values are coverage values: the rural rows of capitals, and municipalities whose split is missing in some years.
Tunja shows both treatments of a capital, and loses none of its 16 zone-years from 2016 to 2023. Its 8 urban rows took the municipal total for coverage, flagged in water_coverage_from_total, and its 8 rural rows took the rural median of their year, flagged in water_coverage_imputed. The check also turns up something the flags do not mark: the total that the urban row for 2021 took is the 0 that the Tunja section (Section 10.3) flagged as probably “not reported”. The analysis keeps it as published, as the data’s README does. Treating such zeros as missing would be a defensible change, but one to make in prepare() and report, never silently.


Pause and think


Suppose prepare() treated Tunja’s reported 0 as missing. What would happen to that row, and to its coverage z-score?



Answer

With no total to take, the urban row for 2021 would go to step 3 and be filled with that year’s urban median, flagged in water_coverage_imputed. Its coverage z-score would move from −1.9, far below the year’s average, to about +0.8, an ordinary head town’s: an unflagged error would become a flagged guess.

title: 11  From Table to Features
text:
11.3 Why scale?
k-means groups rows by straight-line, or Euclidean, distance: the square root of the sum of squared differences across the features. A feature’s share of the expected squared distance, between two rows picked at random, is proportional to its variance, the square of its standard deviation. In raw units, the features measured in thousands, such as millimetres of rain and metres of altitude, dwarf those measured from 0 to 100 (Figure 11.1).








Figure 11.1: Each feature’s share of the squared distance between rows, in raw units (SGP as its logarithm) and after z-scores. Kept rows, 2016–2023.





Unscaled, rainfall and altitude together would make up 99.8% of the distance, so the clusters would be climate zones and the water variables would hardly count. After z-scores, every feature has variance 1 and contributes the same share, about 11%. The log of SGP matters too. In raw pesos, its variance would be about 3,100 times rainfall’s, so it would dominate even rainfall; after z-scores, the log keeps a few very large transfers from sitting far from every other row, cutting the largest z-score from 7.3 to 4.3.
Two real rows show what scaling changes (Table 11.2): the urban zones of Tunja, high in the Andes, and Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast, in 2023. Both are capitals, so their coverage is each municipality’s total. In raw units, their difference in altitude makes up 98% of their squared distance, and a 43-point gap in piped-water coverage makes up less than 1%. In z-scores, coverage counts for 16%, and altitude still leads, at 68%, because height is where the two towns really differ most. Scaling does not make every difference count the same; it stops the units from deciding.



Table 11.2: The urban zones of Tunja and Cartagena in the last year of the analysis: how far apart they are on each feature, in raw units (coverage, poverty, IRCA and MDM in points), and each feature’s share of their squared distance, in raw units and in z-scores. Pause and think


Suppose rainfall were recorded in metres instead of millimetres. What would happen to its share of the distance, unscaled and after z-scores?



Answer

Unscaled, its values would shrink a thousandfold and its variance a millionfold, so its share would all but vanish and altitude would dominate alone. After z-scores nothing would change: the unit cancels, because a z-score divides a distance from the mean by the standard deviation, both in the same unit.








TipIn practice



Equal weight is itself a choice, not a neutral default. Nine z-scored features count equally, so the three safety-and-coverage variables count for 33% of the distance and context for the rest. Equal weight per feature is not equal weight per idea, either: water and sewer coverage are strongly correlated (r = 0.77 over the kept rows, where the correlation coefficient r runs from −1 to 1 and 1 would mean they rise together along a straight line), so what they share counts twice. If water safety should weigh more, that is a decision to make explicitly and report, not to leave to the units the data happened to come in.

Two prompts write the four steps into the project’s script. The first selects and transforms:

The build script writes it from the DIVIPOLA codes, where each capital is numbered 001, except that Cundinamarca’s capital is Bogotá, so 25001 (Agua de Dios) is not one: a detail the agent can only get right by reading the data’s README.
The second imputes and standardises, and saves the result:



Ask your coding agent

The finished project’s version of the imputation and scaling, slightly trimmed, shows how little code each decision takes once it is clear:

title: 12  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
12.1 k-means in four steps
The water data now have 11,235 prepared rows, each described by nine z-scores. Nobody can read that many rows. Clustering turns them into a few kinds that a person can name, compare and act on: these municipal zones are like each other, and unlike those. An official can ask which kinds need which help; a council can see which kind its own zones belong to. Clustering needs no labels, so it is a first look at data nobody has categorised, and an odd cluster can point to a data error or a special case. What it cannot do is explain: clusters describe, they do not show causes.
If the mathematics sounds daunting, it need not be. The algorithm is simple enough to watch step by step, and the judgement it needs, how many kinds to look for, is a decision you can write down and check before seeing the answer.
k-means needs one number up front: \(k\), how many clusters to find. It makes one start, then repeats two moves until they change nothing:
Neither move ever raises the inertia, the sum of squared distances from each point to its centre,
\[\text{inertia} = \sum_{i} \lVert x_i - c_{\ell(i)} \rVert^2 ,\]
where \(x_i\) is point \(i\) (for the water data, a row’s nine z-scores), \(c_{\ell(i)}\) is the centre it is assigned to, and \(\lVert x_i - c_{\ell(i)} \rVert\) is the straight-line distance between them (Section 11.3). On z-scores, inertia is in squared standard deviations, a unit with no everyday meaning, so only its changes matter. There are only finitely many ways to group the points, so the algorithm always stops. It does not always stop at the best answer: a bad start can trap it in a worse grouping. Figure 12.1 shows the algorithm on 560 synthetic points in three groups, which are toy data made up for the illustration, not the water data.
Figure 12.2: The same algorithm on the toy points, flattened to two of their three dimensions: the random start, the first assignment, an assignment halfway, and the stable result.
Different starts can end in different groupings, so the real analysis runs k-means from 20 starts (scikit-learn’s n_init) and keeps the one with the lowest inertia. The starts are random, but repeatable: a fixed random seed, the number that starts the computer’s random-number generator, makes them the same on every run, so your project, the deck and this book all get the same clusters.

text:
Drop \(k\) centres at \(k\) randomly chosen data points.
Assign every point to its nearest centre.
Move each centre to the mean of the points assigned to it.
Repeat 2 and 3 until nothing changes.







● point◉ centre━ its path⏸ fix123456789101112start 1start 2start 3This 3-D view needs WebGL. The four steps are listed above.


1. drop 3 centres at random points


Figure 12.1: k-means on synthetic toy points. The numbered buttons step through the algorithm and “fix” stops the autoplay; “start 1” to “start 3” pick one of three random starts, of which two reach the best grouping and one gets stuck. Drag to turn.











NoteWhy this works



The real starts are not dropped at random, as in the toy. scikit-learn’s default, k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii, 2007), picks the first centre at random from the data and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centre already chosen. That spreads the centres out and makes a stuck start less likely; scikit-learn uses a greedy variant that draws several candidates at each step and keeps the best.

12  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means

title: 12  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
12.2 Choosing k
k is a hyperparameter: a setting the algorithm cannot learn from its own objective, because inertia always falls as k grows, down to zero when every point is its own cluster. So the analysis fits k-means for k from 2 to 8 and reads two measures (Figure 12.3). The first is where inertia stops falling much, the elbow. The second, the silhouette, scores from −1 to 1 how much closer each point is to its own cluster than to the next one, averaged over the points. It needs every distance between points, so it is computed on a fixed sample of 5,000 rows, which keeps it fast.








Figure 12.3: Choosing k: inertia and silhouette for k = 2 to 8, fitted on all kept rows. The chosen k is marked.





The rule, written into choose_k() in the analysis script, has three parts, and Table 12.1 applies it row by row:

k = 2 is excluded. Two clusters mostly split urban from rural rows, which we knew already: they match the zone for 86% of rows. The script measures this with the adjusted Rand index (ARI), which scores how far two groupings agree beyond what chance would give: 1 means identical, 0 no better than chance. Here it is 0.50.
The elbow: take the smallest k from 3 up after which one more cluster cuts inertia by less than 10%. Here that is k = 4: a fifth cluster cuts inertia by only 7%.
The silhouette check: k’s silhouette must be within 0.01 of the best for k ≥ 3. At k = 4 it is 0.195. The check rules out only k = 8 here.

The elbow is marginal. The fourth cluster itself cuts inertia by 10.8% (the row for k = 3), only just above the 10% threshold, so a threshold of 11% would pick k = 3 instead. And the four clusters account for 41% of the spread in the data, one minus the ratio of their inertia to that of a single cluster; the rest is difference within the kinds.
Two more checks follow the fit. Stability: refits from 5 other seeds agree, with an adjusted Rand index of at least 0.998, so the result does not depend on the start. That says nothing about other data, features or k; refitting on rows drawn again at random (a bootstrap), or leaving out one year at a time, would test that. Ordering: clusters are numbered by their centre’s IRCA, from lowest to highest, so a re-run keeps the same numbers and colours.






WarningCommon pitfall



A silhouette near 0.2 is low. In the subjective reading Rousseeuw and colleagues propose, a best average silhouette of 0.25 or less means that “no substantial structure has been found” (Struyf, Hubert and Rousseeuw, 1997, Table 2), and the best here, at any k, is 0.24. The kinds overlap: they summarise a continuum rather than separate islands of data. So treat k as a judgement call, and do not force a number of clusters to make a nicer story. Writing the rule down before seeing the result is what keeps such a choice honest; choose_k() at least makes the rule explicit, so anyone can check it and see how close the call was.




Pause and think


An official reads the report and asks: “So Colombia has four kinds of municipal zone?” What do you answer?



Answer

That four is a useful summary, not a discovery. A written rule chose it by a narrow margin, and a threshold one percentage point higher picks three; the low silhouette says the kinds overlap. The clusters describe typical combinations of water, services and context, and a zone near the edge of one could as well sit in the next.

title: 12  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
12.3 A picture of the clusters
Nine dimensions cannot be drawn. Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions in which the data vary most and projects the rows onto them. Each direction, a principal component, is a weighted sum of the nine z-scores, and its weights, called loadings, say what it measures. Figure 12.4 uses the first two components, which keep 30% and 21% of the variance.








Figure 12.4: Each dot is a zone-year on the first two principal components of the nine z-scored features, coloured and shaped by cluster. PCA is only for the picture: k-means used all nine features.





Overlaps in the picture can be separations in the dimensions it leaves out. Adding a third component, which keeps another 16% of the variance, shows how much (Figure 12.5). On two components, on average 78% of a zone-year’s 15 nearest neighbours are in its own cluster; on three, 94%. The third component rises with altitude and falls with rainfall, its two largest loadings. Cluster 3, the most mixed in two dimensions, sits below the others along it: it is the lowest and wettest of the kinds.

Cluster 2’s urban zones stand highest, with a median altitude of 1,766 m, and 56% of them are in the region Centro Oriente (DANE’s regional grouping). Cluster 3’s stand lowest, at 130 m, and 53% of them are in Caribe. This shows where the kinds are, not why they differ. Tunja’s head town stands at 2,695 m, and all 16 of its zone-years, urban and rural, fall in cluster 1.
The map draws urban zones only, one column per municipality, because the altitude is the head town’s. So it shows little of cluster 4, whose zone-years are 91% rural. Its few urban columns stand low, at a median of 159 m, but the median head-town altitude of its rural zone-years is 1,475 m, so the map says little about where that kind is found.

section: 12.5 Use the model, or build it
text:
12.5 Use the model, or build it
There are two routes through the modelling, and both end with the same outputs/ and the same pages:

Use it (the normal route): copy the finished analysis.py from this step’s checkpoint, run it, and spend your effort on checking what it chose and on the publications.
Build it (a challenge): give the agent the prompt below and have it write the clustering step itself.

This is a book about publishing, so using the finished model is the normal route, not a fallback. But a copied script is only as trustworthy as your reading of it, so the route has two prompts: one runs the script, the other makes the agent explain what it printed.



Ask your coding agent

Copy ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/07-water-cluster/scripts/analysis.py over scripts/analysis.py (keep mine as scripts/analysis-before-07.py), run it with `uv run python scripts/analysis.py`, and tell me k.



Expect it to run

copies the script, keeping yours · uv run python scripts/analysis.py · reports k = 4


Among its output, the script prints the table behind Figure 12.3 and then its verdict in one line, which on this book’s data reads:

k = 4: the next cluster cuts inertia by only 7% (< 10%), and its silhouette 0.195 is within 0.01 of the best k >= 3 (0.196).

Ask the agent to take that line apart:



Ask your coding agent

Explain what scripts/analysis.py printed about k: what `inertia`, `silhouette`, ari_vs_zone and inertia_drop mean for each k, and which test in choose_k() chose k. Quote the lines of choose_k() that decide it.



Expect it to run

reads the printed table and choose_k() · explains each column and the rule, quoting the code




Pause and think


While it explains: which test in choose_k() chose k, and which could only have ruled one out?



Answer

The elbow chose it: k = 4 is the smallest k from 3 up after which one more cluster cuts inertia by less than 10%. k = 2 is excluded before any test, and the silhouette check only vetoes: it rules out only k = 8 here. Check the agent’s explanation against this and Table 12.1: one that says the silhouette chose k has misread the rule.


To build it instead (optional):



Ask your coding agent

title: 12  Finding Kinds of Places: k-Means
text:
Summary


k-means assigns points to the nearest centre and moves centres to their points’ mean; it can stall, so it keeps the best of many seeded starts.
k is chosen by a rule written beforehand: exclude k = 2, take the elbow, let the silhouette veto.
The elbow is marginal and the silhouette low: the kinds summarise a continuum.
Agreement across seeds shows independence from the start, not from the data or features.
PCA and the map show where the kinds stand, not why, and the map leaves rural zone-years out.
Using the finished model is legitimate if you can explain what it chose.


The kinds so far are only numbers, from cluster 1, lowest centre IRCA, to cluster 4: the next chapter works out what sets each one apart, names it by a rule, and compares the outcomes the clustering never saw.

title: 13  Interpreting Clusters
text:
13.1 What sets each cluster apart
Cluster 4 is a number, and a number is hard to act on. “Rural, low-coverage, high-risk water” is a phrase an official can repeat and a council can argue over, and anyone can check it, provided a rule produced it rather than someone’s eye. The names carry most weight in the comparison the analysis was built for: infant mortality, exam scores and school dropout, which the clustering never saw, kind by kind. That comparison is where readers draw conclusions, so it is where honesty matters most, and it gets three views, because each hides something the others show.
A cluster’s profile is the mean of each feature over its rows, in z units (Section 11.1): +1 means one standard deviation above that year’s average across all kept rows (Figure 13.1). Read along a cluster’s line to describe it, and along a feature’s line to see which feature separates the clusters.
Figure 13.1: Cluster profiles in z units: standard deviations above (red) or below (blue) the year’s average. IRCA: utility-supplied. Altitude: derived SRTM point.
The highest-IRCA cluster, cluster 4, stands out on three things at once: piped-water coverage (−1.3 SD), poverty (+1.0 SD) and IRCA (+0.8 SD). Each cluster is such a combination, which is exactly what a single variable could not have found.

title: 13  Interpreting Clusters
text:
13.2 Name them by a rule
Names make clusters usable, and they also make them persuasive, so they need a rule that anyone can check. The analysis script’s name_rule() builds each name from three parts:

Setting, tested in this order: “Rural” if fewer than 40% of the cluster’s rows are urban zones; otherwise “Cities and large towns” if its rural share is 0.5 SD or more below average, “Lowland towns” if its altitude is 0.5 SD or more below, “Highland towns” if 0.5 SD or more above, and plain “Towns” if none of these holds.
Coverage: “low-coverage” if the cluster’s mean piped-water coverage is 0.5 SD or more below average.
Risk: the Resolución 2115 band of the cluster’s median utility-supplied IRCA, the middle value when its zone-years are sorted by IRCA.

Because the rule reads the profile, the names never depend on which number k-means happened to give a cluster. Two words in them need care. “Low-coverage” is a relative position, not an absolute one: the rural cluster’s mean coverage is 30%, low but not zero, so “unserved” would overstate it. And the risk word describes the cluster’s median, not every zone-year in it: individual zone-years can sit in any band, and a median close to a band’s edge can flip the word.






TipIn practice



Check every name against the heatmap and the profile table before you use it, and keep the rule beside the name in anything you publish. A name is a summary someone else will quote without the table. The thresholds, 40% and half a standard deviation, are choices too: a different one could change a name.




Pause and think


Tunja’s rural water scored in the high-risk band in its early years (Section 10.3). Before reading on, which cluster do you expect its rural zone to fall in, and what could put it somewhere else?



Answer

The rural cluster is the obvious guess. But k-means places a zone-year by all nine features at once, and several of them, such as the rural share and the altitude, belong to the municipality, so they are the same for both of Tunja’s zones. If those sit far from the rural cluster’s centre, they can outweigh the water.

title: 13  Interpreting Clusters
text:
13.3 Where Tunja lands
The cluster that holds all 16 of Tunja’s zone-years, urban and rural, now has a name: cluster 1 (cities and large towns), “Cities and large towns, no-risk water”. For the urban zone, it fits. For the rural zone, the label hides most of what Section 10.3 found. Its water scored in the high-risk band every year from 2010 to 2014, before the analysis’s window opens in 2016, and inside the window its utility-supplied IRCA is never in the no-risk band, and is in the medium band in three of the eight years.
Two things are at work. The risk word describes the cluster’s median, not each member, as Section 13.2 warned. And k-means puts each zone-year in the cluster whose centre is nearest over all nine features at once (Section 12.1), adding up the squared differences feature by feature. Table 13.2 splits that sum in two. On its own four features, IRCA, piped-water coverage, sewer coverage and poverty, Tunja’s rural zone sits nearer the centre of cluster 4 (rural), and two of those, the coverages, are fills (Section 11.2). The other five, rural share, altitude, rainfall, municipal performance and water transfers, are the municipality’s, the same for both zones. On those it sits far nearer cluster 1’s centre, by enough to outweigh the first four. The other two centres are farther still.

title: 13  Interpreting Clusters
text:
13.4 Outcomes by cluster
Now the outcomes, which the clustering never used (Figure 13.2). Each line is a cluster’s median within each year, so a shift that moves every kind in one year cannot pass for a difference between kinds. Infant mortality is compared only in 2017–2019 and 2021–2023: its method changes in 2017, and 2020 looks like another source (the data’s README, caveat 8).








Figure 13.2: Median outcome by cluster and year: infant mortality in 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 only, Saber 11 in its published years. Descriptive only: not causal effects of water safety.





Gaps in the lines are years with no comparable value, drawn as gaps rather than joined across. Infant mortality and dropout are measured for a whole municipality but repeated on both zone rows, so they are counted once per municipality in each cluster and year: for these two the unit is the municipality-year, one municipality in one year, while the features and Saber 11 stay per zone-year.
Figure 13.3 puts the outcomes on the features’ scale: each outcome standardised within its year, a cell being the cluster’s mean z, with the mean itself in brackets.








Figure 13.3: Cluster mean outcome in z units, with the mean in brackets. Red is above average: better for Saber 11, worse for the other two. Descriptive only.





The paleness is the finding. No cluster’s mean outcome is more than 0.65 standard deviations from the average, against 1.32 for the features that formed them: the kinds differ less in outcomes than in what defines them. Part of this is by design: k-means chose the clusters to separate the features, so they should differ more on those than on anything else. Within that: the lowest recorded infant mortality is in cluster 1 (cities and large towns) and the highest in cluster 2 (highland towns); the best Saber 11 scores are in cluster 1 (cities and large towns); and the lowest dropout is in cluster 2 (highland towns).


Pause and think


Suppose unsafe water did harm infants’ health a great deal. Would you still expect the outcome heatmap to be paler than the features’?



Answer

Yes. k-means chose the clusters to separate the features, so they differ most on those by construction. The outcomes differ only as far as they go with the features, and small places’ noisy rates blur them further. Paleness alone is no evidence that water does not matter.


The highest recorded infant mortality is not in the cluster with the worst water, cluster 4 (rural). That is a good moment to slow down rather than to explain it away, because two things in the data push the same way. The first is small numbers. The rates of cluster 2 (highland towns) come from the smallest places of any kind, a median of 10,680 people per municipality-year, where a handful of deaths moves a rate a long way.
The second is what is missing. From 2017 the series looks like observed rates rather than modelled estimates, so a municipality where no infant died that year should show a rate of 0, yet no zero appears anywhere: a blank may be a recorded zero. 50% of this kind’s municipality-years are blank, against 32% of all clustered municipality-years. Leaving the blanks out drops what may be zeros, which raises small places’ averages most. That is selection on the outcome: whether a row is kept depends on the value being measured, so the rows kept are not typical. It may account for part of this kind’s place at the top. Small numbers, reporting and many other differences between the kinds all sit between a cluster’s water and its outcomes, and Chapter 14 takes that up directly.

title: 13  Interpreting Clusters
text:
13.5 Every variable, cluster by cluster
Means and medians hide overlap. Box plots show it: how each variable spreads within each cluster (Figure 13.4). Each box holds the middle half of a cluster’s values, with a solid line at the median and a dashed line at the mean, and its whiskers reach from the 5th to the 95th percentile, so they span the middle 90% of values. Features cover every zone-year 2016–2023; outcomes count in their years, municipal ones once per municipality.



IRCA, utility-supplied (0–100)Piped water coverage (%)Sewer coverage (%)Multidimensional poverty, 2018 (%)Rural share of populationAltitude of head town, derived SRTM point (m)Rainfall (mm/year)Municipal performance, MDMWater transfers per person (log SGP)Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births)Saber 11 mean score (0–500)School dropout, public schools (%)


Figure 13.4: Every feature and outcome, cluster by cluster: pick a variable. Boxes hold the middle half of each cluster’s values; whiskers the middle 90%.



The boxes make the overlap visible. Clusters differ sharply on the features that built them and overlap on the outcomes, and a gap between two clusters’ boxes is a description of the data, not an effect of water safety.
So Part III’s second question has an answer, and it is descriptive: infant mortality, exam scores and dropout do differ between the kinds of place, exam scores most, but by no more than 0.65 standard deviations in any cluster’s mean, and for every outcome the middle 90% of each kind’s values overlaps every other kind’s.

title: 13  Interpreting Clusters
text:
Summary


A cluster’s profile, its mean z-score on each feature, describes it as a combination of traits that no single variable could have found.
A written rule names each cluster from its profile (setting, relative coverage, median IRCA band), so anyone can check the name.
“Low-coverage” is relative and the risk word describes a median: Tunja’s rural zone, never no-risk inside the window, sits in a cluster named for no-risk water, carried there by what it shares with its urban zone.
The outcomes, never used to form the clusters, differ between the kinds less than the features do, partly by design, and their distributions overlap.
The highest recorded infant mortality is not where the water is worst, and small places and blank rates make that ranking fragile.
All of it is description: a gap between kinds is not an effect of water safety.


Yet a description like this invites a causal reading. Chapter 14 tests the link inside each kind of place, where poverty, rurality and coverage are more alike than across the country.

title: 14  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
14.1 Worse water, more infant deaths?
The analysis was built to ask whether places with worse water have worse outcomes, and the temptation, once there is a chart, is to read the answer as an effect: worse water causes more infant deaths. The data cannot support that sentence, and this chapter shows why, with the analysis’s own numbers.
One more comparison, the association between water safety and infant mortality within each kind of place, comes out weak in every kind, and in one as large as across all of them. But neither a strong association nor a weak one could settle the causal question here, and the reasons decide how the results must be written. That last part is not a formality: the sentence a reader quotes is the one you publish.
The measure is Spearman’s \(\rho\) (rho), which asks whether two variables rise and fall together in rank order: sort the places by each variable, and see whether the two orders agree. It runs from −1 (perfectly opposite) through 0 to +1 (perfectly together), where 0 means no monotonic relation, one in which a variable tends to rise as the other rises, though not necessarily along a straight line. Because it uses ranks, it is not thrown by extreme values, which matters with small municipalities’ noisy rates.
Across all municipality-years with both values in 2017–2019 and 2021–2023, \(\rho\) between utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality is +0.10 (n = 4,016, the number of municipality-years compared). Figure 14.1 shows what so weak an association looks like: a cloud with no visible slope.
Figure 14.1: Every municipality-year with both values, 2017–2019 and 2021–2023: utility-supplied IRCA, the mean of its scored zones, against infant mortality (log scale). Descriptive only.
A small positive association across all places could come from water, or from everything that differs between places with safe and unsafe water. The clusters offer a partial control, a way of comparing like with like: within a cluster, places are more alike in poverty, rurality, coverage and altitude than across the country, though far from equal (Table 14.1).

The first is range. The clusters were formed partly on IRCA, so inside clusters 1 and 2 it varies far less than across all places, and inside clusters 3 and 4 more. A narrower range tends to weaken a rank correlation, but that does not explain these four: \(\rho\) is largest in cluster 2, where IRCA varies little, and closest to zero in cluster 4, where it varies most.
The second is chance. To see how far \(\rho\) could move with another draw of places, the book redraws each set’s municipalities 1,000 times, with replacement and keeping each municipality’s years together, and recomputes \(\rho\) every time; the middle 95% of those values is the interval in Table 14.2. Each cluster’s interval reaches 0.06 to 0.08 either side of its \(\rho\), more than the gaps between neighbouring values, so these data cannot rank the four. The intervals for clusters 1, 3 and 4 include zero; the pooled one does not.
The third is the unit, because the unit follows the outcome. Infant mortality is measured for a whole municipality, so each municipality-year counts once, with the mean IRCA of its zones: all of them for the pooled figure, only those in the cluster for a cluster’s. That mean is unweighted, and it covers only the zones with a score: in 54% of the pooled municipality-years only one zone has one. So the IRCA beside a rate is one zone’s score or the plain mean of two, not what the average resident drinks.
It would be easy to read this as “water does not matter”. That reading is as unsupported as the first one.

title: 14  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
Pause and think


Within cluster 4, \(\rho\) is close to zero. Write the sentence a councillor might wrongly take from it, and an honest one.



Answer

Wrong: “In rural, low-coverage places, water quality makes no difference to infant deaths.” Honest: “Within the rural, low-coverage kind, municipality-years with higher utility-supplied IRCA did not have markedly higher recorded infant mortality (2017–2019 and 2021–2023). This does not show that water has no effect: under-reporting, blank rates and the mismatch between zone and municipality could hide one.”

title: 14  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
14.2 What else could explain it
Figure 14.3 draws the paths between water and infant mortality that the data cannot separate.






Figure 14.3: What else could explain it. The dashed arrow is the question; every other path can create an association without an effect, or hide an effect that exists.



Poverty and rurality are likely confounders. A confounder is a third variable that affects both the exposure, here water safety, and the outcome, here infant deaths, so the two move together even if one has no effect on the other. Poorer, more rural places tend to have less safe water and, for other reasons, more infant deaths, so they can produce an association between water and mortality with no effect of water at all. Health-service access carries part of that path: poorer and remoter places have less of it, and less access means more infant deaths.
Reporting quality is a problem of measurement, and it works the other way: places with weak birth and death registration record fewer infant deaths than occur, and if those are also the places with unsafe water, under-recording can hide a real effect. Blanks add a second problem. The series holds no zeros, so a blank rate may mean no deaths were recorded, and 32% of the clustered municipality-years in these years are blank. Leaving them out drops what may be recorded zeros, which raises small places’ averages most: a selection on the outcome itself (Section 13.4).
Then there is the ecological level. IRCA is measured for an urban or rural zone, infant mortality for the whole municipality. A pattern across places need not hold for the people in them: the infants who died need not be the ones drinking the worst water. Drawing individual conclusions from aggregate data is known as the ecological fallacy.
Tunja shows the mismatch in one place. In this check each of its six municipality-years counts once in cluster 1, with the mean IRCA of its two zones: in 2018, for example, 9.15, halfway between its urban water’s 0.5 and its rural water’s 17.8, a value neither zone had. The mean weighs the two zones equally, though at most 5% of Tunja’s people live in the rural one, and the infant mortality beside it is the whole municipality’s.
The clusters narrow some of these differences without removing them: within a cluster, places still differ in poverty and access (Table 14.1). And small municipalities produce extreme rates, which add noise that flattens any line.


Pause and think


Pick one of these paths. Could it hide a real effect, or create a fake one?



Answer

Poverty can create a fake one: if poorer places tend to have both less safe water and, for other reasons, more infant deaths, the two move together without water doing anything. Reporting quality can hide a real one: if unsafe-water places under-record deaths, their measured rates are too low, and a real effect looks smaller than it is. Only the first is a confounder; the second is a problem of measurement. Each path pushes one way, but several act at once and their sizes are unknown, so the net bias could go either way, which is why a correlation cannot settle the question.


Table 14.3 sorts the paths by the kind of problem each one is.

yes
yes


Noise
small places’ extreme rates
no
yes






A causal claim needs a design that handles these paths, not a better chart: for example, comparing places before and after a change in water treatment, against comparable places without the change, a design known as difference-in-differences. That is a different study, with different data; Hernán and Robins, in Further reading, cover such designs.

title: 14  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
14.3 Writing it honestly
Every output of this analysis says the same thing in the same words, because the project’s rules require it: comparisons between clusters are descriptive and do not establish a causal effect of water safety. In practice that means a few habits:

Describe what was compared, and over which rows: “within each cluster, 2017–2019 and 2021–2023, municipality-years with both values”.
Use verbs of association (“is higher in”, “varies with”), not of effect (“raises”, “reduces”, “leads to”).
Name the data’s limits beside the result: the utility-supplied IRCA, the method change in infant mortality, the zone-versus-municipality mismatch.
State what the result does not show, in one sentence a reader could quote.







WarningCommon pitfall



The causal sentence usually arrives in the last step: a slide title, a blog post’s headline, a summary for a council. Ask the agent to check every title and summary against the project’s rules, and read them yourself. “Utility-supplied water risk (IRCA) and infant mortality in Colombian municipalities” is a fair title; “How unsafe water kills infants” is not, however strongly you suspect it.

title: 14  Correlation Is Not Causation
text:
Summary


Spearman’s \(\rho\) measures whether two variables rise and fall together in rank order; across all places, utility-supplied IRCA and infant mortality are only weakly associated (\(\rho\) = +0.10).
Within the clusters, where places are more alike but far from equal, \(\rho\) runs from −0.04 to +0.10; range, chance and a different unit mean these values cannot be ranked or set beside the pooled one at face value.
Poverty and rurality are likely confounders that can create an association with no effect, while weak reporting and blank rates can hide a real one.
IRCA is measured per zone and infant mortality per municipality, and reading a pattern across places as one about the people in them is the ecological fallacy, as Tunja’s averaged zones show.
Neither a strong nor a weak association settles the causal question; that needs a design, such as before-and-after comparisons with comparable places.
Write about association: name the rows compared, use verbs of association, put the limits beside the result and say what it does not show.


Check every title and summary against that rule before it goes out. Chapter 15 takes the results, and those sentences, to the officials and the council, in every format they need.

Robinson, “Ecological correlations and the behavior of individuals”, American Sociological Review 15(3), 351–357 (1950), doi:10.2307/2087176, the classic account of the ecological fallacy; cited in examples/water/references.bib and checked against its publisher’s page (2026-11-01; pages from the paper’s 2009 reprint in the International Journal of Epidemiology, checked 2026-11-12).

title: 15  Publish Many
text:
15.1 The report, in Word and PDF
The officials will read the findings as a report, so they need it in the formats offices pass around: Word and PDF. The municipal council will see them on a screen in a meeting, and will look to the last slide for the conclusion. Both will look for where to act, and anyone else needs a link. So the project gets a report, slides and a website with a blog post, and not one of them may compute anything. Each reads outputs/, and that is what makes the chapter’s last test fair: change one setting in the analysis, predict what follows, rebuild, and check that every publication followed.
The prompt lists the report’s sections, and three of its choices carry the lessons of the last chapters. “Utility-supplied” is in the data section because Section 9.2 showed what the label hides. “Correlation ≠ causation” is a section, not a footnote. And the figures are matplotlib, because Word, PowerPoint and PDF cannot run the JavaScript that interactive Plotly charts need (Figure 15.1).
Every number in the text is inline code reading outputs/, never typed: a report that quotes the number of kept rows quotes whatever the analysis last computed. You should have report.html, report.docx and report.pdf, each with the heatmap, the outcomes and the within-cluster figure.

15.3 The report as an e-book (optional)



Ask your coding agent

In report.qmd, add an epub format (toc: true), set lang: en, and add ePub to the html `format-links`. Render report.qmd and check that report.epub contains the three figures and the sources.


An EPUB is a zipped set of web pages whose text reflows to fit the reader’s screen. Most e-book readers do not run JavaScript, so figures must be static images, which the report’s already are. lang: en records the book’s language (without it the file declares an unknown one), and toc: true adds a table of contents. Open the result in Apple Books on a Mac or in Calibre: it should hold the three figures and the sources.
The book in your hands is the same thing at a larger scale, and building it showed where a report-sized EPUB stops being enough. Parts and part pages disappear from a Quarto book’s EPUB; content marked for HTML also appears in EPUB unless it is marked for HTML with JavaScript; Quarto’s built-in callout and code colours vanish on a reader’s night theme; and an EPUB checker rejects markup that every browser accepts. Appendix H describes each problem and its fix.

title: 15  Publish Many
text:
15.4 A website with a blog
The publications become one website, with a blog post that tells the story in prose:
# _quarto.yml
project:
  type: website
1  execute-dir: project
2  pre-render: scripts/analysis.py
execute:
3  freeze: false

1

Every page, including a post in posts/…/, reads outputs/ and data/ from the project folder.

2

Quarto runs the analysis before every render, including a single page’s render: outputs/ is always fresh.

3

Every render re-executes every page, so every page shows the outputs just written.


# index.qmd
listing:
1  contents: posts

1

A listing turns every posts/*/index.qmd into an entry on the home page: a blog.





Ask your coding agent

Make this folder a Quarto website: _quarto.yml (execute-dir: project, `pre-render` scripts/analysis.py, freeze: false, render list, navbar), index.qmd listing posts/, and one post titled with the real k, e.g. "Four kinds of municipal zone". Render it; check the links.



You do

uv run quarto preview


The preview’s home page should list one post, whose title states the real k.
The post’s title states the number of clusters, so a change in the analysis could leave it wrong. The finished post protects itself with one line in its setup cell, assert k == 4, which fails the render if the analysis ever finds a different k (Figure 15.3). That line is a guard: it stops the render when a sentence’s words, not only its numbers, no longer match the data, because a loud failure is better than a quiet falsehood. This book guards its own sentences the same way. Section 13.4 says that the highest recorded infant mortality is not in the cluster with the worst water; if new data made that false, the book would stop building rather than print it.






Figure 15.3: The finished blog post, whose title states the number of clusters the analysis found. Rendered from examples/water/posts/four-kinds-of-municipal-zone/index.qmd.




15.4.1 Fresh or frozen?
freeze: false is the simple, safe setting: every render recomputes everything, so nothing can be stale. The cost is time, every render, for every page. freeze: auto is the alternative: Quarto stores each page’s results in _freeze/ and re-executes a page only when its own source changes.
The catch is in that last phrase. Quarto does not know which files a page reads, so a change to data/ or to outputs/ is not detected, and a frozen page keeps its old numbers. With freeze: auto you need a rule for throwing results away: delete _freeze/ (or render that one page directly, which ignores the cache) whenever the data or the analysis change.


Pause and think


Your site uses freeze: auto. You change MAX_MISSING in scripts/analysis.py and run uv run quarto render. Which pages show the new numbers?



Answer

Only pages whose own source changed, and you changed none. pre-render still rewrites outputs/, but every frozen page reuses its stored results, so the site shows the old numbers beside new output files until you delete _freeze/ or render each page on its own.








TipIn practice



Start with freeze: false and switch only when renders become slow enough to matter, and when you do, write the invalidation rule down where the next person will find it. This book uses freeze: auto, so the EPUB rebuilds quickly and reproducibly, and its rule is written in its configuration and README: after any change to the examples’ data or analysis, run make book-fresh, which deletes _freeze/ and re-executes every chapter.

15.5 Publish it



Ask your coding agent

If this folder is not yet a Git repository, run `git init -b main`. Check that .gitignore covers _site/, .quarto/, .venv/, outputs/ and *_files/. Replace README.md in this folder with a short one linking to https://<your-github-username>.github.io/water-quality/ and listing the files in the site's Downloads menu. Commit everything not ignored, then create a public GitHub repository named `water-quality` with gh and push to it. Set the repository's website to the same URL with `gh repo edit --homepage`. Show me the README and the website URL you set.



You do

approve gh · when it shows the website URL, in the second tab: uv run quarto publish gh-pages, then Enter at “Publish site … (Y/n)” · open the live address


The steps are Part II’s (Section 8.4). The repository has existed since Section 9.7, so the push carries the analysis’s whole history; its .gitignore also leaves out outputs/, which the pre-render step rebuilds. In a test run on 2026-11-01 the first publish took about two minutes, then GitHub Pages built the site in 20 to 35 seconds.
The data are public, and publishing them with the site is fine, provided the attributions travel with them. data/README.md lists each source’s terms: CC BY-SA 4.0 for DANE’s DIVIPOLA list and the INS, ICFES and MEN tables, CC BY 4.0 for TerriData and CHIRPS, citation terms for DANE’s population and boundaries, and none for SRTM. CC BY-SA adds a ShareAlike condition: anything built from those data, such as water_municipal.csv, must be shared under the same licence (CC BY-SA 4.0, checked 2026-11-12).


Pause and think


While it publishes: what is the difference between your folder and the live site?



Answer

The live site is the last _site/ you published. Changes in your folder, including re-rendered outputs, do not appear online until you publish again.








ImportantTry it



Build the report, the slides and the website, then publish.

You’re done when https://<your-github-username>.github.io/water-quality/ opens in a browser, with the report, the slides and the blog post.

text:
15.7 A dashboard and a white paper (optional)
A dashboard can show the clusters on a map. The first prompt builds a Plotly choropleth, a map whose areas are coloured by a value, here each municipality by its urban zone’s IRCA band, with a year slider; the second adds pages for the kinds, the outcomes and the method:



Ask your coding agent

Create dashboard.qmd (format: dashboard): a Plotly choropleth of the IRCA band of the "urban" rows of outputs/clusters.parquet on data/municipios.geojson (featureidkey="properties.divipola"), a year slider over their years (frames update only z), an itables table of outputs/clusters.parquet (maxBytes=0); end each chart cell with `fig`. Make it polished: IRCA bands in order from no risk to unfit, light to dark, with a legend, titled cards and readable labels. Add it to the navbar; render, check it looks good at laptop size and report errors.


When the map page looks right, the second prompt adds the other pages:



Ask your coding agent

Add Kinds, Outcomes and Method pages to dashboard.qmd from outputs/ only: a heatmap of cluster_profiles.csv's `z_` columns; outcomes_by_year.csv medians by `year` and `cluster`, and irca_infant.csv's ρ; k_selection.csv's inertia and silhouette by k. Use each cluster's `color` and axis units; say it is descriptive, not causal. Render; check each page at laptop size.








Figure 15.4: The finished dashboard’s map page. Rendered from examples/water/dashboard.qmd.









WarningCommon pitfall



Three traps, all met building the example. The boundary file follows the GeoJSON standard (exterior rings counter-clockwise) and Plotly expects the opposite, so without reversing the rings every municipality is drawn as “the world minus the municipality”, a grey rectangle; the finished script’s load_geojson() reverses them. Animation frames must update only the colours (z): if every year repeats the 2.7 MB of boundaries, the page balloons. And a dashboard cell shows every top-level expression, not only the last, so a bare fig.add_vline(…) draws the chart twice; assign it, fig = fig.add_vline(…), and end the cell with fig.


The searchable table needs maxBytes=0, or itables silently drops rows to keep the page small.
The same outputs can also become an academic paper, as London’s did (Section 8.6), now with numbered equations ($$ … $$ {#eq-kmeans}, referred to as @eq-kmeans) and citations of the papers behind each method:



Ask your coding agent

Create whitepaper.qmd from outputs/: A4 Typst, "New Computer Modern"; an abstract (no inline code), numbered Introduction, Methods with equations, Results and Conclusions, then References via `#set bibliography(title: [References])`. Cite data/README.md's sources and the k-means, silhouette and ARI papers in references.bib; open each DOI. Add it to `render` and the "Downloads" menu; render; check equations and citations. Figures must be vector: set `fig-format: svg` and check that the files in `figure-typst/` end in .svg.








WarningCommon pitfall



“Open each DOI” is there for a reason: an agent can produce a plausible reference that does not exist. A DOI is a document’s permanent identifier, and https://doi.org/ followed by it opens the publisher’s page, so it is a quick test that a reference exists. Ask the agent to drop any reference it cannot open rather than guess, and check the reference list yourself. The finished paper cites Lloyd (1982) for k-means, Rousseeuw (1987) for the silhouette, Hubert and Arabie (1985) for the adjusted Rand index and Pedregosa et al. (2011) for scikit-learn, each checked against its publisher’s page on 2026-11-01.

title: 15  Publish Many
text:
15.8 Further challenges
These have no checkpoints. Each extends the analysis with data already in the project, or names one that is not yet available:

Moves between kinds. Count how municipalities’ zones move between clusters from 2016 to 2023, and draw it as a Sankey diagram (Plotly’s go.Sankey).
Positive deviants. Find municipalities whose rural zone is in the high-risk kind yet whose recorded infant mortality is low, and check first whether that is small numbers, blanks or under-registration.
Other clusterings. A Gaussian mixture model gives each row a probability per cluster instead of a hard label; HDBSCAN finds dense groups and leaves outliers unclustered. Do the kinds survive?
A better outcome. Diarrhoeal disease in children under five is the outcome most directly linked to water. Its incidence is not in the open data of SIVIGILA, Colombia’s public-health surveillance system, which publish only deaths; the data’s README records it as a source to add when it becomes available.

title: 15  Publish Many
text:
Summary


Every publication reads outputs/ and none computes, so one analysis reaches each reader in the format they use: Word and PDF for officials, slides for a council, a website for anyone.
Word, PowerPoint, PDF and most e-book readers cannot run JavaScript, so their figures must be static images.
pre-render re-runs the analysis before every render and freeze: false re-executes every page, so nothing is stale; freeze: auto is faster but cannot see data/ or outputs/, so it needs a written rule for clearing _freeze/.
A guard turns a sentence that no longer matches the data into a failed render instead of a quiet falsehood.
The live site is the last _site/ you published, and changes only when you publish again.
A changed setting reaches every page that reads outputs/ and nothing else: predict that, rebuild and check.


That last exercise holds the part’s design, and it is the book’s method at full size. The afterword takes it back to its three verbs, and to a project of your own.

Exercise III.6: Report, slides and e-book

You’re done when report.docx and report.pdf open with the heatmap, the outcomes and the within-cluster figure; slides.html and slides.pptx both have six slides; and, if you made it, report.epub opens with the three figures and the sources.

title: Exercises for Part III
section: Transfer tasks: your prompt, your check
text:
Transfer tasks: your prompt, your check
Each task applies one of Part III’s rules to something the chapters did not do. Write the prompt yourself, one task with concrete file and column names, and write the check before you run it: what will you look at, and what would tell you the agent got it wrong?

Follow another municipality. Choose one you know, or another department’s capital, and list each of its zones’ clusters by year from outputs/clusters.parquet, with every flag that marks a filled value.

You’re done when you can say which kind each zone falls in, whether either moves between kinds, and which of its values were filled rather than measured.

Dropout within each kind. Repeat the within-cluster check (Worse water, more infant deaths?) for school dropout instead of infant mortality, and add it to clusters.qmd. The prompt has to carry the rules that apply to dropout: the years OUTCOME_YEARS gives it, and the level at which it is measured.

You’re done when the page shows \(\rho\) and n per cluster beside a sentence saying the check is descriptive, and you can explain why its n differs from the infant-mortality check’s.

Guard a sentence. Find a sentence in report.qmd or the blog post whose words, not only its numbers, depend on the data, such as one naming the kind with the lowest coverage. Make the page fail its render if the data stop supporting it, as assert k == 4 does for the post’s title.

You’re done when the page renders with the guard, and fails with a message naming the sentence when you temporarily reverse the guard’s condition.

Another reader. Suppose a regional health office asks for one page: a PDF with one figure, one table and the sentence saying what the comparison does not show. Build it from outputs/ only.

You’re done when brief.pdf renders, every number in brief.qmd is inline code, the IRCA is labelled utility-supplied, and the last sentence says the comparison does not establish a causal effect of water safety.

title: Exercises for Part III
text:
Review questions

A colleague suggests adding infant mortality to the features, since it says more about health risk than altitude does. Why does Part III never cluster on an outcome?
Why is the IRCA called “utility-supplied” every time it appears, and where does the label matter most?
Most rural rows have no IRCA, and the analysis drops them. What can the rural cluster’s results claim, and what can they not?
Why does the analysis cluster z-scores standardised within each year, rather than the raw values?
The silhouette at the chosen k is only 0.19. Did the clustering fail?
Tunja’s rural zone had medium-risk water in some of the analysis’s years, yet sits in a cluster named for no-risk water. Is the name wrong?
Two draft titles for the council’s last slide: “Safer water lowers infant mortality” and, after the within-cluster check (Worse water, more infant deaths?), “Water quality makes no difference to infant mortality”. What is wrong with each, and what would you write instead?
In the within-cluster check, each of Tunja’s municipality-years carries the mean IRCA of its two zones. Why is that not the water Tunja’s infants drank, and what is it called to read it as if it were?
After you change MAX_MISSING and rebuild, the clusters page, the report and the post show new numbers, but the explore page and the live site do not. Why? And what would go wrong if the site used freeze: auto?

title: Exercises for Part III
text:
Answers to the review questions

Because the analysis then compares outcomes between the kinds. If infant mortality helped define them, they would differ in infant mortality by construction, and the comparison would find exactly what was put in (Features and outcomes). Outcomes describe the clusters; they never define them.
The open table holds the IRCA of systems run by water utilities, not the national figure. Self-supplied systems, which have no utility, score far worse (Scoring water risk: the IRCA), so the data understate the risk wherever people rely on self-supply, and say nothing where no utility exists. Without the label, a reader would take the figure for the national one, and think water safer than it is wherever self-supply is common.
They describe sampled rural systems only: those run by a utility and tested. The gaps are not missing at random. They depend on the zone, and perhaps on the risk itself, since the zones least often scored are the riskiest where they are scored, so every rural result should say which systems it covers (Rural: less data, more risk, What the steps keep).
k-means groups rows by straight-line distance, where a feature counts in proportion to its variance. In raw units, rainfall and altitude would decide the clusters on their own, and the kinds would be climate zones. z-scores give every feature the same weight, and computing them within each year removes shifts that move every place at once, such as transfers in pesos not adjusted for inflation, so a cluster means the same relative position in every year (Why scale?, Four steps from table to features).
No, but the kinds overlap: they summarise a continuum rather than separate islands of data. That is why k is chosen by a rule written down before seeing the result, and why the kinds are described, not treated as natural types. Refits from other seeds agree, which shows only that the result does not depend on the start, not that it would survive other data or features (Choosing k).
Right about the kind, wrong about this member: Tunja’s rural water was never in the no-risk band in 2016–2023. The risk word is the band of the cluster’s median IRCA, not a claim about every zone-year in it, and k-means places a row by all nine features, several of which Tunja’s two zones share as one municipality (Name them by a rule, Where Tunja lands). A statement about Tunja needs Tunja’s rows.
Both read a description as an effect. The first turns a difference between kinds into a cause, though poverty, rurality, health-service access and reporting differ between the kinds too. The second reads a weak association as no effect, though weak reporting can hide deaths and small municipalities add noise (What else could explain it). Instead, say what was compared over which rows, with verbs of association, and add one sentence saying the comparison does not establish a causal effect of water safety (Writing it honestly).
The mean weighs the two zones equally, though only a small share of Tunja’s people live in the rural one, and it lies between two values that neither zone had. IRCA is measured per zone and infant mortality per municipality, so a pattern across places need not hold for the people in them; reading it as if it did is the ecological fallacy (What else could explain it).
pre-render re-runs the analysis, which rewrites outputs/, and freeze: false re-executes every page, so every page that reads outputs/ is fresh. The explore page re-runs too, but it reads only data/water_municipal.csv, which did not change (Table 15.1). The live site is the last _site/ you published, and changes only when you publish again (Publish it). With freeze: auto, Quarto would re-execute a page only when its own source changed: it does not see outputs/ or data/, so pages would keep their old numbers until the cache was cleared (A website with a blog).

title: Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next
text:
What you can now do
Near the end of Part III, one setting changed in one script, and the officials’ report, the council’s slides, the blog post and the dashboard all changed with it, without a number retyped. That moment is what the two projects were for. The London guide and the water analysis each started from plain text and data, became a shelf of documents for different readers, and rebuild with one command. The projects will date. The method will not, and it fits on a card.
Part III added four habits that travel to any analysis. Follow one case, your own Tunja, through every step, because aggregates hide what a single place shows. Label each variable for what it measures, as “utility-supplied” did for the IRCA. Never define groups by the outcome you will compare them on. And open every reference an agent gives you before you cite it.
The formats were never the goal. Work with data, software and AI applications pays off when its audience engages with it and acts on it: a manager decides, a council funds a water supply, a reader tries the method. Quarto, git and a hosting service make that work reproducible, so others can trust it, act on it and build on it; an agent makes it fast; checking keeps it right. What stays with you is the judgement no tool makes: who the work is for, and what would make them read it.
If you worked through both parts, you can:
If one of these is shaky, go back to that part’s exercises, starting from a known-good state in Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers.
