title: Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next
text:
Three projects of your own
The London guide and the water analysis were practice. The three projects here are the kind of document you already make, or will soon be asked for, built the book’s way. Each ends with the same proof, a rebuild from a fresh copy, so you know that someone else could make it too.
Inside each project the order is the one the book followed. Start with one output for one reader; make it compute, so that no number is typed; then add formats. The second format is where the approach starts to repay the setup; the first change to the data is where it pays for itself.






TipWhich project first?



Choose the one with a real reader and a date: a brief your manager reads on the first Monday, a supplement due with a resubmission, a report due in three weeks. Then check that you are allowed to use its data with an agent (below). If two qualify, start with the smaller. Finish one project, fresh clone included, before you start another; the second goes faster.



Start every project the same way
Make the project folder and go into it (Get the files): for the brief, mkdir ~/metrics-brief then cd ~/metrics-brief. Make a data/ folder inside it (mkdir data) and copy your files in, unchanged; Finder or File Explorer will do. Start the history with git init -b main and commit the data, git add data then git commit -m "Data, as exported" (Start a history). Then hand the agent the setup, with rules written before the first request (Rules that persist: AGENTS.md). This prompt and the ones below are examples: change the file and column names to yours.



Ask your coding agent

Set up this folder for a Quarto report with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas matplotlib`. Write AGENTS.md: files in data/ are inputs, never edit them; every number comes from data/ through code; run quarto through `uv run`. Write a .gitignore for .venv/, .quarto/ and the rendered outputs. Show me `git status`.


It writes AGENTS.md, pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .gitignore; the layouts below show the rest. New files appear in git status as untracked, not in git diff, so open and read them, then commit them yourself. From then on, read each change with git diff (Hand the fix to the agent) and commit after every prompt whose result you checked, so that a bad turn is one git restore away.






TipKeep private data private



What an agent reads is sent to the model on its vendor’s servers (Model plus harness). Customer records, sales figures, unpublished results, participant data and student marks are not yours to send anywhere you like. Before a confidential file meets an agent, read your organisation’s AI and data policy, and ask whoever owns it if the policy is silent. If your agent is not approved for the data, do not paste it, open it or name its path in a prompt: build the project on a public or made-up file with the same columns, labelled as such, then swap in the real file and render it yourself. Keep such a project off public hosting.




An internal metrics brief
Who it is for. Anyone who sends the same figures every month: an analyst, an operations lead, a manager. Each month you export a CSV from your own tool (a CRM, a ticketing system, a finance package) and turn it into a one-page brief, as a web page and a Word file. Start with:
metrics-brief/
├── AGENTS.md
├── data/
│   ├── 2026-09.csv   each month's export, saved unchanged
│   └── 2026-10.csv
├── brief.qmd         the agent writes it
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
You build brief.html and brief.docx. The first prompt makes one output that computes:



Ask your coding agent

Write brief.qmd with formats html and docx. Read the newest file in data/ (files are named YYYY-MM.csv) and state its month, its number of rows and the total of `amount`, each as inline code. Render, and tell me which file it read.


Then the comparison a reader acts on:



Ask your coding agent

In brief.qmd, add a table of total `amount` by `region` for the newest month and the one before, with the change, and a bar chart of the change with a caption and alt text. Render both formats; check that the table's total equals the sentence's.


An export can change shape when someone renames a column, so make the brief say so instead of printing nonsense, and let code choose the words of the one sentence that depends on the data:



Ask your coding agent

Make brief.qmd stop with an error naming the column if the newest export lacks `date`, `region` or `amount`. Test it on a renamed copy in a temporary folder, then delete the copy and render again.



Ask your coding agent

Add a sentence saying whether the total rose or fell since the month before, its wording chosen by code from the two totals. Render, and show me the sentence.


Checks only you can do. Open the export in its own tool and compare one region’s total with the brief’s. Open the Word file: does it fit one page? Show it to one reader and ask what they would do differently after reading it; if the answer is “nothing”, the brief needs a different question, not more charts.
The rebuild test is next month’s file. When it arrives, save it in data/, predict which numbers will change, render, and compare (Predict, change, rebuild). To rehearse now, remove the newest export (rm data/2026-10.csv), predict, render, then bring it back with git restore data/2026-10.csv.

You’re done when next month’s export rebuilds both formats with no other edit, one region’s total matches the tool’s, and the fresh-clone test gives the same brief.



A reproducible research supplement
Who it is for. Researchers with a paper in progress. The supplement holds the paper’s figures and tables, each computed from the data, with captions, alt text and citations, as a web page and a PDF that reviewers can open and you can rebuild after every revision. Start with:
paper-supplement/
├── AGENTS.md
├── data/
│   ├── README.md        each file's source, licence and date
│   └── measurements.csv your data, unchanged
├── references.bib     the agent writes it
├── supplement.qmd     the agent writes it
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
You build supplement.html and supplement.pdf, the PDF made with Typst as in One source, three formats.



Ask your coding agent

Write supplement.qmd with formats html and typst. Add Table S1 from data/measurements.csv: n, mean and standard deviation of `value` by `group`, with a caption. Render both; check that the n values add up to the file's rows.



Ask your coding agent

Add Figure S1, `value` by `group` as a box plot, with a caption and alt text that says what the figure shows, not only what it is (`fig-cap`, `fig-alt`). Render both formats; check that the figure and caption appear in the PDF.



Ask your coding agent

Add a Data section citing each source in data/README.md, from a new references.bib set as the `bibliography`. List every DOI and URL you used so that I can open each one; cite nothing you could not find.



Ask your coding agent

Add an "AI use" section naming the agent and its version and the tasks it did here, with a TODO where I will list the checks I made. Render, and show me the section.


The last prompt follows Using AI in research: say it, own it: the tool is never an author, you are responsible for what it produced, and you say how you used it. The checks are yours to write, because only you made them.
Checks only you can do. Compare every number in the paper’s text with the supplement’s. Open every reference, since an agent can produce a plausible one that does not exist (A dashboard and a white paper (optional)), and read the sentence that cites it. Confirm that you may share the data: consent, ethics approval and data agreements decide, not the agent. Read the journal’s rules on supplementary material and on AI use.

You’re done when every figure and table in both formats comes from a cell and has a caption and alt text, every citation opens to the work it names, the AI-use statement names the tool, the tasks and your checks, and the fresh-clone test gives the same supplement.



A coursework report
Who it is for. Students with an assignment that involves data. You build report.pdf and hand it in with the source, so that a marker can rebuild it and see that every number came from the data. Start with:
coursework/
├── AGENTS.md
├── data/survey.csv   the data the assignment gives you, unchanged
├── README.md         how to rebuild it (the agent writes it)
├── report.qmd        the agent writes it
├── pyproject.toml
└── uv.lock
Coursework has a rule the other two projects lack: the work being marked must be yours. Start with the course’s AI policy, before any other prompt.



Ask your coding agent

Add to AGENTS.md the rules from my course's AI policy, pasted below, and that data/survey.csv must never be edited. Then list, one line each, what you may and may not do for me under them.



Ask your coding agent

Write report.qmd with format typst and the sections the assignment brief asks for (pasted below), and one inline-code sentence giving the number of responses in data/survey.csv. Render report.pdf; tell me how you checked the number.



Ask your coding agent

Write README.md: what the project is, and how to rebuild report.pdf from a fresh copy (install uv and Quarto, then `uv run quarto render report.qmd`). Then add an AI-use statement at the end of report.qmd in the form my course asks for. Render, and show me both.


If the policy forbids an agent for assessed work, build the project by hand, as in 4  A First Report, by Hand: everything here except the prompts still applies.
Checks only you can do. Read the policy yourself, and ask the course leader when it is unclear; the agent’s summary of it is not permission. Make sure you can explain every line of code and every sentence, since a marker may ask. Check the brief’s length and format rules against the PDF. Hand in the source the way the course asks; for a zip of exactly what you committed (no .venv/, no rendered files), run git archive -o coursework-source.zip HEAD.

You’re done when report.pdf answers the brief, the AI-use statement matches both what you did and what the policy allows, and the fresh-clone test, run by following your own README.md, gives the same PDF.



The fresh-clone test
The last check of every project is the one a colleague, a reviewer or a marker will make: rebuild it from what you committed, on a clean copy. Anything that lived only on your machine, a file never committed or a step done by hand, shows up here instead of in their inbox.

In the project folder, run git status. If it lists anything, commit it (Start a history) until it says nothing to commit, working tree clean.
Clone the project into a new folder and render it there. For the brief:
git clone ~/metrics-brief ~/metrics-brief-check
cd ~/metrics-brief-check
uv run quarto render brief.qmd
The clone has no .venv/ and no outputs, because .gitignore kept them out of the history, so the first render builds the environment again, as in Render it yourself. A local clone copies between folders on your own computer; nothing is uploaded. For the other projects, use their folder and file names.
Open each output from both folders side by side and compare every number.

A failed render or a different number is a finding, not a failure: commit the missing file, or turn the manual step into code, and clone again. When the two agree, delete the check folder; it is only a copy.
Agents, models and Quarto’s options will keep changing, and some details in this book with them. The loop does not. Prompt for one thing. Check it against the data. Publish only what you checked, from one source, as often as the data change.

title: Afterword: What You Built, and Where Next
text:
Where next

Quarto’s Guide covers everything this book used and much it did not: books like this one, manuscripts, interactive documents and more output formats (checked 2026-10-30).
Dashboards, Typst and publishing to GitHub Pages are the official references for the three areas readers usually extend first (checked 2026-10-30).
For the causal questions Part III left open, Miguel A. Hernán and James M. Robins, Causal Inference: What If (Boca Raton: Chapman & Hall/CRC, 2020; free online), on confounding and the designs that can answer them (checked 2026-11-12).
Quarto’s Citations page, and its Manuscripts, projects that write a scholarly article in several formats and publish it as a website, take the research supplement further (checked 2026-11-17).
In this book: Appendix C — Cheatsheet for the commands, Appendix D — Troubleshooting when a render fails, and Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers for every known-good state.
The workshop’s slides are online, and its examples and checkpoints are in its GitHub repository.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Before you start
This appendix is step 1 of the setup (Section 3.2) for Windows. The workshop’s tools are made for Linux, so on Windows you install Ubuntu, a widely used version of Linux, inside Windows with WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux. Think of Windows as your house, with your browser, files and apps, and Ubuntu as a room inside it, a window where you type commands. Everything in this book happens in that room, your Windows browser still opens what you make, and nothing on Windows is removed.
Why not PowerShell, Windows’s own command window? Because the book’s commands, and the way the setup was tested, are for Linux. Some tools have Windows installers, but their paths and commands differ, and each variant is another way to go wrong.
Figure A.1 shows the whole procedure in one window. The steps below go slowly, with a restart in the middle, and the first time Ubuntu opens it also asks you to choose a username and password, which the animation skips.
Do one step, compare your screen with You should see, then go on. If something looks different, see If you are stuck.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
About 20 minutes and one restart.
An administrator account on this computer. On a work laptop, ask IT first; if IT types the password for you, stay signed in as yourself. Without one, WSL cannot be installed: arrange to work with someone else’s computer.
Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 or newer (Settings → System → About shows yours).
Plugged in, on a strong connection: Ubuntu is a big download.
These instructions on a second screen or a phone, because the restart closes your browser.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Step 1: open PowerShell as administrator
PowerShell is a Windows window for typing commands; you need it for a few minutes only.

Press the Windows key, or click the Windows logo on the taskbar, and type PowerShell.
Right-click “Windows PowerShell” and choose Run as administrator.
Choose Yes when Windows asks.




Searching for PowerShell from the Start button. A drawing of Windows 11; on Windows 10 the button sits at the left, and the steps are the same.





The right-click menu, with Run as administrator circled.








NoteYou should see



A window whose title starts with “Administrator”, ending in a line like PS C:\WINDOWS\system32>.



The administrator window.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Step 2: turn on WSL
Paste this into the PowerShell window (Ctrl+V, or a right-click if that does nothing) and press Enter:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch

PS C:\WINDOWS\system32> wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch
Installing: Virtual Machine Platform
Virtual Machine Platform has been installed.
Installing: Windows Subsystem for Linux
Windows Subsystem for Linux has been installed.
Installing: Ubuntu
Ubuntu has been installed.
The requested operation is successful. Changes will not be effective until the system is rebooted.







NoteYou should see



A message that you must restart, such as “Changes will not be effective until the system is rebooted”. If instead it says Ubuntu is installed or “already exists”, skip to step 5.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Step 3: restart the computer
Save your work, then Start → Power → Restart.






NoteWhy this works



The command runs twice because, when a restart is needed, the first run only turns on Windows features and installs no Linux at all (checked against WSL’s source code, version 3.0.3, on 2026-11-06). --no-launch keeps Ubuntu’s first start out of the administrator window, whose folder is a Windows system folder.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Step 4: download Ubuntu

Open a normal PowerShell window, not as administrator: press the Windows key, type PowerShell, and press Enter. Ubuntu is installed for the account that runs this line, so it must be yours.
Paste the same line and press Enter:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch
This is the long wait: the download can take many minutes, and the percentage may stand still for a while.






NoteYou should see



That it finished, or “already exists”. Both mean go on. Keep this window open.


You will now have two windows, and their last line tells them apart: PowerShell’s ends in > (like PS C:\Users\Ana>), Ubuntu’s in $ (like ana@LAPTOP:~$). PowerShell is only for steps 1, 2, 4 and 6; everything else happens in Ubuntu.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
section: Step 5: open Ubuntu, and choose a username and password
text:
Step 5: open Ubuntu, and choose a username and password

Press the Windows key, type Ubuntu, and press Enter. The first start unpacks files: wait.
Username: one short word in lower case, with no spaces, such as ana. It need not match your Windows name.
Password: type one you will remember, press Enter, and type it again.







WarningCommon pitfall



Nothing appears while you type the password: no dots, no stars. That is normal; keep typing and press Enter. Write the password down: sudo asks for it in step 8.








NoteYou should see



A prompt, the line that means “ready for a command”, with your own names: ana@LAPTOP:~$. ana is you, LAPTOP this computer, ~ your home folder, and $ where you type. In this Ubuntu window, type whoami and press Enter: it prints your username.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
section: Step 6: check that Ubuntu runs on WSL 2
text:
Step 6: check that Ubuntu runs on WSL 2
In the PowerShell window (its line ends in >):
wsl -l -v






NoteYou should see



Ubuntu with a 2 in the VERSION column:
  NAME      STATE           VERSION
* Ubuntu    Running         2


If it says 1, run wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2 and wait. Then type exit to close PowerShell.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Step 7: practise copy and paste



Table A.1: Copy and paste in Windows Terminal. The keyboard way does nothing in some older windows; the mouse always works.











With the mouse
With the keyboard




Copy
select the text, then right-click
select the text, then Ctrl+Shift+C


Paste
right-click with nothing selected
Ctrl+Shift+V












WarningCommon pitfall



Ctrl+C with nothing selected does not copy: it stops whatever is running. If that happens, run the command again.


Copy echo "Paste works", paste it into Ubuntu and press Enter; the next line should say Paste works.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Step 8: install two small tools
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git
sudo means “do this as administrator” and asks for your Ubuntu password from step 5, hidden again; apt is Ubuntu’s installer; && means “and then, if that worked”. A lot of text scrolls past. When the $ comes back, check:
curl --version && git --version






NoteYou should see



A version number for each, such as git version 2.43.0. Yours may differ.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Step 9: four habits
Stay in your home folder. Keep project folders there, not in Documents, Desktop or OneDrive. If the prompt shows /mnt/c, you are in a Windows folder: cd ~ goes home. (Windows drives appear under /mnt/; keeping projects in ~ is also faster.)
See your files in Windows. explorer.exe . opens the current folder in File Explorer, where you can double-click what you made.
Open a second tab. Ctrl+Shift+D duplicates the tab; you will need one while the agent is busy in the first. A new tab may start in the home folder, so cd back into your project.
Copy sign-in links whole. Ubuntu may not be able to open your browser, so tools print a link: copy all of it into your Windows browser, and if the website shows a code, paste it back into Ubuntu.






WarningCommon pitfall



Don’t install the Windows versions of Quarto, Python or a coding agent for this book. Ubuntu needs its own copies, and the Windows ones can get in the way.


Step 1 is done when wsl -l -v shows Ubuntu with VERSION 2, an Ubuntu window shows a prompt ending in $, git --version prints a version in Ubuntu, and you know your Ubuntu password. Continue with Section 3.3. Next time, open Ubuntu from the Start menu: your files are still there.

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
Useful PowerShell commands



Table A.2: Three WSL commands worth knowing (Microsoft’s WSL documentation, checked 2026-10-31).









Command (in PowerShell)
Does




wsl -l -v
lists each Linux with its state and WSL version (from Ubuntu: wsl.exe -l -v)


wsl --user root
opens a root shell, the documented way to reset a forgotten password with passwd <username>


wsl --shutdown
stops every running Linux at once, including the agent and any preview: save your work first

title: Appendix A — Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
If you are stuck



Table A.3: What to do when installing goes wrong (steps 1 to 5).









You see
Do this




The install stuck at 0.0%
Close it, then in PowerShell run wsl --install --web-download --no-launch -d Ubuntu


No Ubuntu in the Start menu
Do step 4 again in a normal window, not as administrator; still none? In PowerShell type wsl ~


Error 0x80370102, or “virtualization is not enabled”
Virtualization is off in the computer’s BIOS; without BIOS access this cannot be fixed


A list of options and no install
Windows is too old: run Windows Update, restart, repeat step 2


“Access denied”, or no Run as administrator
You need an administrator account


“Already exists”
Ubuntu is installed: go to step 5


wsl is “not found”
You are in Ubuntu: use PowerShell, whose line ends in >


Ubuntu closes or won’t start
Restart the computer and open Ubuntu again









Table A.4: What to do when Ubuntu runs but a step goes wrong.









You see
Do this




Nothing moves, and the title starts with “Select”
A click paused the window: press Esc


A download fails on a work network
Try another network, such as a phone hotspot


The prompt starts with root@ and ends in #
The username step was skipped: ask for help before going on


sudo says “Sorry, try again”
Wrong password: type it again slowly, it stays hidden


Forgotten Ubuntu password
In PowerShell, wsl -u root, then passwd ana with your username, then exit


command not found right after an install
Open a new tab or window and try again






For anything else, copy the command and the full error into a web chat, say “Windows, Ubuntu on WSL”, and try one suggested fix at a time, never pasting a password.
These steps were written from Microsoft’s WSL documentation (install, setup, basic commands, file systems and troubleshooting, checked 2026-11-06) and have been checked on a Mac against that documentation, not yet on a clean Windows machine. Exact messages can differ between Windows versions.

title: Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits
text:
The keyboard
If you mostly type prose, four things in this book may be new: keys that each program treats differently, the symbols that code is full of, the paths that name files and folders, and the keys and habits that make a terminal predictable, including how to read an error. Skip what you already know. Chapter 4 is the place to practise all of it: almost everything in it is typed by hand.
crumbs: B  Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits

title: Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits
text:
Table B.1: Keys whose effect depends on the program you are in. Mac keys from Apple’s “Mac keyboard shortcuts” page (checked 2026-11-16).









Keys
What to know




Shift, Caps Lock
hold Shift for one capital letter, or for the upper symbol on a key; Caps Lock stays on until you press it again


Backspace, Delete
Backspace deletes to the left of the cursor, Delete to the right; on a Mac the key labelled Delete is Backspace, and Fn-Delete deletes to the right


Enter (Return)
starts a new line in a document, sends a message in a chat, and runs the command in a terminal


Tab
moves to the next field in a form and indents in an editor; in a terminal it completes names (below)


Ctrl, Command
a shortcut means holding the first key while you press the second: Ctrl+Z undoes on Windows and Linux, Command-Z on a Mac
crumbs: B  Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits

title: Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits
text:
Symbols this book uses
Code uses punctuation that prose rarely needs, and one wrong symbol stops a command. Each symbol below appears in the book’s prompts, commands or files.



Table B.2: The symbols the book types most, and where each one appears.










Symbol
Name
Where you meet it




`
backtick (grave accent)
around code in Markdown; three of them open a code block (Section 5.9)


~
tilde
your home folder in a path: ~/quarto-workshop


_
underscore (Shift and the minus key)
file and column names: _quarto.yml, water_coverage_total


-
hyphen, also called dash or minus
options to a command: quarto --version; type the key itself, not a longer dash


:
colon
YAML settings, with a space after it: title: "Visit London" (Section 6.2)


', "
single and double quotes
keep words with spaces together: cd "My Documents"; text in Python and YAML


&&
double ampersand
runs a second command only if the first worked: mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide


;
semicolon
runs two commands on one terminal line, one after the other; rare in this book


{ }
braces, or curly brackets
executable cells such as {python}, and attributes such as {.unnumbered}


( )
parentheses, or round brackets
Python calls such as len(df), and a Markdown link’s address: [text](url)


[ ]
square brackets
a Markdown link’s text, and Python lists: ["html", "pdf"]


/
forward slash
between folders on a Mac, Linux and WSL, and in web addresses: data/visits.csv


\
backslash
between folders in Windows (C:\Users); at the end of a terminal line it continues the command on the next


#
hash
a Markdown heading, and a comment in Python, YAML and Bash scripts (not at a zsh prompt on a Mac, where it is passed to the command)












WarningCommon pitfall



Two traps change a symbol without telling you. Word processors and notes apps turn straight quotes into curly ones (“ ”) and two hyphens into a dash (—). A terminal and Python read those as different characters, so a quoted name or an option such as --version stops working: copy prompts and commands from the book or a plain-text editor. And some keyboard layouts make symbols dead keys, which wait for the next key to accent it: Windows’ United States-International layout does this to `, ', ", ~ and ^ (Microsoft’s layout page, checked 2026-11-16), and Spanish layouts to ` and ^. Press Space after a dead key to get the symbol itself.
crumbs: B  Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits

title: Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits
text:
Terminal keys
A handful of keys make the terminal much faster and less error-prone. They are defaults in Bash, Ubuntu’s shell, and zsh, the Mac’s, and in Windows Terminal and the Mac’s Terminal app (GNU Bash and zsh line-editor manuals; Microsoft and Apple keyboard documentation; all checked 2026-10-31).



Table B.3: Terminal keys worth knowing: running, completing, recalling, stopping, copying and pasting.









Keys
Does




Enter
runs the command you typed; press it once the whole command is there


Space
separates a command’s parts, so put quotes round a name that contains one: cd "My Documents"


Tab
completes a file or command name; lists the choices when several match


Up arrow, Down arrow
step back and forward through earlier commands; edit one, then press Enter to run it


Ctrl+C
stops the running command (in Windows Terminal, copies instead when text is selected)


Ctrl+Shift+C, Ctrl+Shift+V
copy and paste in Windows Terminal and Ubuntu (Mac: Command-C, Command-V)


right-click
in Windows Terminal: copies a selection, or pastes when nothing is selected












WarningCommon pitfall



Ctrl+C in the agent’s tab interrupts the agent, not a command. In Windows Terminal it copies only when text is selected; with nothing selected it stops what is running.


Other keys edit the line you are typing, clear the screen or find a command you typed before:



Table B.4: Terminal keys for editing the line, clearing the screen and searching earlier commands.









Keys
Does




Ctrl+A, Ctrl+E
jump to the start and the end of the line


Ctrl+U
delete to the start of the line (the whole line in zsh); Ctrl+K deletes to the end


Ctrl+L
clear the screen


Ctrl+R
search earlier commands as you type; Ctrl+R again for older matches, Enter runs it, Ctrl+G gives up












ImportantTry it



Open a second tab (Ctrl+Shift+D in Windows Terminal, Command-T on a Mac), type ls ~/quarto-w and press Tab, then Enter. Press Ctrl+L, then Ctrl+R and type ls; then Ctrl+A, Ctrl+E and Ctrl+U.

You’re done when Ctrl+R found your ls command and Ctrl+U cleared it.
crumbs: B  Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits

title: Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits
text:
Paths
A path names a file or folder by the folders that lead to it, separated by /. An absolute path starts at the top of the computer’s folders, /, and means the same wherever you are: /home/ana/first-report on Linux and WSL, /Users/ana/first-report on a Mac. A relative path starts from the folder you are in: in ~/first-report, data/visits.csv is the file visits.csv in its data folder, and from your home folder the same path finds nothing.



Table B.5: The short forms of paths that this book’s commands use.









Path
Means




~
your home folder: ~/first-report is the folder first-report inside it, from anywhere


.
the folder you are in: open . opens it on a Mac


..
the folder above: cd .. goes up one, and ../quarto-workshop is a folder beside this one


data/visits.csv
relative: visits.csv in the data folder of the folder you are in






A “no such file” error often means a relative path read from the wrong folder: pwd says where you are, and ls what is there.
A space separates a command’s parts, so a name with a space reads as two names. Each shell says so in its own words:

$ mkdir "my reports"
$ cd my reports
bash: cd: too many arguments

That is Bash on Ubuntu (5.2); zsh on a Mac answers cd: string not in pwd: my. Either way, keep the name in one piece: put it in quotes, cd "my reports", or put a backslash before the space, cd my\ reports. Easiest of all, type cd my and press Tab: the shell completes the name and types the backslash for you. Names you choose yourself are simpler without spaces: my-reports.
crumbs: B  Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits

title: Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits
text:
Reading an error
A failed command often prints more than you need. Read it in this order.
The first line. It says what went wrong, usually after ERROR: or error:. Run uv run quarto render report.qmd in the wrong folder and the line is:

ERROR: No valid input files passed to render

Stack trace:
    at _Command.actionHandler (file:///Applications/quarto/bin/quarto.js:142967:11)
    ...

Quarto found no report.qmd here: you are in the wrong folder, or the name is misspelt.
Not the stack trace. The lines after Stack trace:, each starting at, show where inside Quarto the error surfaced. They are for Quarto’s developers, not for you: skip them.
The caret. A mistake in a file’s YAML ends with the lines around it, numbered, and a caret, ^, under the place where YAML gave up. Here format: html lost the space after its colon:

ERROR: YAMLException: can not read a block mapping entry; a multiline key may not be an implicit key (4:1)

 1 |
 2 | title: "Five London Sights"
 3 | format:html
 4 |
-----^

The numbers count lines from the opening ---, which is line 1, and (4:1) means line 4, character 1. YAML often notices a mistake one line after it, so look at the line the caret points to and the line above: here the culprit is line 3.
When you ask for help, copy the whole thing all the same: the command and every line it printed, stack trace included. The person or web chat helping you may need the part you skipped. Section 4.6 makes three common mistakes on purpose, and Appendix D lists the messages seen in practice, with their fixes.
crumbs: B  Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits

title: Appendix B — Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits
text:
Habits

Know where you are. Run pwd before starting an agent: its answer is the agent’s root folder (Section 2.4).
Two tabs. Keep the agent in one tab and commands such as quarto preview in another, both in the project folder.
New tab after installing. A terminal learns where programs are when it starts, so a program installed a moment ago is “not found” until you open a new tab.
Read before you run. Whether a command comes from the book, a web chat or the agent, read it before you press Enter or approve it, especially anything with sudo or rm.
Copy errors whole. When something fails, copy the command and the entire error text; the useful line is rarely the last one.
Edit small files in the terminal. nano AGENTS.md opens a file in a simple editor: Ctrl+O, then Enter, saves it, and Ctrl+X leaves. On a Mac, nano opens Pico, which uses the same keys (checked on macOS 26, 2026-11-12); both list their keys along the bottom of the screen.
crumbs: B  Keys, Symbols and Terminal Habits

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
Front matter (YAML)
A one-page reference for the patterns this book uses, with the chapter that explains each.
One source, several formats (Chapter 6):

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
---
title: "Project Report"
author: "Author Name"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    format-links:
      - docx
      - {format: typst, text: PDF}
  docx: default
  typst:
    papersize: a4
  pptx: default
  revealjs:
    output-file: report-slides.html
  epub:
    toc: true
lang: en
---

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
Code cells and inline code
Options go at the top of a cell, as #| comments (Section 6.4):

#| label: fig-name numbers the figure and lets the text refer to it as @fig-name.
#| echo: false hides the code and shows the output.
#| eval: false shows the code without running it.
#| fig-cap: "…" is the caption under a figure.
#| fig-alt: "…" is the alt text screen readers announce.
#| tbl-cap: "…" is the caption of a table.
#| output: asis treats printed text as Markdown.

Inline code puts a computed value in a sentence (Section 6.3):
The dataset contains `{python} len(df)` rows across `{python} df['year'].nunique()` years.

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
Dashboards
A level-1 heading starts a page, a level-2 heading a row, and each cell’s output becomes a card (Section 7.1):
---
title: "Operations dashboard"
format: dashboard
---

# Overview

## Row {height=30%}

::: {.valuebox icon="trophy" color="primary"}
Most visited
`{{python}} top_name`
:::

## Row

```{python}
#| title: Visits by attraction
fig = px.bar(attractions, x="visits_2025", y="attraction")
fig
```
Assign Plotly figures and end the cell with fig; never call fig.show() in a dashboard.

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
Websites
_quarto.yml turns a folder into a website (Section 8.3, Section 15.4):
project:
  type: website
  execute-dir: project
  pre-render: scripts/analysis.py
  render:
    - index.qmd
    - report.qmd
website:
  title: "My project"
  navbar:
    left:
      - {text: Report, href: report.qmd}
      - text: Downloads
        menu:
          - {text: "Report (PDF)", href: report.pdf}
execute:
  freeze: false

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
Commands



Table C.1: The commands used in this book.









Command
Does




uv init --bare
starts a uv project in this folder


uv add pandas matplotlib
adds packages to pyproject.toml and uv.lock, and installs them


uv run quarto preview file.qmd
renders and serves a page, re-rendering on every save


uv run quarto render file.qmd
renders one file in all its formats; --to docx for one format


uv run quarto render
renders the whole project


uv run quarto publish gh-pages
the first publish to GitHub Pages, interactive


uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt
later updates, once the gh-pages branch exists


uv run quarto check jupyter
shows which Python and Jupyter Quarto will use

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
Check and undo with Git
Run them in the project folder, before and after every change, yours or the agent’s (Section 4.4, Section 4.5, Section 8.1):



Table C.2: Checking and undoing with Git.









Command
Does




git init -b main
starts a history in this folder, on a branch called main (once per project)


git status
lists the files changed, added or untracked since the last commit


git diff
shows the changes not yet added, line by line: - the old line, + the new


git add .
adds every change to the next commit; git add report.qmd adds one file


git commit -m "What changed"
records the added changes as a commit, with a message saying what changed


git log --oneline
lists the commits, newest first, one line each


git restore data/visits.csv
throws away the uncommitted changes to one file, back to its last commit

title: Appendix C — Cheatsheet
text:
Prompts
A reliable prompt (Section 2.6):

Names the inputs and outputs: file names and column names, in backticks.
Does one task.
Ends with a check: “render it and tell me which file it wrote”, “check the PDF is one page”.
Respects the data: “compute every number from the cited files; never invent one”.

title: Appendix D — Troubleshooting
text:
Setup
Problems seen while building and teaching the workshop, and the mistakes Section 4.6 makes on purpose, with fixes that were tested. Reading an error says which line of an error to read first. For setup on Windows, see also the Windows stuck table. For anything not listed: copy the command and the whole error into a web chat with your system’s name, try one suggested fix at a time, and never paste passwords or keys.

title: Appendix D — Troubleshooting
text:
Table D.1: Setup problems.









Problem
Fix




Mac: a pop-up asks to install “command line developer tools”
Expected the first time git runs. Click Install and wait (or run xcode-select --install first); if the agent is waiting, tell it done


command not found for uv, claude, codex or agy just after installing
Open a new terminal tab. On a Mac, Claude Code’s installer prints a line to add under “Setup notes”: paste it, then open the tab


quarto: command not found in Ubuntu, though it works in PowerShell
Windows installers put tools where Ubuntu cannot use them: install Quarto inside Ubuntu (Section 3.5)


The prompt shows /mnt/c/...
You are in a Windows folder: cd ~, and keep projects there


gh auth login or the agent cannot open a browser
Expected in WSL: copy the link or code it prints into your Windows browser (for gh: github.com/login/device). Codex: codex login --device-auth


Downloads or git clone fail on a company network
A proxy can block curl, git and uv: try another network


git commit says “Please tell me who you are”
Set your name and email with the two git config --global lines from the setup check


not a valid Python environment
A stale .venv: delete it (rm -rf .venv); uv run rebuilds it

title: Appendix D — Troubleshooting
text:
The terminal



Table D.2: Terminal messages.





Message
Cause and fix




zsh: command not found: quatro (Mac) or quatro: command not found (Ubuntu)
A typo in the command’s name. Press the up arrow, correct it, then Enter (Section 4.6). If the name is right, see the command not found row in Table D.1


error: Failed to spawn: `quatro`, then No such file or directory (os error 2)
The same typo after uv run: uv found no program of that name. Press the up arrow, correct it, then Enter


bash: cd: too many arguments (Ubuntu) or cd: string not in pwd: my (Mac)
The folder’s name has a space, so cd read two names: cd "my reports", or type cd my and press Tab (Paths)

title: Appendix D — Troubleshooting
text:
Rendering and preview



Table D.3: Rendering problems.









Problem
Cause and fix




ERROR: No valid input files passed to render
Quarto found no file of that name in this folder: you are in the wrong folder, or the name is misspelt. pwd and ls show where you are; cd to the project, such as cd ~/first-report (Section 4.6)


ERROR: YAMLException: …, with numbered lines and a caret (^)
A mistake in the front matter. YAML often notices it one line after it, so check the line the caret points to and the line above: a missing space after a colon (can not read a block mapping entry), a stray indent (bad indentation of a mapping entry), a missing closing quote (unexpected end of the stream within a double quoted scalar). Fix it by hand, or undo every change since the last commit with git restore report.qmd (Section 4.6)


readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb', or a locked file
A render ran while quarto preview was rendering the same file. Let the preview render, or stop it (Ctrl+C) before rendering several formats, then restart it (Section 6.7)


Typst PDF fails: cannot parse length '60px'
Typst does not accept CSS pixels in image sizes: write {height=60} or {width="30%"}


A Plotly chart appears twice in a dashboard card
The cell both calls fig.show() (or a bare fig.add_…()) and returns the figure: assign, and end the cell with fig


itables drops rows from a dashboard table
Its default size limit: show(df, maxBytes=0)


A Plotly map is a grey rectangle
The GeoJSON’s rings wind the other way from Plotly’s expectation: reverse them (load_geojson() in the water project’s script)


A page shows old numbers after the data changed
freeze: auto reuses results until the page’s own source changes: delete _freeze/ and render again (Section 15.4)

title: Appendix D — Troubleshooting
text:
Python and Jupyter



Table D.4: Python and Jupyter messages.









Message
Meaning




quarto check says Jupyter is not available
Harmless during setup: each project gets its own environment from uv, and Quarto runs Python through uv run


Kernel is running over TCP without encryption, after [IPKernelApp] WARNING
Harmless: the connection is between Quarto and a Python process on your own computer


There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv
Run Quarto through uv run, which activates the project’s environment


A water checkpoint has no data
Water checkpoints hold sources only: cp -R ../quarto-workshop/examples/water/data .






Backups that copy .venv/ are slow and pointless, because uv run rebuilds it. The checkpoints’ backup command leaves it out, and works on macOS, Linux and WSL:
b="../project-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)" && mkdir "$b" && tar -cf - --exclude=.venv . | tar -xf - -C "$b"

title: Appendix D — Troubleshooting
text:
Publishing



Table D.5: Publishing problems.









Problem
Fix




The first publish fails: “the remote origin does not have a branch named gh-pages”
The first quarto publish gh-pages must be interactive: run uv run quarto publish gh-pages and press Enter at the question. --no-prompt works once the branch exists


A push fails with HTTP 400, “RPC failed”
git config http.postBuffer 524288000, then push again


404 right after publishing
GitHub Pages takes 20 to 60 seconds to deploy: wait a minute and reload (Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac, Ctrl+F5 elsewhere)


A link checker reports 403 Forbidden for a museum’s site
Some sites block automated requests: open the link in a browser

title: Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers
text:
Every checkpoint
Each checkpoint is a folder in quarto-workshop/checkpoints/ holding a project as it stands at the end of one hands-on block, with a README listing the steps to catch up: back up your folder (all but .venv/) to a new time-stamped folder beside it, copy the checkpoint in (and, for the water project, data/ if it is missing), render and check a named output. Paste Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/<path>/README.md into your agent, or follow the README by hand, then carry on from the section whose catch-up box you used. The README names the workshop slide at the same point. There is no checkpoint 03.
Reading on your own, diagnose before you catch up. Check where you are (pwd), what changed since your last commit (git status, then git diff) and the error’s first line (Reading an error, Appendix D), and try the one fix it points to. Catch up only if that fails. Afterwards, open the output the README names and see that it shows what the book describes at the catch-up box.
Chapter 4 has no checkpoint either. Its project is small and typed by hand, and its starter, starters/first-report/ in the same repository, is its fresh start: to begin again, rename your copy with mv ~/first-report ~/first-report-old and copy the starter again as in Section 4.1. Within the chapter, your last commit is the known-good state: git restore takes a file back to it.

title: Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers
text:
Answer: changing a London input
The task (Section 8.5): set the Tower of London’s visits_2025 to 8,000,000.
What changes. Every page that loads attractions.csv (Table 8.3) is rebuilt with the new count, and what it shows depends on its code. The guide, in every format it writes (web page, Word and PDF, and PowerPoint, slides and EPUB if made), the dashboard’s value boxes and bar chart, and the partner brief (london-email.docx) find the top attraction with idxmax() and the total with .sum(), so the Tower of London becomes the most visited attraction and the total rises. The square advert, if made, uses only idxmax(), so it names the Tower too. The white paper names no top attraction: its sums by admission change, but its table keeps ALVA’s rank_uk column from the file, so it would still rank the Tower ninth in the UK beside the most visits of the ten. A copied column goes stale too.
What does not. The flyer, which copies its facts and quotes no visit counts; the covering email (london-email-message.md), which quotes no numbers and is not rendered; the dashboard’s line chart and the 3-D map, which read visits.csv, not attractions.csv; any output not rebuilt; and the live site, until it is published again.
Why. Every render re-runs every page’s code (freeze: false), and each changed output is linked to the input by a line of code that loads it. A strong answer names that line.
Follow-up questions worth asking. Where would the change appear if the number had been typed into the prose instead of computed? (Nowhere: the typed number would silently disagree with the chart.) What would change if visits.csv were edited instead? (The dashboard’s line chart, the 3-D map and the white paper’s trend.) Why does the render re-run every cell? (Because nothing is cached; see Section 15.4.)

Answer: changing a water setting
The task (Section 15.6): set MAX_MISSING = 1 instead of 2 in scripts/analysis.py. Computed here by running the finished analysis both ways:

The prediction. Every row missing more than one of the nine features goes. Department capitals have no zone-level coverage, so their rural zones reach that rule with both coverage values missing (imputation comes after the rule): every one of their rural zone-years goes, Tunja’s eight among them, while Tunja’s urban zone, which takes the municipal total, stays.
What the rebuild shows. The stricter setting drops 652 more rows, every one of them missing both coverage values: the capitals’ 135 rural zone-years and 517 other zone-years whose coverage split is missing that year, seven of them capitals’ urban zones with no municipal total either. Nothing else goes. Tunja’s urban zone stays in cluster 1 in every year. k stays 4, so the blog post’s assert k == 4 still passes (a setting that changed k would make the post fail its render, by design), the names stay, and 98% of the remaining rows keep their cluster.
What changes. pre-render re-runs scripts/analysis.py, which rewrites every file in outputs/ (clusters.parquet, cluster_profiles.csv, k_selection.csv, stability.csv, outcomes_by_year.csv, irca_infant.csv, irca_infant_bins.csv and summary.json), and freeze: false re-executes every page, so every page that reads outputs/ changes (Table 15.1): the clusters page, the report in every format, the slides, the blog post, the dashboard and the white paper, which also quotes the setting itself.
What does not. data/, the page sources, the post’s title (k is still 4) and, until it is published again, the live site. Nor does the explore page: it re-runs, but reads only data/water_municipal.csv.
Why. Compute once, publish many: one setting in one script, read by every publication. Strong answers name the mechanism (pre-render, outputs/, freeze: false) and check at least two outputs against the new row counts. Undo with git restore scripts/analysis.py.

title: Appendix F — Reading in Another Language
text:
The book is written in English, but its tools need not be used in English.
The website edition can be translated by your browser. In Chrome, the Google Translate extension translates the page in place (checked 2026-10-30). Code stays as written: translators skip code, so commands, file names and the prompts in the agent boxes remain in English. That is deliberate. The prompts name files, columns and options that must match your project exactly, and a translated file name would no longer be found.
The agent understands many languages. You can write your own prompts in Spanish, or any other language the model knows, and keep the literal names in backticks so they are not translated. To have the agent answer in Spanish while leaving code alone, make your first prompt:



Ask your coding agent

Responde siempre en español; deja el código y los nombres de archivo en inglés.


(“Always reply in Spanish; leave code and file names in English.”)
The workshop’s slides, which this book follows, were designed for browser translation: their prompts are translated for reading, while file names, columns and options are marked to stay in English.






TipIn practice



A translated page can mistranslate technical words. In testing, Google Translate rendered the column name mdm as “señora” and “Render” as “Prestar”. When a translated sentence seems odd, check the original, and always copy literal names from the code, never from translated prose.

title: Appendix H — How This Book Is Built
text:
One source, two editions
This book is a Quarto book project in the book/ folder of the workshop repository, built into two editions from one set of chapter files: an EPUB e-book and a website. It is a worked example of the book’s own subject, and its problems are worth recording, because most of them were invisible until the EPUB was checked on a phone screen or by a validator.
The chapters are .qmd files. Their Python cells compute every number from the repository’s data, by reading the London files and by importing the water project’s analysis.py, so the book quotes exactly what the projects compute. Results are cached with freeze: auto, so the EPUB rebuilds quickly and the same way each time; the rule for clearing the cache, written in the configuration and the README, is to run make book-fresh after any change to the examples’ data or analysis.
Content meant for one edition is marked for it. Live 3-D scenes and data explorers are wrapped in ::: {.content-visible when-format="html:js"}, and their EPUB stand-ins, animations with a link (and, for the London map, a QR code), in when-format="epub". The HTML edition runs the workshop’s own three.js bundle, unchanged, through a small script that imitates the slide framework the bundle expects.
crumbs: H  How This Book Is Built

title: Appendix H — How This Book Is Built
text:
What the EPUB needed



Table H.1: Problems met building the EPUB edition, and their fixes.









Problem
Fix




Quarto 1.10.20 drops a book’s parts, and the part pages’ content, from the EPUB
Part pages are ordinary chapters in the EPUB; a post-render script nests each part’s chapters under it in the table of contents


A profile’s chapter list is added to the base list, not substituted for it
One master list (_chapters.yml) generates a chapter list for each edition


when-format="html" also matches EPUB
HTML-only content uses when-format="html:js"


Rendering one edition empties the other’s output folder
Each edition has its own output folder


Quarto’s figure wrapper carries an alt attribute that EPUB’s XHTML forbids
The post-render script removes it (the image keeps its alt text)


No landmarks for the copyright page or the start of the text
Added by the post-render script, which also puts the copyright page before the preface


Callout titles and code have fixed light backgrounds and dark text, invisible in a reader’s night theme
The stylesheet lets the reader’s colours through


Code lines do not wrap on a phone, and cell outputs scroll sideways
The stylesheet makes long lines wrap and outputs fit


Wide diagrams are unreadable on a phone
Diagrams are drawn portrait, 700 pixels wide with text of at least 19 pixels, and supplied as PNG at double resolution






The finished EPUB passes EPUBCheck 5.4.0, the W3C’s validator, with no errors and no warnings.

title: Appendix H — How This Book Is Built

Media
All media are rebuilt by one script, media/build.py, run by make media:

Diagrams are SVG files with a shared style, rasterised to PNG by Chrome. The website uses the SVG, the EPUB the PNG, chosen by Quarto’s default-image-extension for each edition.
3-D animations are recorded from the website edition’s live scenes: a script opens the page in Chrome, runs the scene’s views and drags, captures frames and assembles a GIF with ffmpeg’s palette filters.
Terminal animations are recorded with VHS from scripted tapes that run real commands under a demo account, so no personal path appears; the agent session is a scripted illustration, because the repository’s rules rule out paid agent sessions for teaching material.
Every GIF opens on its final frame, held for two seconds, because e-readers that do not animate show a GIF’s first frame. Each also has a still PNG, which the website shows to readers who ask their system for reduced motion. GIFs are kept under 2 MB.

title: Appendix I — Running This as a Workshop
text:
The day
The book follows a six-hour, hands-on workshop, and can be taught that way: 300 minutes of teaching in four sessions, of 65, 65, 85 and 85 minutes, with two 15-minute breaks and a 30-minute meal. The workshop’s slides are the course resource on the day; this book is the reading behind them. Participants do the setup in Chapter 3, and the reading on agents, costs, AI policy and Markdown, at home before the day.
Chapter 4, the first report by hand, is book-only: the slides do not include it, and nothing on the day depends on it. It fits the pre-work, after the test run, because it needs only the tools and the workshop’s files that setup installs, and its starter (starters/first-report/) comes with those files. Offer it as optional pre-work, about 45 minutes: participants who do it arrive having rendered a report, checked it against its data and undone a change with Git themselves.
Table I.1 and Table I.2 map the day to the book: each block’s start and length in minutes, the checkpoint that ends it where there is one, and the chapters it covers.
Exercise times are planning estimates that never fill a block: the rest is for concept slides, showing results and recovering from a failed command. If the venue fixes the meal time, move the start, not the meal: the meal belongs between the two parts, so that everyone starts Part III together.

title: Appendix I — Running This as a Workshop
text:
Before the day

Collect test-run confirmations. Ask every participant to confirm the setup check and the test run (Section 3.7), and contact anyone who has not.
Windows. Ask for wsl -l -v output showing VERSION 2 before the day. Participants without an administrator account, or with virtualisation off in the BIOS, cannot install WSL: pair them with a neighbour. The Windows procedure has been checked against Microsoft’s documentation and on a Mac; run it once on a clean Windows machine before teaching.
The network. Check that the venue’s Wi-Fi allows GitHub, uv’s package downloads and GitHub Pages, and copes with everyone downloading at once.
crumbs: I  Running This as a Workshop

title: Appendix I — Running This as a Workshop
text:
The two-minute rule
The rule that keeps the room together: anyone stuck for two minutes on a command, an agent error or a typo does not debug in front of the room. They paste the exercise’s catch-up line (Figure 2), and everyone is hands-on together again at the next block. Demonstrate the catch-up once, live, early in the first block, so that nobody treats it as failing. In the 0:15 block, a helper sits with anyone whose setup check or test run failed while the presenter carries on.
From the Cluster block on, keep the room on the normal route, which copies each block’s finished analysis.py. The challenge route, writing the analysis, is for people well ahead of the room; agenda times assume the normal route.
crumbs: I  Running This as a Workshop

title: Appendix I — Running This as a Workshop
text:
Publishing
The first publish of each site takes about two minutes from creating the gh-pages branch to pushing the site, and GitHub Pages then builds it in 20 to 35 seconds (dry run, 2026-11-01). Use the wait: show one of the finished example sites, or explain how the gh-pages branch works. The three commonest problems are the first publish (it must be interactive), a push failing with HTTP 400 (raise http.postBuffer), and a render colliding with a running preview (stop the preview first); Appendix D has the fixes.
crumbs: I  Running This as a Workshop

cd ../water
uv run python scripts/analysis.py
uv run quarto render
test -f _site/index.html && test -f _site/dashboard.html && test -f _site/whitepaper.pdf && echo "Part III OK"

title: Appendix J — Glossary
text:
The terms in this book that a newcomer may not know, each with a short definition and the section that explains it in context, where it comes with its reasons and an example. Code and file names are listed by their letters, without punctuation.


A


absolute path

A path that starts at the top folder, /, so it names the same place from any folder: /home/ana/first-report. See Paths.

adjusted Rand index (ARI)

A score of how far two groupings agree beyond chance: 1 means identical, 0 no better than chance. See Section 12.2.

AGENTS.md

A plain Markdown file of rules at the top of a project, which the agent reads at the start of every session. See Section 2.5.

alt text

The description that screen readers announce, and that appears if an image cannot load. See Section 5.7.

ALVA

The Association of Leading Visitor Attractions, the source of the London visitor counts; it counts only its member sites. See Section 1.1.

API

The vendor’s programming interface; API prices are what a program pays per token when it calls a model directly. See Section 2.2.



B


blank line

A line with nothing on it. In Markdown it starts a new paragraph, and a list needs one above it. See Section 5.1.

block quote

A quotation set off from the text beside a bar, typed with > at the start of each line. See Section 5.1.

bootstrap

Refitting on rows drawn again at random, to test whether a result survives other data. See Section 12.2.

box plot

A box holding the middle half of a group’s values, with lines at the median and the mean, and whiskers spanning the middle 90%. See Section 13.5.

branch

A movable label on a line of commits. See Section 8.1.



C


catch-up box

The one line to paste into your agent where the book reaches a checkpoint; after catching up, you carry on reading from the box. See Section 5.11 and Figure 2.

cell options

Instructions for a code cell in its first lines, written as comments that start with #|. See Section 6.1 and Section 6.4.

checkpoint

A folder in the workshop’s checkpoints/ holding a project as it should be at the end of a hands-on block, with a README of catch-up steps. See Section 5.11 and Figure 2.

choropleth

A map whose areas are coloured by a value. See Section 15.7.

CI job

A build that a host such as GitLab runs on each push. See Section 8.2.

cited copy

Facts typed into a source from a cited file; they do not follow the file when it changes. See Section 5.8.

clone

To copy a repository, with its history, to your computer. See Section 3.6.

cluster

A group of zone-years that are similar to each other on the chosen variables, found by k-means. See Section 9.1.

code cell

A fenced block of code whose language is in braces, such as {python}; it runs when the document renders. See Section 1.2 and Section 6.1.

code fence

Three backticks that open and close a block of code; the word after them names the language, and the text inside is shown exactly as typed. See Section 5.9.

coding agent

A program that writes files and runs commands at your request, acting in your project folder in a loop until the step is done, where a web chat hands you text to copy. See Figure 1 and Section 2.1.

command-line program

A program you run by typing a command in a terminal. See Section 1.2.

commit

A recorded state of the project’s files, with a message saying why it changed. See Section 4.4 and Section 8.1.

CommonMark

A precise specification of Markdown, which GFM extends. See Section 5.1.

confounder

A third variable that affects both the exposure and the outcome, so the two move together even if one has no effect on the other. See Section 14.2.

context

Everything sent to the model with a request: the conversation so far, the files read and the project’s rules. See Section 2.3.

control

Comparing like with like, so a third variable cannot explain a difference; the clusters offer a partial control. See Section 14.1.

correlation coefficient (r)

A measure from −1 to 1 of how two variables move together; 1 would mean they rise together along a straight line. See Section 11.3.

CSV

A table in plain text, one line per row, with commas between the columns. See Section 5.8.



D


dashboard

A page of charts and key numbers arranged in a grid. See Section 7.1.

diff

The lines a change added and removed. See Section 2.6 and Section 4.5.

difference-in-differences

Comparing places before and after a change with comparable places that did not change. See Section 14.2.

display-only fence

A code fence whose language is not in braces, such as python: the code is shown and never run. See Section 6.1.

div

A block of Markdown between two lines of three colons, whose class in braces tells Quarto what to make of it. See Section 7.1.

DIVIPOLA

DANE’s list of Colombia’s municipalities, which gives each a five-digit code: two digits for the department and three for the municipality. See Section 9.4.

DOI

A document’s permanent identifier; https://doi.org/ followed by it opens the publisher’s page. See Section 15.7.



E


ecological fallacy

Drawing conclusions about people from data about places. See Section 14.2.

effort

How long a model reasons before answering. See Chapter 2.

elbow

The k after which inertia stops falling much. See Section 12.2.

environment

A folder holding one version of Python and the packages one project uses, kept apart from every other project’s. See Section 5.10.

EPUB

An e-book format: a zipped set of web pages whose text reflows to fit the reader’s screen. See Section 6.6 and Section 15.3.

escape

A backslash before a Markdown mark, such as \*, which keeps the mark as typed. See Section 5.1.

Euclidean distance

Straight-line distance: the square root of the sum of squared differences across the features. See Section 11.3.

execute-dir

A project setting that makes every page read files from the project folder. See Section 15.4.



F


feature

A variable the clustering sees, and so one that defines the kinds. See Section 9.5.

flag column

A column that marks every value that was filled. See Section 11.1.

freeze

Quarto’s cache of computed results; with freeze: auto a page re-runs only when its own source changes, not when the data it reads change. See Section 1.4 and Section 15.4.

front matter

A block of settings in YAML between two lines of three dashes at the very top of a file. See Section 6.1 and Section 6.2.



G


gh

The GitHub command-line tool. See Section 3.5.

Git

The version-control tool: something like Track Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history. See Section 1.4 and Section 8.1.

git add

Chooses what goes into the next commit; git add . takes every file in the folder that .gitignore does not leave out. See Section 4.4.

git diff

Shows the lines changed since the last commit: a line starting - was removed, one starting + added. See Section 4.5.

git log

Lists the commits, newest first; git log --oneline gives one line to each. See Section 4.4.

git restore

Puts a file back as it was at the last commit. See Section 4.5 and Section 8.5.

git status

Says which files have changed since the last commit, and which ones Git does not track. See Section 4.4.

GitHub

The website that keeps a copy of a repository online. See Section 8.1.

GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM)

The dialect of Markdown GitHub uses for README files and issues: CommonMark with tables, task lists, strikethrough and automatic links. See Section 5.1.

.gitignore

The list of files and folders Git should not track. See Section 4.4 and Section 8.3.

guard

A line that stops the render when a sentence’s words, not only its numbers, no longer match the data. See Section 15.4.



H


harness

The program on your computer that gives a model its tools, carries out its requests and asks you first. See Section 2.1.

home folder

Your own folder, written ~. See Section 3.3.

horizontal rule

A line across the page, typed as --- between blank lines. See Section 5.1.

hyperparameter

A setting an algorithm cannot learn from its own objective, such as k. See Section 12.2.



I


impute

To fill a missing value with an estimate. See Section 11.1.

index.qmd

The source of a website’s home page. See Section 8.3.

inertia

The sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster’s centre. See Section 12.1.

infant mortality

Deaths under one year of age per 1,000 live births. See Section 9.5.

inline code

Code in a sentence, such as {python} name, whose value Quarto writes into the sentence when the document renders. See Section 1.2 and Section 6.1.

IPM

The multidimensional poverty index: the share of a zone’s people who are poor in several respects at once, from the 2018 census. See Section 9.5.

IRCA

Colombia’s risk index for drinking water, from 0, every test passed, to 100, every test failed. See Section 9.2.

IRCA risk bands

Resolución 2115’s five ranges of the IRCA: no risk, low, medium, high and unfit. See Section 9.2.



J


join

Matching the rows of two tables by a column they share. See Section 9.4.

Jupyter

The computation engine that runs Python code cells (knitr does the same for R). See Section 1.2.



K


k

How many clusters k-means is asked to find. See Section 12.1.

kernel

The running Python process that executes a document’s cells, top to bottom. See Section 6.7.

k-means++

scikit-learn’s way of choosing starting centres that are spread out, which makes a stuck start less likely. See Section 12.1.



L


lead

The agent session that starts sub-agents, waits for them and checks their results. See Section 7.2.

line break

A new line inside a paragraph, made by ending the line with a backslash. See Section 5.1.

listing

A page that lists other pages, such as every post of a blog, made by Quarto. See Section 15.4.

loadings

The weights of a principal component, which say what it measures. See Section 12.3.

lockfile

A file such as uv.lock that records the exact version of every package, for every system. See Section 5.10.

logarithm

A scale that measures ratios rather than differences: every doubling adds the same amount. See Section 11.1.

low-coverage

In a cluster’s name, half a standard deviation or more below the year’s average coverage: a relative position, not an absence of service. See Section 13.2.



M


Markdown

A way of writing structured text with a few punctuation marks, such as # before a heading. See Section 1.2 and Section 5.1.

MDM

DNP’s score of a municipality’s management and results, from 0 to 100. See Section 9.5.

median

The middle value, with half the values below it. See Section 10.1.

missing not at random

Gaps that depend on the unmeasured value itself, which no fill can repair. See Section 10.2.

model

A large language model: it reads and writes text and can reply with a request to use a tool. See Section 2.1.

monotonic

A relation in which one variable tends to rise as the other rises, though not necessarily along a straight line. See Section 14.1.

municipality-year

One municipality in one year: the unit of the municipal outcomes, infant mortality and dropout. See Section 13.4.



N


naming rule

A written rule that names each cluster from its profile: setting, relative coverage and the band of its median IRCA. See Section 13.2.

nano

The terminal’s own simple text editor: Ctrl+O and Enter save, Ctrl+X leaves. See Section 4.5 and Section 5.5.

nominal pesos

Pesos not adjusted for inflation. See Section 11.1.



O


outcome

A variable the analysis only compares between the kinds and never clusters on. See Section 9.5.



P


package

An add-on library that Python code imports, such as pandas for tables or matplotlib for charts. See Section 5.10.

Pandoc

The document converter inside Quarto that turns the executed Markdown into each output format. See Section 1.2.

Pandoc’s Markdown

The Markdown Quarto reads: GFM’s core marks, plus attributes in braces, footnotes, definition lists, citations and mathematics. See Section 5.1.

Parquet

A file format for tables that keeps each column’s type, so a code such as 05001 stays text. See Section 9.6.

path

The name of a file or folder through the folders that lead to it, separated by /: data/visits.csv. See Paths and Section 4.1.

PATH

The list of folders a terminal searches for programs, read when the terminal starts. See Section 3.4.

percentile

The value below which a given share of the values lies; the 5th and 95th bound the middle 90%. See Section 13.5.

platform tag

The part of a package file’s name that says which system and processor it was built for. See Section 5.10.

pre-render

A script Quarto runs before every render of a project, even of a single page. See Section 15.4.

principal component

A direction in which the data vary: a weighted sum of the features. See Section 12.3.

principal component analysis (PCA)

A method that finds the directions in which the data vary most and projects the rows onto them. See Section 12.3.

profile

A cluster’s mean of each feature over its rows, in z units. See Section 13.1.

prompt

The request you type into the agent. See Section 2.6.

Prompt, Check, Publish

The loop this book teaches: prompt an agent for one small step, check what it did, and let Quarto rebuild every output from the checked source. See Figure 1.

prompt (terminal)

The line ending in $ (or % on a Mac) that shows the terminal is ready, and who and where you are. See Section 3.3.

pull request

A proposal to merge a branch, which shows the difference line by line. See Section 8.1.

push

Copying commits to the shared repository on GitHub. See Section 8.1.



Q


quarto preview

Renders a file, serves it on a local address and renders it again every time the file is saved; Ctrl+C stops it. See Section 5.1 and Section 5.4.

Quarto project

A folder that a _quarto.yml file at its top turns into one website or book. See Section 8.3.



R


random seed

The number that starts the computer’s random-number generator, so random starts are the same on every run. See Section 1.4 and Section 12.1.

raw block

A block that Quarto passes untouched to one format, such as a raw Typst block. See Section 7.4.

relative path

A path that starts from the folder you are in, such as data/visits.csv or ..; it means something else from another folder. See Paths.

render

To build a document’s outputs from its source; quarto render executes, converts and typesets. See Section 1.2 and Section 5.1.

repository

A project folder with its Git history. See Section 1.4 and Section 4.4.

reproducible

Someone else, or you later, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command, and see where every number came from. See Section 1.4.

root folder

The folder you start an agent in, where it reads, edits and runs commands. See Section 2.4.

rural zone

A municipality’s smaller settlements and dispersed countryside. See Section 9.4.



S


Saber 11

ICFES’s national exam for students finishing upper secondary school, with a global score from 0 to 500. See Section 9.3.

selection on the outcome

Keeping or dropping rows by the value being measured, so the rows kept are not typical. See Section 13.4.

self-supplied system

A water system that no utility runs. See Section 9.2.

SGP

Colombia’s system of national transfers to municipalities; the feature is its allocation for drinking water and sanitation, per person. See Section 9.5.

ShareAlike

The condition of a CC BY-SA licence that anything built from the data is shared under the same licence. See Section 15.5.

shell

The program behind the terminal that runs your commands. See Section 3.4.1.

silhouette

A score from −1 to 1 of how much closer each point is to its own cluster than to the next one, averaged over the points. See Section 12.2.

SIVIGILA

Colombia’s public-health surveillance system. See Section 15.8.

skewed

Mostly moderate values with a few very large ones. See Section 11.1.

slash command

A command such as /model, /clear or /exit, typed into the agent itself. See Section 2.3.

small numbers

In small places a handful of deaths moves a rate a long way, so extreme rates are fragile. See Section 13.4.

Spearman’s ρ

A measure, from −1 through 0 to +1, of whether two variables rise and fall together in rank order. See Section 14.1.

stack trace

The list of what was running inside a program when it stopped, printed after some errors; it is for the program’s developers, and the error’s first line is what to read. See Section 4.6.

standard deviation

Roughly, the typical distance of a value from the mean, in the variable’s own unit. See Section 11.1.

static site

A folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and documents, with no program running on a server. See Section 8.2.

strikethrough

Text crossed out, written between two tildes on each side, ~~Car~~. See Section 5.1.

sub-agent

A separate agent session that your agent starts for one task, with its own context. See Section 7.2.

sudo

Runs a command as the administrator, after asking for your password. See Section 3.2.

SVG

A drawing written as text, which a model writes as it writes code. See Chapter 2.



T


Tab completion

Pressing Tab in the terminal to finish a file or folder name; twice lists the names that fit. See Section 4.1.

task list

A bulleted list whose items start with a box, [ ] empty or [x] ticked. See Section 5.1.

terminal

A window where you type commands instead of clicking. See Section 3.3.

three checks

What every change passes: before it is committed, scope (which files changed) and correctness (one number against its source row); after, rebuild (what was committed renders on its own, from a fresh clone). See Section 4.7.1.

token

A fragment of text a few characters long: the unit models read, write and are priced by. See Section 2.2.

Typst

A modern typesetting system that ships inside Quarto and makes its PDFs. See Section 1.2.



U


untracked

A file Git can see in the folder but does not yet record. See Section 4.4.

urban zone

A municipality’s head town (cabecera municipal). See Section 9.4.

utility-supplied IRCA

The IRCA of samples from systems a water utility runs (“prestadores”), which understates risk where people supply themselves. See Section 9.2.

uv

The tool that installs Python and manages each project’s packages. See Section 3.5 and Section 5.10.

uv run

Runs one command in the project’s environment, first bringing .venv up to date with uv.lock. See Section 5.10.



V


value box

A dashboard box that shows one key number with a label. See Section 7.1.

variance

The square of the standard deviation. See Section 11.3.



W


WebGL

The browser’s built-in 3-D graphics. See Section 7.5.

working tree

The project’s files as they are now; “clean” means they match the last commit. See Section 4.4.

WSL

The Windows Subsystem for Linux, which runs Ubuntu inside Windows. See Chapter 3.



Y


YAML

A format for settings in which indentation is meaning. See Section 1.2 and Section 6.1.



Z


zone variable

A variable measured separately for a municipality’s urban and rural zones; a municipal variable has one value for the whole municipality, repeated on both rows. See Section 9.5.

zone-year

One municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year: one row of the water data, and Part III’s unit of analysis. See Section 9.4.

z-score

A value’s distance from its year’s mean, in standard deviations; it has no unit. See Section 11.1.

title: Appendix K — Facts That Change
text:
Agents, chats and models
Prices, plans, accounts and free allowances change from month to month, so this book keeps them in one place: a file in its source, book/facts.yml, which this appendix prints in full. The chapters quote it rather than typing a price or a plan, so when a fact changes, one edit and a rebuild update every page that mentions it, and this list. Each fact carries the date it was checked against the official page linked beside it. By the time you read this, some will have changed: follow the link, and trust the page over the book.

Haiku’s price is for prompts up to 100,000 tokens; longer ones cost five times as much. Subscriptions count usage differently from API prices, and which models you can choose depends on your plan and the agent’s version. Sources: Anthropic’s pricing and models pages and OpenAI’s models pages.
These are API prices: what a program pays per token when it calls the model directly (Section 2.2). Read them as a snapshot of the spread between small and large models, not as numbers to plan with.
